News.title: Cairngorms wildfire declared major incident as horror blaze tears towards homes
News.content:
Cairngorms wildfire declared major incident as horror blaze tears towards homes

Police Scotland has declared a major incident as fire crews continue to battle a wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park

View Image Police Scotland have declared a major incident over the wildfire (Image: Highland, Islands, Moray and Aberdeenshire Weather/Facebook)

Police Scotland has declared a major incident as firefighters battle a wildfire in the Cairngorms National Park.

‌



The force said the decision followed a "significant change" in weather conditions, with strengthening winds making the fire more unpredictable and causing it to spread towards Nethy Bridge.

‌



All residents of Nethy Bridge are being evacuated as a precaution and directed to a respite centre at the Macdonald Aviemore Resort. Access roads into the village have been closed.

‌



The Scottish Fire and Rescue Service (SFRS) has deployed more than 500 firefighters over the course of the incident, which was first reported on July 15. Firefighters have been supported by specialist wildfire appliances, all-terrain vehicles, helicopter water-bombing operations and partner agencies.

Superintendent Judy Hill said: "The weather conditions experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation. With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution."

She said additional police officers are being deployed to help people leave their homes and maintain cordons around restricted areas.

‌



"We understand this is a very concerning time for residents, businesses and visitors to the Cairngorms region," Supt Hill said. "Please be assured that the multi-agency response remains fully committed to bringing this incident to a safe conclusion as quickly as possible."

Deputy Assistant Chief Officer Kenny Barbour, of the SFRS, said firefighters, specialist resources and partners have "worked tirelessly" over the past nine days to respond to this "challenging and complex wildfire".

He said: "The combination of prolonged dry conditions, strengthening winds and challenging terrain has created an extremely complex operational environment. Large areas of the fire ground are inaccessible by vehicle or on foot, making helicopter water-bombing operations and specialist wildfire tactics essential to our response.

‌



"Throughout this incident, partnership working has been fundamental. I would like to thank Forestry and Land Scotland, the Cairngorms National Park Authority, landowners, estate gamekeepers and our emergency service partners, whose expertise, local knowledge and continued support have been invaluable in helping us protect communities and the natural environment."

Mr Barbour urged people to continue following the advice of Police Scotland and to stay away from the affected areas while firefighters tackle the wildfire.

News.title: Essex explosion live: Inferno after huge blast as 100 firefighters tackle flames
News.content:
More than 100 firefighters are tackling a massive fire at a farm off Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon in Essex

A massive explosion at a farm in Essex has shaken buildings up to 15 miles away, with footage showing an enormous ball of flames erupting from the scene.

Essex County Fire and Rescue Service said more than 100 firefighters are at the scene of a "large industrial unit fire" off Southend Road between East Hanningfield and Rettendon, near Chelmsford.

The blaze, which is understood to be at Highlands Farm, has been declared a major incident because of its size. East of England Ambulance Service said it is responding to a "significant incident", and police have cordoned off a huge area around the blaze.

"If you live or are travelling nearby, please continue to keep your windows and doors closed," the fire service said. "Please avoid the area while we deal with this incident."

Did you see or hear the explosion? If so, please get in touch by emailing livenews@reachplc.com

News.title: Westminster Bridge live: Multiple casualties in horror police boat crash on Thames
News.content:
Police boat was travelling at 'high speed' before 'slamming into wall'

A couple from the United States said they heard "an explosion" when a police boat travelling at "high speed" struck Westminster Bridge on the River Thames today, injuring five officers.

Jim Bagley, from Gloucester, Massachusetts, told the Press Association: "We were standing in line to get onto the city cruise hop on, hop off tours, and we saw two police boats coming up the river.

"One was an orange boat that went under the bridge and left a great big wave, and then there was a black boat that came up behind it, the police boat.

"It looks to me that he got stuck in the wake of the other boat that had just passed through the bridge and slammed into the wall on the opposite side.

"We didn’t see it happen, but we heard the explosion… the next thing we saw was three people in the water, coming down the river."

He added: "We were wondering why they were under way at high speed to begin with."

Katherine Bagley said: "They were both in pursuit of something farther down the river, but they never… the second boat never got to it because it crashed into the bridge with a big bang."

News.title: PlayStation Network goes down worldwide as thousands unable to connect servers
News.content:
Video game giant Sony has confirmed that all PlayStation services were 'experiencing issues' amid thousands of reports from users around the globe

Gamers around the world, including thousands in the UK, reported issues with the PlayStation Network, with many saying they were unable to connect to the server.

Problems started around 11.30am today (Friday, July 24) with video game giant Sony later confirming all PlayStation services were "experiencing issues". It added that it was working to resolve the problem as soon as possible and thanked users for their patience. The firm has not yet given a reason for the outage.

Tens of thousands of network problem reports had been logged in the UK on outage-tracking website Downdetector.

One frustrated UK user wrote on Downdetector: "Can't load any digital games at all bought or free. Can't connect to servers to verify licences, doesn't matter what I try to load - I get the same message every time."

News.title: Heatwave hell sparks summer of chaos as THOUSANDS queue for holidays and wildfires force Brits to flee hotels
News.content:
Heatwave hell sparks summer of chaos as THOUSANDS queue for holidays and wildfires force Brits to flee hotels

As 6.3 million people embark on road trips, the UKHSA has issued a yellow heat health alert with a risk to life for the elderly and vulnerable

View 5 Images Beach goers sit on the beach of Moutchic in Lacanau, southwestern France (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

More than six million people are hitting the roads as the summer holidays begin – battling 30C temperatures and nose-to-tail traffic jams.

‌



The AA predicts 6.3 million of us will make journeys between now and Thursday. Yellow heat health alerts are in place across much of the country until tomorrow morning and the UK Health Security Agency is warning of minor impacts on health and social care services and an increased risk to life for vulnerable people.

‌



The Port of Dover is braced for its busiest weekend of the summer. Holidaymakers faced gridlock as they waited for ferries today, and tomorrow is set to be the same. Ferry company DFDS said its wait times at Dover were up to 60 minutes at border controls.

‌



View 5 Images The UKHSA has issued a yellow heat health alert for much of the country (Image: Getty Images)

Are you worried about the extreme summer weather? Take our poll and have your say READ MORE :

But officials hope it will be smooth sailing compared to the May half-term getaway, when waiting times hit four-and-a-half hours due to technical issues with the new border check Entry Exit System.

The RAC’s Simon Williams warned: “Drivers should be ready for some very busy roads this weekend and expect delays. The best advice is to plan journeys and think about setting off earlier or later in the day to avoid traffic jams.”

‌



Opting to stay at home this week will also come with its challenges. Millions of Brits are now subject to hosepipe bans and a drought has been officially declared for large parts of north and mid-Wales.

The rest of Wales, along with much of central, southern and eastern England, is in the “prolonged dry weather” ­category – one stage below a drought. But parts of Britain might be in for some light relief from Sunday, as high pressure retreats and brings outbreaks of rain.

View 5 Images Many areas are on the brink of drought (Image: Ben Whitley/PA Wirere)

‌



Showers could be heavy in the north and the west of the UK, with 20mm possible in parts of north west Scotland. The rain will be much patchier further south and east, with large swathes of England and Wales forecast to get just a few millimetres at most. And it’s likely some locations in the south of England will not see a drop.

The Met Office’s Dan Suri said: “After a prolonged spell of hot, dry and settled weather, some will see a temporary change this weekend as weather fronts move south east across the UK. While some areas, particularly in the north and west, will see rain and showers, many places are likely to receive ­relatively little rainfall.

“For much of southern England, dry conditions are expected to remain the ­dominant feature, with ­temperatures recovering quickly next week and the potential for very warm or locally hot weather to return.”

‌



View 5 Images Ferry passengers face queues at Dover (Image: Gareth Fuller/PA Wire)

Meanwhile, British holidaymakers were among thousands evacuated from the Cap Ferret peninsula as wildfires raged across south-west France. Tens of thousands are being forced to leave the upmarket resort, including hundreds escaping by boat.

Headmaster David Morton, 53, from Gloucester, was holidaying in the coastal village of Petit Piquey with his wife and sons when they received an emergency text message at 3am.

‌



He said: “We got in our car, packed everything up as quickly as we could... and then set off and joined a very long, slow-moving queue of traffic. We could see several fires in the distance. The whole forest was on fire.”

View 5 Images A forest burns close to a residential area during a wildfire near Lege-Cap-Ferret, southwestern France (Image: AFP via Getty Images)

The fire has so far consumed around 10,000 hectares – nearly the size of the city of Manchester – with water-bombing planes deployed in a bid to keep the flames under control. French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez said 40,000 people either had been or were preparing to evacuate from the Cap Ferret peninsula.

Article continues below

Firefighters also battled blazes in Le Porge and Lacanau in the Gironde department of south-west France, while smoke from the fires dominated the skyline in nearby Biscarrosse.

Elsewhere in Europe, Spain has declared a national emergency after 20,000 people were forced to flee due to fires near Madrid, while the Italian island of Sicily has also been hit.

News.title: Donald Trump berates them and calls them 'Piggy', yet the press are still buying him dinner
News.content:
Donald Trump berates them and calls them 'Piggy', yet the press are still buying him dinner

The rescheduled White House Correspondents Dinner takes place tonight in Washington DC - and the entertainment will be a magician, because that's who you book to perform at a party for a toddler

View Image Trump will be guest of honour at a party to celebrate people he brands corrupt and dishonest on a daily basis (Image: Getty Images)

Tonight, the leading lights of American journalism will put on tuxedoes and frocks and share expensive steak and fine wine with the guy who wants to destroy them.

‌



And you've got to wonder why.

‌



The rescheduled White House Correspondents Dinner takes place this evening in Washington DC. The previous edition, you'll remember, was abandoned after someone ran in with a homemade shotgun and tried to assassinate Trump and his cabinet.

‌



The event is supposedly a celebration of the first amendment, which protects freedom of the press and free speech. But in order for the President to agree to attend, the event was radically changed. Out was the comedian host who would gently roast the President and his cabinet - and in his place? A magician.

Because who else would you book as the entertainment for a party where the guest of honour is an overgrown toddler? I suppose we should think ourselves lucky it's taking place in a swanky hotel and not at a soft play centre.

The do-over will take place at the Waldorf Astoria - formerly the Trump Hotel in DC - and comes at a time when Trump's attacks on the media have reached unprecedented levels, even by his standards.

‌



The Justice Department is currently in court demanding phone records from New York Times journalists, their spouses and in one case, their MOTHER, to try and smoke out who leaked sensitive information to the paper about a story.

Donald Trump spirals into on-air meltdown over Iran war plan

And which story prompted the administration to take such unheard of, antidemocratic, frankly un-American action?

‌



The stupid story about Trump's Qatari jet not having the security features it needed to fly the President around safely. A story that was so obvious to most people that it barely needed telling.

(It's also quite funny that it's this story they chose to send subpoenas over, and not the leak to the same newspaper's reporters of recordings of meetings held in the Situation Room. Presumably because they already know who leaked those.)

The move will almost certainly be blocked by judges - but that's not the point. As with most of Trump's legal fights with the media - from the AP to CBS News to the Wall Street Journal to the BBC - the process is the punishment. It's not about winning in court, it's about intimidating journalists and - more importantly - their sources.

‌



Of course, this is just Trump's latest attack on the press. He frequently swerves questions he doesn't like by attacking the journalist, or their employer, as dishonest or corrupt, accusing them of lying, calling them "piggy". It's particularly dicey being a woman in the White House Press Corps, unless you're one of the paid propagandists from organisations like Lindell TV, who Trump has invited into the press room to dilute the proper questions he and his team are subjected to.

And it doesn't end with Trump. His public description of anyone trying to hold him to account as "fake news" was understandably attractive to politicians around the world that it rapidly became the done thing to attack the media. Nigel Farage does it, Jeremy Corbyn did it. I spent a lot of time at CPAC GB last week, and was personally described from the stage as the "enemy" for accurately writing and reporting what was going on there.

‌



So I return to my earlier question. If you're a journalist in Washington, why would you ever accept an invitation to a dinner where the guest of honour is Donald Trump?

The New York Times have the right idea. They have a longstanding policy of not attending as guests, but instead turning up to cover it as an event.

Of course, if nobody turned up to the dinner last year, nobody would have been there to report on the shots fired and the scramble to safety. But there's no reason a night of reporting on Trump has to come with a plate of chateaubriand. In a normal world the reaction to Trump's behaviour would be empty tables and dozens of reporters standing around the walls.

‌



Even better, the White House Correspondents Association could just...disinvite Trump. It's happened without the President before. There is absolutely no requirement for an organisation to invite a guy who calls its members "piggy" and undermines them whenever possible over for dinner. It's like the National Association of Electric Cars inviting Jeremy Clarkson to speak at their annual conference.

Other groups have managed not to invite him to things, most notably the Nobel Committee. The worst that could happen if he wasn't invited is that he'd get a bit upset and Gianni Infantino would have to invent a "FIFA CHAMPION OF THE NEWS" medal to give him.

They could just...not invite him.

Article continues below

But they won't.

News.title: Toddler dies after being 'left inside baking nursery minibus for seven hours'
News.content:
Toddler dies after being 'left inside baking nursery minibus for seven hours'

Police have launched an investigation after an 18-month-old girl was allegedly left inside a nursery transport vehicle for several hours before she was discovered and pronounced dead at the scene

View 3 Images The 18-month-old was pronounced dead despite prolonged efforts to save her (stock image) (Image: Getty Images)

An 18-month-old girl died after she was allegedly left inside a nursery transport vehicle for several hours.

‌



The toddler, known only as Sofia, was reportedly collected at about 8am and is said to have remained inside the vehicle after being picked up for nursery in Portugal. Nursery staff were unaware the child was missing, until her mother arrived to collect her later that afternoon and was told she had never attended nursery.

‌



Sofia’s grandmother said the toddler was normally dropped off at the same time each day and that her arrival should have been recorded. She said: “She’s dropped off every year, every day, at the same time. And whenever she isn’t dropped off, there’s a record of it. And there’s a record of the time she arrived, and it wasn’t possible to provide a record.”

‌



The child attended a nursery in the Pragal area, but the vehicle had reportedly been parked outside another site run by the same institution on Avenida do Cristo Rei.

View 3 Images Local reports said the vehicle was the personal car of an employee at the institution (Image: Getty Images)

Family of tragic two-year-old launch memorial appeal for bench inspired by favourite TV character READ MORE :

Police missed chances to stop attacker who went on deadly synagogue rampage READ MORE :

Her grandmother said Sofia’s mother arrived to collect her only to find that staff did not know where she was. She said: “My daughter had come to pick up her daughter and nobody knew where she was. It was only then that they told us. They said no.

‌



“They came running over here to find out what was happening and had to break down the door to get in and rescue my granddaughter. I don’t know how many children are in the care of this institution."

Firefighters, an INEM emergency medical team and PSP officers were dispatched to the scene. By the time emergency crews arrived, a window of the vehicle had reportedly already been smashed in an attempt to reach the little girl. Paramedics immediately began advanced life support and cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but Sofia was pronounced dead at the scene despite prolonged attempts to save her.

Police said the case was being treated as a suspecious incident in which a child was inadvertently left inside a school transport vehicle. Portugal’s Judicial Police launched an investigation into the circumstances surrounding Sofia’s death. Local reports said the vehicle was the personal car of an employee at the institution, although a school transport sticker was displayed on its windscreen.

‌



View 3 Images The president of the Commission for the Protection of Crime Victims said the fatal ordeal was due to negligent (Image: Getty Images)

The president of the Commission for the Protection of Crime Victims said the circumstances appeared to point towards alleged negligence rather than an intentional act.

He said: “It doesn’t seem to me that this is a case of someone setting out to take her life. In other words, this is a type of case, as happens in accidents caused by swerving, where there is no intent, but the fact remains that a death has occurred. And so, if a death occurs, and if someone kills someone...

‌



“Here, the girl was not killed by someone’s direct action; the baby was not killed by a direct act, but because of an oversight. And so, leaving her in a van for seven hours; that’s negligent.”

He said the van was parked at a different nursery to the one Sofia attended. He added: “What is certain is that they didn’t check whether all those children were inside the school, and apparently she wasn’t; she was in a minibus that was actually parked outside - not at the nursery for children of her age, but at another one.”

He said: “I’d say that everything that could have gone wrong did go wrong - there was no proper procedure in place. Now, there is clearly a case of negligence here, and that’s where the difference lies, in my view, and that’s where the investigation will focus.”

Article continues below

He added: “I think everyone has already been severely punished. This includes the headteacher, the staff, and above all the child’s parents and family, who, alongside the child herself, are the main victims in this case due to her death.”

News.title: Man describes trying to save mother and daughter who drowned off Essex beach
News.content:
A day-tripper has told the BBC how he dived into the sea in an attempt to save a mother and daughter who drowned off an Essex beach.

Craig Bowe, 42, battled the incoming tide at West Mersea, near Colchester, three times after hearing screams on Wednesday evening.

The kitchen fitter, who was on a day trip from Hertfordshire to celebrate his daughter's 10th birthday, managed to haul Shally and Samiha Rahman from the waves and also helped a seven-year-old boy onto a lifeboat.

Despite his efforts, the pair - aged 41 and 15 - died in the desperate attempt to bring the boy to shore.

The boy, who became stranded during a family day out from Barking, east London, was airlifted to hospital and remained there in a critical condition on Friday.

Three others were taken by ambulance to another hospital after the incident unfolded at about 17:35 BST.

Bowe, from Northaw, sprang into action after hearing a man screaming in the water and seeing bodies floating.

"When I got there, the first two people I saw were actually face down, so [it was] more serious than I initially thought," he told the BBC.

Bowe pulled Shally Rahman to shore where bystanders began administering CPR. He then dashed back out to sea to rescue her daughter.

Having done so, he then returned to the water to help load the seven-year-old boy and another child, who were about 150 yards (137m) out at sea, onto a lifeboat.

"I helped sort of shoo him onto the boat, because he was face down too... but the seven-year-old was not in a good way," said Bowe, who was helped by an unnamed man.

"The waves were hitting me in the face. The current was definitely stronger."

News.title: Law student is charged over intercepted bomb in car
News.content:
A 25-year-old law student has appeared in court charged over a bomb which was discovered in a car in the Republic of Ireland.

Isobella Perrie Sullivan, from Abbeylands Park in Clane, County Kildare, was charged with the possession of explosives.

It was alleged she was driving the car which was intercepted by gardaÃ­ (Irish police) near Carrickmacross, County Monaghan, on Wednesday.

A defence solicitor told the court his client had been asked to take a bag to Northern Ireland and had not been aware what was in it.

Earlier on Friday, gardaÃ­ (Irish police) told reporters their interception was part of an operation targeting dissident republican activity.

The accused, who was arrested on Wednesday, was brought before a special sitting of Trim District Court in County Meath on Friday evening.

A member of the Garda Special Detective Unit told the court the car she was driving was stopped by officers on N2 at Aclint, south of Carrickmacross.

News.title: Andy Burnham's first week pledges - how much do they add up to?
News.content:
Andy Burnham is ending his first week as prime minister by working out of Manchester in the new No 10 North for the first time.

He spent this week making a series of spending announcements mostly aimed at tackling the cost of living, including capping bus fares.

BBC Verify has looked at Burnham's first week of spending commitments, how much they cost and how the government says they will be paid for, which comes to about Â£1.5bn.

Here's how that breaks down and what could later be coming down the line.

News.title: Angela Rayner rules out rent controls in England
News.content:
Housing Secretary Angela Rayner has said Prime Minister Andy Burnham is not looking at bringing in rent controls in England.

She told BBC Breakfast that changes made through the Renters' Rights Act, which came into effect in May, were "already having a significant impact on the market".

She added that controls which had been implemented in some areas of the UK over the past few years had not "necessarily brought rents down".

In 2023 when he was the mayor of Greater Manchester, Burnham called for freezes to private sector rents until the cost of living crisis was over.

But Rayner told the BBC on Friday: "I don't think that rent freezes, rent controls, is a way forward at the moment.

"Three years ago, Andy called for that because there was a significant crisis in the rental market.

"We implemented between then the Renters' Rights Act which is giving renters more power and control."

Temporary rent controls were introduced in Scotland in October 2022 but expired last year.

Under new legislation, ministers in Holyrood will be able to designate certain places in Scotland as rent control areas - expected to come in by 2027.

Councils will be able to cap rent increases on some properties at a maximum of 6%.

Green Party leader Zack Polanski has said he wants to see rent controls brought in for all rented property in England.

Responding to Rayner's interview, he described Burnham as "continuity Starmer", posting on X: "The new prime minister talks a lot of about helping with the cost of living crisis. This is the one single measure that would help the most and save billions. All talk."

Jeremy Corbyn, who pledged to bring in rent controls during the 2019 general election when he was the Labour leader, described Rayner's announcement as "extremely disappointing".

"There is no hope of ending homelessness if we do not stand up to vested interests and take action against extortionate private rents.

"We need rent controls, and we need them now."

Sir Sadiq Khan, the mayor of London, has also long called on the government to implement a cap.

But Gareth Bacon, the Conservative's shadow housing minister, said rent controls would be "disastrous" and "intensify the damage done by Labour's agenda that has driven landlords from the market and reduced choice for renters".

"Labour are clearly divided. Burnham's pick for housing secretary has disowned a policy he himself has repeatedly backed," he said.

The term rent controls describes a range of measures a government can implement - from capping price increases to freezing them for a period of time.

Landlord groups say they may exacerbate the housing crisis by putting owners off renting out property.

The Renters' Rights Act was brought in to give more stability and security to the 11 million people who rent from private landlords.

Under the legislation, fixed-term tenancies have been banned and it is now significantly harder for landlords to evict tenants.

Rents can also only be increased once a year to the property's "open market rent".

News.title: Heatwave reveals lost archaeological sites across Wales
News.content:
Lost archaeological sites have emerged in grasslands across Wales after a prolonged spell of hot and dry weather.

Wales has seen about 5% of the average rainfall for July, after a series of back-to-back heatwaves and a drier than usual April to June. A drought has also been triggered in parts of Wales.

Experts said these dry conditions have brought to light a range of hidden archaeological remains, including Roman buildings and practice trenches from World War One.

Many are only visible from the air as distinctive marks in crops and grass, with some not being seen for "two or three decades", according to the Royal Commission on the Ancient and Historical Monuments of Wales (RCAHMW).

News.title: Officers hurt as police boat hits Westminster Bridge
News.content:
Five Metropolitan Police officers have been injured after a police boat struck Westminster Bridge in central London.

The Met said the incident occurred at about 15:40 BST and involved a boat from the Marine Policing Unit which was carrying armed officers.

One officer has since been discharged from hospital and the others have serious but non-life-threatening injuries.

The police confirmed that no members of the public were involved or injured in the crash.

The police boat was responding to a report of a person in the water near Battersea.

The Met said in a statement: "As a result of the collision, three officers were thrown from the boat into the water. They were recovered by those on nearby boats.

"Additional officers responded alongside the London Ambulance Service and London Fire Brigade."

The Met's Cmdr Nick John thanked river users "who came to the aid of the officers, as well as other police and emergency service colleagues who immediately made their way to the scene to assist".

He added: "The quick-thinking and professionalism of all those involved undoubtedly prevented any further injuries."

News.title: ICC top prosecutor removed over sexual misconduct allegations
News.content:
Members of the International Criminal Court (ICC) have voted to dismiss Karim Khan as chief prosecutor for alleged sexual misconduct.

Elected the ICC's third prosecutor in 2021, Khan was suspended last month. The decision to remove him was passed with 82 votes in favour.

The court's oversight body found in June he had committed a "serious breach of duty and serious misconduct" by engaging in an improper sexual relationship with a junior ICC staff member and seeking to stop her pursuing her complaint.

Khan has repeatedly denied all the allegations against him.

His lawyers have described his suspension as "unlawful, procedurally unfair and unsupported by evidence".

This process goes beyond the fate of a single prosecutor and could reshape the world's only permanent warâcrimes tribunal.

The misconduct investigation has put the institution under a glaring spotlight, intensified divisions inside it and played out alongside an unprecedented campaign to weaken, and in fact dismantle, the ICC in its entirety.

The fear among its supporters is that the court will emerge weakened and less able to face the gravest global threats.

Khan, a prominent British lawyer, has been on voluntary leave to fight the allegations since May 2025. He remains suspended from practising law in the UK, after the Bar Standards Board imposed an interim ban while it conducts its own inquiry.

He was unable to attend the vote, held in the United Nations headquarters in New York, because he is barred from entering the United States under sanctions imposed by the Trump administration over the ICC's investigation into alleged war crimes by Israeli officials in Gaza.

Regardless of his removal, the controversy is unlikely to end there.

The decision follows a highly sensitive process that has left the court under intense scrutiny.

In May 2024, allegations that Khan had engaged in sexual misconduct involving a female staff member were reported to the ICC by a third party.

The court's Independent Oversight Mechanism (IOM) opened an investigation, but the case was later closed after the alleged victim declined to participate.

Critics of the process argued that the investigation had been mishandled, undermining confidence in the IOM.

Investigators ultimately said there was insufficient evidence to substantiate the allegations.

A second referral was made in October 2024. The matter was then transferred to the United Nations Office of Internal Oversight Services (OIOS), which conducted a broader investigation into allegations of sexual misconduct and abuse of authority.

That inquiry ran from November 2024 to December 2025 and generated more than 5,000 pages of evidence and testimony.

The OIOS findings were subsequently reviewed by a panel of three judges tasked with advising whether Khan's conduct amounted to serious misconduct, less serious misconduct, or no misconduct.

The allegations have unfolded during a period of exceptional pressure on the ICC, coinciding with wider political tensions.

The United States imposed sanctions on Khan after he sought arrest warrants for Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu and former Defence Minister Yoav Gallant over alleged crimes linked to the war in Gaza.

Washington's attitude to the court in general has become increasingly hostile in recent years.

Earlier this month, the US launched a new "wholeâofâgovernment" campaign to dismantle the ICC "brick by brick" in what it calls a threat to American sovereignty, promising visa bans, asset freezes and diplomatic pressure on allies to withdraw from the court or reject its jurisdiction over their nationals.

The United States, Russia and Israel are not members of the ICC. However, the court can exercise jurisdiction over crimes committed by their nationals on the territory of ICC member states.

News.title: PlayStation Network down, leaving thousands of gamers unable to play
News.content:
Gamers have been unable to connect to the PlayStation Network, leaving some unable to play digital games for several hours.

According to Down Detector, which tracks outages, tens of thousands of people have reported problems globally, external with the service - although some reported they were able to get back online since.

The outage, which affects gamers' ability to launch games, apps or network features on their PlayStation, has prompted some to highlight their concerns around Sony's plans to no longer release new PlayStation games on discs from January 2028.

Sony's status page, external currently reads all services are "experiencing issues" and it was "working to resolve the issue as soon as possible".

The BBC has approached PlayStation for comment.

"Can't play digital games till you fix it. Yet I can put my disc in and play. The all digital future looks great," read one comment on X, external.

Sony said in a blog post earlier this month, external that new games would still be able to be bought in shops, but they would come with a digital code.

The problems began to appear around the same time as an alert from Amazon Web Services that some servers were facing issues, however this has since been resolved, external.

News.title: Police declare 'major incident' as weather change increases Cairngorms wildfire risk
News.content:
Police Scotland has declared a major incident as emergency services continue to tackle a wildfire which has been burning in the Cairngorms National Park for 10 days.

The force said it followed "a significant change in weather conditions" which has increased the risk of fire spreading towards the village of Nethy Bridge.

All Nethy Bridge residents have been evacuated to allow emergency services to continue their response.

Smoke from the wildfire can now be seen 59 miles away in Aberdeen following a change in wind direction.

Supt Judy Hill said: "The weather conditions experienced within the Cairngorms over the last 24 hours have added further complexities to this situation.

"With evidence suggesting the fire is spreading towards Nethy Bridge, the decision has been taken to declare a major incident and evacuate residents as a precaution.

"Additional police resources are being deployed to assist in contacting those who need to leave their properties and to maintain cordons around restricted areas while our fire service colleagues continue to tackle the wildfire."

News.title: Slapping therapist jailed over death 'released early'
News.content:
An alternative healer jailed over the death of a woman at one of his workshops has been released from prison just 18 months into a 10-year sentence, it is understood.

Hongchi Xiao, 63, from California, was convicted and sentenced in 2024 for the manslaughter by gross negligence of 71-year-old Danielle Carr-Gomm in 2016.

Carr-Gomm, who was diabetic, died while taking part in a therapy event in Wiltshire, which involved people being slapped or slapping themselves repeatedly.

On Friday, during a Court of Appeal hearing where an application to overturn his conviction was quashed, it emerged Xiao had been returned to the US and was believed to no longer be in custody. The BBC has approached the Ministry of Justice for comment.

In his judgment, Lord Justice Dingemans said it seemed Xiao had been returned to the US on 2 July through the Facilitated Return Scheme as a foreign national offender, as well as through the Early Release Scheme.

However, he added: "Other information suggests he was deported on 30 June 2026. It seems that Mr Xiao is not in custody in the USA."

Xiao had been extradited from Australia for the trial into Carr-Gomm's death. He had previously been prosecuted there after a six-year-old boy also died when his parents withdrew his insulin medication after attending Xiao's workshop in Sydney.

It was announced on Wednesday that new Prime Minister Andy Burnham was pausing an upcoming scheme that would have seen thousands of prisoners in England and Wales eligible to be released from prison early.

News.title: Southport killer Axel Rudakubana appears to be manipulating the system, families' lawyer says
News.content:
A lawyer for the families of the children murdered by Southport killer Axel Rudakubana has said his transfer from prison to a psychiatric hospital may be an attempt to "manipulate the system".

Rudakubana, 19, was given a life sentence for the murder of three children - Alice da Silva Aguiar, 9, Bebe King, 6, and Elsie Dot Stancombe, 7 - and attempted murder of eight other children and two adults.

On Thursday, he was moved from HMP Belmarsh to Broadmoor psychiatric hospital in Berkshire.

Prisoners who are considered to present a risk to staff, inmates or themselves because of mental disorders can be moved to hospital under the Mental Health Act.

Next Wednesday marks two years since Rudakubana carried out the attack at a Taylor Swift-themed dance class on 29 July 2024.

Lawyer Chris Walker, who represents the three bereaved families, said they "don't believe the merits" of the transfer on the basis of a mental health issue and is calling for more information from ministers.

"In my mind this is a new event, this is something which occurred whilst he was at prison, and we at this stage don't believe the merits of it in terms of him because I've seen no evidence at all until today which suggests he has a significant mental health disorder," Walker told BBC Radio 4's Today programme.

He added: "We do have an evil person but being evil does not mean that you're suffering with psychosis of some sort.

"We need to know is this a single event, is this a recurring event, is this him playing the system and we need those answers."

The Prison Officers' Association told the BBC that Rudakubana was transferred due to a deterioration in his mental health.

Walker added in a separate statement that the news would "devastate" the families at any time but "the fact that this has occurred as we approach the second anniversary in our view is another move by AR who would appear to be attempting, once again, to manipulate the system".

He continued: "We have been given the barest of details and whilst we are supporting the families through this we are urgently seeking a meeting with the appropriate authorities to understand the situation before commenting further."

A lawyer for the families of the attack's survivors said they did not want to give "notoriety" to Rudakubana and that attention should be focused on supporting the children around the anniversary.

Nicola Ryan-Donnelly of Fletchers Solicitors said: "The focus of public outrage should not be on moves that this perpetrator has made, it should be examining how we are two years on from this attack and some of these girls are still not receiving the proper psychological care and support that they should be to recover from this."

Prior to Rudakubana's sentencing last year, his defence lawyer told the court no psychiatric evidence could suggest a mental disorder contributed to his actions.

The court also heard how Rudakubana presented as having high functioning autism and did not have any associated learning disabilities.

Stan Reiz KC added that his client had appeared to have been a "normal child" until he reached 13, adding: "However, he did make a transition from a normal, well-disciplined child to someone who was capable of committing acts of such shocking and senseless violence."

Rudakubana was deemed mentally fit to be detained, interviewed and stand trial. His late guilty plea meant his mental health was not discussed in detail in court during a trial.

He was given a 52-year prison sentence in January 2025 but the judge was unable to impose a whole life order due to Rudakubana being 17 when he carried out the attack. He will likely never be released.

News.title: Mega dinghy carries record 165 migrants to UK
News.content:
A record 165 migrants reached the UK in a single boat, the Home Office has confirmed.

The number broke the previous record from July, when 128 crossed the Channel from France in one vessel.

Border Security Command was pictured towing a mega dinghy - estimated to be the same size as a standard bus at 13m (42ft) long - when it arrived in Dover on Thursday afternoon.

A Home Office spokesperson said the crossing served as a "stark reminder that criminal gangs have no regard for the safety of those they claim to help".

"The reality is clear and lives are being lost in the Channel," they added.

A total of 162 people died, external in the busy waterway between 2018 and 2025, according to the University of Oxford's Migration Observatory.

This rises to 257 when considering other migration-related deaths in the area, such as accidents involving people trying to board lorries bound for the UK, it added.

News.title: Dad who murdered four-week-old son jailed for 18 years
News.content:
A man who murdered his four-week-old son after drinking up to nine pints of beer on a night out has been jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Tony Bartlett returned to the family home in Chard, Somerset, on 16 July 2022 and shook baby Atticus in what the sentencing judge described as "a sudden fit of anger".

The 39-year-old caused serious injuries to his son's spinal cord and ribs, as well as brain damage so severe he never regained consciousness or the ability to breathe independently. Atticus died seven days later.

Bartlett, who was convicted after a trial at Bristol Crown Court earlier this month, was jailed for life with a minimum term of 18 years.

Warning: This story contains details which readers may find distressing.

The trial heard the former postman, from Axminster in Devon, had gone to a pub and comedy club with his then-partner Evelyn Ballentyne on the night Atticus was fatally injured.

It was their first evening out since their son's birth.

After they returned home, Ballentyne went upstairs and left Bartlett alone to feed Atticus.

News.title: Fifty women tell BBC they were pressured into having sex with strangers
News.content:
Warning: This story contains details of sexual acts

Fifty women have told the BBC they were pressured or coerced by their partners into having sex with strangers.

They got in contact following an investigation which told the story of a woman who said she had been pressured into having sex with more than 100 people she did not know.

Many of the women who came forward said they had sex through swinging despite not wanting to, either because they feared the consequences of refusing or felt they had to keep their partners happy.

They spoke of deep, long-lasting trauma.

"I remember many nights of my partner keeping me up all night screaming at me, threatening me, and attempting to gaslight me into believing this was something I wanted," said one woman. "It was never what I wanted."

Another told us: "I felt like I had been given away. I felt used. I felt so dirty."

Most encounters were arranged via the website FabSwingers, say the women, which claims to have more than half a million UK active monthly accounts.

Six women told BBC News they had been raped by men met through the site.

One said her partner had forced her to have sex with more than 90 men through FabSwingers. On one occasion, he held her down by the ankles, she told us.

Sixteen said intimate photos of them had been uploaded to the website without their permission.

News.title: Sarah Ferguson's charity formally closes down
News.content:
Sarah Ferguson's charity, Sarah's Trust, has formally wound up and is marked as "removed" on the public register of charities.

The charity said in February it would close "for the foreseeable future" days after new details emerged about the former Duchess of York's friendship with the late sex offender Jeffrey Epstein.

Among more than three million documents released by the US Department of Justice (DoJ) earlier this year were emails appearing to show Ferguson was in contact with Epstein while he was in prison for soliciting sex from a minor. Being named in the documents does not indicate wrongdoing.

The BBC has contacted Ferguson's representatives for comment on the closure of her charity.

Established in 2020, Sarah's Trust was "dedicated to supporting frontline, grassroots work to address the humanitarian and environmental crisis, the hunger crisis and issues perpetuating cycles of extreme poverty", according to its website.

In February, a spokesperson for the foundation said the decision to close had come after "some months" of discussion.

The foundation did not provide further details behind its decision to close at the time.

The massive drop of files by the DoJ earlier this year suggested Ferguson had been closer to Epstein than previously thought.

In the files, Ferguson was seen praising the late sex offender in 2009 as "the brother I have always wished for".

The emails also suggest she took her daughters along for lunch with him in Miami, days after his release from prison.

Ferguson's representatives have not responded to previous requests for comment on the documents.

The former duchess has already been dropped by multiple charities over her Epstein links.

In October, she lost her duchess title when her ex-husband, Andrew Mountbatten-Windsor, relinquished his Duke of York title over his links with Epstein, and she was also forced to move out of his Windsor mansion, Royal Lodge, where the couple lived together, despite having divorced in 1996.

News.title: Nine men in court over historical child sexual exploitation offences
News.content:
Nine men have appeared in court charged with a total of 41 historical sexual offences, relating to eight victims who were children at the time.

The men, aged between 54 and 76, were arrested in Newport, Swansea, London, Birmingham, Lancashire, Edinburgh and the Argyll and Bute area of Scotland earlier in July.

Gwent Police initiated Operation Oak after several women reported the abuse, which took place in south Wales between 1985 and 1996.

Appearing at Newport Magistrates' Court, the defendants were told most charges were so serious that the cases would be transferred to Crown court.

The men, who are all British citizens, were granted bail. They will appear at Cardiff Crown Court on 21 August.

Operation Oak has been described by the force as a "complex and long-running investigation into group-based child sexual exploitation in south Wales".

Many of the charges relate to the rape of children.

No pleas were entered during the short hearings at Newport Magistrates' Court on Friday.

The defendants spoke only to confirm their names, dates of birth and addresses. One appeared via video-link.

President Donald Trump on Friday said he does not believe the Russian or Chinese governments are providing military or intelligence assistance to Iran — based solely on the denials of their leaders — contradicting the assessment of his own defense secretary during a Senate hearing just days ago.

Taking questions in the Oval Office during an appearance focused on nuclear energy, Trump was asked to defend a Truth Social post in which he claimed Chinese President Xi Jinping had said “he would not, under any circumstances, give or sell Weapons to the Islamic Republic of Iran” and said Russia’s Vladimir Putin had promised, “he would not sell Weapons to Iran.”

He also wrote that in his view, both countries were “not participating” in Iran’s ongoing conflict with the U.S. while warning that “it would be very bad for them” if they did.

When a reporter noted that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth told the Senate Appropriations Committee on Tuesday that there were “ways in which both of those countries” were “enabling” Tehran “at different levels” and asked how he differentiates “enabling” from assisting, Trump dismissed the question.

“Well, I don't know that they're enabling. I mean, I will tell you that President Xi said he will not partake, and President Putin said the same thing ... I trust them,” he said.

Trump contradicts Defense Secretary's prior statement on Chinese and Russian aid to Tehran ( AFP/Getty )

“There could be some things you do, but thus far, at least, has not been major. I don't think they'd want to have me disappointed,” Trump added.

Despite his professions of trust in the Russian and Chinese leaders, both Moscow and Beijing have long provided significant logistical assistance to Tehran short of selling munitions to the Islamic Republic.

Both countries have reportedly supplied intelligence and technical assistance, including access to Russian satellite reconnaissance photographs used for targeting purpose and Chinese satellite data, plus access to Beijing’s BeiDou navigation network for the purposes of guiding missiles and drones to their targets.

Additionally, China is understood to be a major supplier of the precursor chemicals and other raw materials Tehran needs to manufacture fuel for the ballistic missiles that have wrought damage to U.S. and allied bases across the Middle East.

Beijing also supplies dual-use technological components used in the manufacture of one-way attack drones.

Additionally, China remains the major purchaser of Iranian oil exports, providing Tehran with tens of billions of dollars worth of revenue that can be directed to the Iranian military budget.

The war between the U.S. and Iran has continued to intensify since the U.S. began attacking Iranian infrastructure nearly two weeks ago.

The Pentagon is now reportedly moving weapons, medics and special forces to the Middle East to broaden options as hopes of a diplomatic resolution wane, with sources telling the Wall Street Journal that Trump is growing increasingly impatient at the pace of the war, which remains broadly unpopular with the American public.

Massive forest fires raging across southwestern France and central Spain have forced 135,000 people from their homes.

A blaze near Cap Ferret, located just 37 miles from Bordeaux on France's Atlantic coast, has consumed some 48 square miles since Wednesday and has placed the this area, known for its stunning landscapes and upmarket resorts, under severe threat.

In Spain, the government declared a national emergency for wildfires for the first time as blazes in Madrid and the nearby province of Ávila prompted the evacuation from towns west of the capital.

Dozens of firefighters have been injured, authorities said, but no deaths were reported in either France or Spain.

open image in gallery Firefighters work to extinguish flames during a wildfire in Lege-Cap-Ferret in the Gironde department, amongst worsening drought conditions following a heatwave and water shortages across much of France. ( Reuters )

Authorities also believe the cause of both fires was accidental.

France's interior minister Laurent Nuñez said on Friday evening that 110,000 people have been displaced so far, while in Spain, 25,000 people have been evacuated, with more than 20,000 are in lockdown.

"It's quite impressive and even frightening," said Laurent Moretti, a resident in the town of Arès, France.

"An evacuation on this scale has never happened before. All we really hope is that the firefighters can quickly get it under control."

Local authorities in the Gironde department said 53 homes and a campsite have been ravaged by flames, adding that 42 firefighters were injured.

Around 1,500 people who fled the peninsula arrived by sea in the city of Arcachon, some aboard small water taxis and others on larger boats.

open image in gallery Fiirefighters spray water in a burning forest in the Lège-Cap-Ferret region ( AP )

Hundreds of French firefighters have been deployed and additional ground and aerial reinforcements were sent Friday to tackle the blaze.

Meanwhile, another major wildfire burned further south down the coast and was not contained as strong winds did not help firefighters.

French president Emmanuel Macron said France will receive EU reinforcements including two Croatian Canadair firefighting aircraft, two Portuguese Air Tractor aircraft, and two heavy-lift Black Hawk helicopters from the Czech Republic and Slovakia.

The national emergency in Spain means that the nation’s interior ministry, which controls police and security forces, has taken charge of overseeing the firefighting efforts that are being fanned by a heat wave, with temperatures expected to top 39 degrees Celsius (102 Fahrenheit) in parts of the country.

The two major fires near Madrid merged into one single blaze that had quickly charred 11.5 square miles by Friday afternoon.

Regional president Isabel Díaz-Ayuso called it the worst in Madrid's history, while Francisco Martín, the central government representative for the region of Madrid, said that 20,000 people had been ordered to shelter at home in towns west of the capital.

Martín said more evacuations could be coming and that the priority now was to protect the town of San Lorenzo, the home of the Escorial, Philip II's 16th-century royal palace and monastery.

Meanwhile, a blaze in Ávila, less than two hours northwest of Madrid, had consumed 34 square miles, causing another 1,500 people to flee.

Spain's Civil Guard arrested one man and is investigating another for allegedly having used heavy machinery in an area where it was prohibited for fire risk. Police believe a spark ignited the fire on Thursday.

open image in gallery Firefighters battle a wildfire in Cebreros area, near Avila, 80 kms west of Madrid on July 24, 2026 ( AFP/Getty )

Spanish interior minister Fernando Grande-Marlaska said that Italy and Greece are each sending two Canadair water-dumping airplanes.

“In my 60 years I have never seen something like this in my village, I have never seen fire of these dimensions,” Francisco Martínez, the mayor of Burgohondo, whose residents were preventively evacuated in Ávila, told Spain’s national broadcaster TVE.

Spanish television showed video taken by retreating residents of walls of flames topped by long plumes of smoke advancing through woods and scrublands. High winds and hilly terrain complicated efforts by firefighters, who combated the blazes with firetrucks and bulldozers.

In southwest France, authorities sent boats to help the evacuation and a total of about 63,000 people, many of them tourists, were told to get out as two major, separate fires threatened homes and campsites, officials said.

"From our home, we had a view of the fires ... We could see the clouds becoming darker and darker," said Yoan Urien, who left late on Thursday after police told everyone in his neighbourhood in the town of Biscarrosse to leave.

"I was able to find ‌somewhere to take shelter with my pets, but ... it's quite a shock," the 26-year-old told Reuters.

open image in gallery Holidaymakers from Lege-Cap-Ferret disembark from a boat upon their arrival in Arcachon during an evacuation operation of the entire Cap-Ferret peninsula ( AFP/Getty )

The other major fire, which began in nearby Saumos, north of Cap Ferret, is threatening to cut off the only road out of the peninsula and is the largest so far this season in France, interior minister Laurent Nunez told local television.

It has ‌torn through more than 10,000 hectares (24,700 acres) of forest and burned 80 homes, completely destroying about 50 ‌of them, he said.

"It's totally apocalyptic," said Ambre Dubos, from the nearby Landes region.

Mapped: Cap Ferret peninsula

In one week, Spain has had the worst fires on record for both the regions of Castilla La Mancha and Madrid.

Firefighters were still trying to extinguish Spain’s second-largest ever fire in the Guadalajara province of Castilla La Mancha after it had destroyed some 320 square kilometers (120 square miles) over the last week.

Thirteen people were also killed in a fire in southern Spain earlier this month, the deadliest fire in recent memory for Spain.

open image in gallery Smoke and flames rise as a wildfire advances near San Martin de Valdeiglesias, Ávila province, Spain. ( AP )

Spanish minister for the ecological transition Sara Aagesen said that Spain has seen 1,140 square kilometres (440 square miles) already burned this year, more than five times the burned terrain it had through the first half of 2025.

Grande-Marlaska said that in addition to the major fires in Madrid and in Ávila that have required the national government to get directly involved, there are nine serious fires in other parts of Spain.

“The day has been complicated by winds that reach 50 kph (31 mph) and high temperatures,” Grande-Marlaska said.

Sánchez called on Wednesday for a pact between political parties to fight climate change that he said is key to adapting to a more fire-prone climate. Spain has experienced record temperatures in recent summers and forest fires of increasing violence.

Sicily is burning

open image in gallery A Canadair drops water over a burning area as a wildfire flares in Sagana in the territory of Monreale, Sicily ( AFP/Getty )

In Italy, wildfires continued to ravage parts of Sicily, with the central-western province of Agrigento particularly hard hit.

Fueled by temperatures that have topped 40C (104F), low humidity and winds, the blazes have forced scattered evacuations and were blamed for the death of a firefighter responding to a fire in Caltanissetta.

Reuters

People are irate after the White House tried to MAGA-ify Jimothy, the beloved Seattle-based raccoon who went viral for having a short spine.

Capitalizing on the viral social media trend, the White House posted an image of Jimothy wearing a red ‘Trump was right about everything’ hat.

“Jimothy spotted on the way to Washington, D.C.,” the caption read.

Within a day, the post had accumulated more than one million views and criticisms that it was “cringe” and the White House was “killing memes.”

One person disputed Jimothy would have voted for President Donald Trump, joking the raccoon was a “Harris voter [for real]” and “maybe uncommitted in the primary.”

The White House posted a photoshopped image of the viral short-spined raccoon Jimothy wearing a red 'Trump was right about everything' hat ( White House / X )

But mostly, critics responded with complaints that the White House was using the trending raccoon to promote Trump.

“I swear y'all go out of your way to try to ruin everyone's fun,” one X user grumbled.

An X user named Evan wrote: “Genuinely the worst propaganda account ever.”

The raccoon named Jimothy has been all over social media, gaining buzz for his uniquely curved back, and stealing the hearts of Seattle locals. In one video posted on Instagram, Jimothy was seen prancing across a lawn before going up concrete steps.

The woman filming the video can be heard saying, “What am I looking at?”

She then said in the post’s caption that she and her partner “were graced with the presence of Jimothy the raccoon with short spine syndrome. Praise Jimothy!!”

The Daily Beast was the first to report on the Jimothy backlash. The White House often uses its social media accounts to post memes or troll Trump’s opponents – a tactic that can resonate with young people and boost morale, even momentarily.

More recently, the White House social media team has engaged with people online by Trump-ifying trending posts. Earlier this month, the White House posted a version of Madison Square Garden’s wedding announcement for Taylor Swift and Travis Kelce by replacing the original text with: “TRUMP Is Your President.”

The concept is popular with companies and brands, which are typically doing so to promote a product.

Other Trump administration agencies followed suit on Jimothy. The Office of Personnel Management posted an image of Jimothy “trying to enter public service” and a personal identification badge indicating “Jimothy J. Raccoon” was now working for the government.

The Interior Department press team promptly responded, claiming Jimothy was now a Park Police Officer.

Scott Kupor, director of the Office of Personnel Management, also chimed in: “We believe in equal employment opportunities - in this case, though, I question the merit-based assessment process.”

Kupor’s tweet referred to Trump’s policy that all hiring in the federal government be “merit-based” after accusing past administration of hiring for diversity, equity and inclusion purposes.

Two sons of a man shot by immigration officers in Houston this month testified at a congressional hearing Friday, describing the horror and confusion of learning their father had been killed, and demanding a transparent investigation into how he died and why.

Lorenzo Salgado Araujo was killed July 7, when Immigration and Customs Enforcement officers chased his white work van through the streets, then shot him through the window in front of his work crew, including his brother.

Salgado Araujo’s sons read from prepared remarks at a Houston hearing with Democratic members of Congress. The sons' voices often choked with emotion as they described their father as a humble and hardworking family man. He had lived without legal status in the U.S. for 35 years, ran a homebuilding business and had never been in trouble with the law.

“He didn’t need anybody to know his name,” Lorenzo Salgado Araujo, Jr. told the hearing, held by the Congressional Hispanic Caucus. “He worked hard to protect and provide for our family, to put me and my siblings through college. He taught us that good things come to those that work hard.”

The Department of Homeland Security said shortly after the shooting that Salgado Araujo had rammed his van into the immigration vehicles chasing him, then “weaponized his vehicle in an attempt to run over an ICE law enforcement officer,” and that the officer fired in self-defense. The officers were not wearing body cameras.

Passengers in Salgado Araujo’s van describe a different version of events

At least two of the passengers in the van have disputed the government's account, saying the officers crashed into the van and were safely on the sides of the vehicle, never in danger of being struck, when the officer fired. All three passengers in the van were arrested and remain in immigration detention. One of them is Salgado Araujo’s brother, Victor, whose account of the killing is not public because his petition for release is sealed.

Harris County District Attorney Sean Teare told the hearing that DHS, which oversees ICE, has ignored his requests for information and evidence, including the name of the officer who fired the fatal shot.

Nevertheless, he said, his office was making “significant progress.” He declined to discuss specific evidence or speculate on when his office’s investigation would end.

Salgado Araujo’s sons said their father would have never run from officers, who were driving unmarked vehicles, if he’d known who they were. They had talked as a family about what they would do if he encountered ICE, and they said he believed he would find a way to get back home to them.

Salgado Araujo’s sons describe an excruciating wait for information

They said he was a man of routine. The day he was killed started as most did: He woke up before dawn, his wife cooked him a hearty breakfast, then he said goodbye to her and their dog. He got into his white van, said a prayer and left before 6 a.m. to pick up his crew.

Ronaldo Salgado said his mother called him around 7 a.m. to say something bad had happened. He saw a Facebook post about an encounter with immigration officers and rushed to the scene. He was there for hours, he said, begging officers and neighbors for information, even asking one homeowner to climb onto her roof to survey the scene.

Then a Facebook video appeared.

“I learned again from a Facebook post that our dad had been shot,” he told the hearing. “Not because I could see him, but because I could hear his voice on videos posted online crying for help.”

He rushed to the hospital. More hours passed before Democratic U.S. Rep. Sylvia Garcia demanded answers, and they learned he was dead.

Garcia said the Democratic delegation has sent multiple letters to DHS and ICE about the shooting and has received no response. The delegation also invited representatives of the department and the administration to attend the hearing, and they declined.

An email sent to DHS by The Associated Press seeking comment Friday was not immediately returned.

Lorenzo Jr. called what happened to them “a kafkaesque nightmare.” They said they mourned not only for their father, but also for the families of others killed by immigration officers, including Johan Sebastián Durán Guerrero, a 26-year-old who was shot in Maine days after their dad.

The sons say they want justice

The sons called on Congress to make sure justice is served.

Lorenzo asked people to imagine what the brothers were experiencing by picturing a loved one “pinned to the ground in pain and yelling out in desperate need of help.”

“Picture the anger and helplessness of watching that person bleed out through a video on your phone. What would you do after?” he asked. “How would you cope with the feeling of losing your protector, your role model, your mother’s loving partner, your grandmother’s little boy?”

He added, “That feeling you feel right now is only a fraction of what my family and I have felt these past 17 days.”

Toy Story 5 is lighting up more than just movie theater screens across America.

The fifth installment of the beloved franchise hit theaters last month and has raked in an impressive $957 million, likely on its way to becoming the highest-grossing film in the franchise.

But its impact is felt beyond the screen thanks to Disney’s long-standing partnership with Starlight Children’s Foundation.

As part of the partnership, the company has converted hospital spaces into immersive screening events for patients and their families. The film became available to patients in more than 400 children’s hospitals globally, including more than 300 across the U.S.

Disney says it distributed more than 18,000 Toy Story 5-themed toys and 34,000 character-inspired hospital gowns to children and families.

open image in gallery More than 18,000 ‘Toy Story 5’-themed toys were distributed to children and families across participating hospitals ( Disney/Pixar )

At the Los Angeles premiere for the film, cast members and guests stopped on the red carpet to write messages of encouragement for children in hospitals.

The heartfelt messages were shown at hospitals in Washington, D.C., Oakland and Orlando, where children were surprised with visits from Woody and Jessie. They also participated in drawing sessions led by Pixar animators and received Toy Story-themed gift packages.

In the latest installment of Pixar's long-running franchise, Woody, Buzz Lightyear and Jessie find themselves competing with a new kind of rival: a frog-shaped tablet called Lilypad, voiced by Greta Lee. The film follows the toys as they struggle to remain relevant after Bonnie becomes captivated by the device, with Pixar describing the story as “Toy meets Tech.”

In the film, Tom Hanks returns as Woody, Tim Allen as the space ranger Buzz Lightyear, and Joan Cusack as the yodeling cowgirl Jessie.

Allen, Cusack, Lee, Tony Hale and Conan O’Brien were among some of the celebrities who sent heartfelt messages to the children as part of the partnership with Starlight Children’s Foundation.

open image in gallery Disney’s long-standing partnership with Starlight Children’s Foundation saw the latest ‘Toy Story’ movie brought into children’s hospitals across the US ( iStock )

“This is amazing! Disney is sending Toy Story to all these fantastic kids in hospitals around the nation,” Hale told The Hollywood Reporter.

Lisa Haines, senior vice president of corporate social responsibility at Disney, said that the film’s cast and crew carried the film’s spirit “onto the red carpet by writing personal messages for children in hospitals before the world even saw the film.”

Haines continued: “Whether it’s a beloved character by a child’s side or a note from the voice of Buzz Lightyear, those simple gestures are incredibly powerful and can create moments of comfort and joy for kids when they’re needed most.”

The film itself was praised for exploring children’s growing dependence on screens, and The Independent’s Charlotte Cripps wrote that the film had such an impact on her kids that one of her daughters gave up using the iPad.

News.title: 11 indicted in smuggling deaths after seven found dead in shipping container in Texas rail yard
News.content:

Eleven people were named in an indictment on Friday for the smuggling deaths of seven migrants who were hiding inside a sealed rail cargo container in Texas, a U.S. attorney announced on Friday.

Six people were found dead inside the shipping container in a rail yard in Laredo, Texas, while a seventh had been left for dead along the way back in May, U.S. Attorney for the Western District of Texas Justin R. Simmons alleges.

“It’s very hard to survive in an un-air-conditioned, sealed container with ... the temperature being what it was on that day,” Simmons said in his indictment.

According to the indictment, the group boarded the train in the border town of Del Rio and headed toward San Antonio, where officials believe was the destination. However, when smugglers opened the door, a man fell out so the smugglers closed the door and fled the scene.

It’s not clear if he was already dead by then, Simmons said.

When the smugglers fled, the remaining six people were left locked inside, including a 14-year-old boy, authorities said.

Sealed from within and stacked high, the shipping container offered no ventilation or cooling. Temperatures that day ranged from 88 to 92 degrees Fahrenheit (31 to 33 degrees Celsius), the U.S. Attorney’s office said.

A worker at Union Pacific Rail Yard saw the container and noticed a leg sticking out, later finding the bodies.

“One of those individuals frantically contacted their family as they were dying from the sweltering heat in that container,” Simmons said.

The migrants were from Honduras and Mexico.

( AFP/Getty )

The Webb County medical examiner suspected the deaths were caused by hyperthermia, or heat stroke.

The 11 people were indicted on two charges: Conspiracy to transport aliens, resulting in death, and aiding and abetting the transportation of aliens resulting in death. Each charge carries a maximum penalty of life in prison, Simmons said.

The migrants paid “generally the equivalent of $1,500 -$10,000 to individuals in Honduras, Mexico, the United States, and elsewhere, to be transported into the interior of the United States,” according to the indictment.

One of the defendants was arrested May 12 in Del Rio, and eight more were arrested over several days last week in central and south Texas. Two of the 11 remain at large, including a man and a woman. Officials said four are U.S. citizens and two are permanent U.S. residents. They didn’t specify any other nationalities.

Smuggling on trains has long been a concern partly because trains headed to the United States often slow or stop in Mexico before crossing the border. That creates an opportunity for smugglers or immigrants to climb aboard or hide drugs or other contraband on a train before it enters the U.S.

The United States has gradually expanded the scope of its attacks against Iran over the course of two weeks of punishing airstrikes that increasingly resemble the war’s opening salvos.

After a brief ceasefire in June following the signing of an interim deal to end the conflict, a battle for control over the Strait of Hormuz erupted, shattering the truce and pushing the countries back to the precipice of an all-out war across the Middle East.

The U.S. started off with intense waves of strikes on Iran’s navy and coastal defenses earlier this month, aiming to blunt Tehran's ability to attack ships in the strait vital to world energy supplies. In recent days, the U.S. has expanded its targets, hitting bridges and infrastructure in the south and striking deeper into the center of Iran and the outskirts of its capital, Tehran.

Despite its growing intensity and scope, the renewed U.S. aerial campaign is not as fierce in either way as the one at the start of the war, which began on Feb. 28. In just the first 100 hours of the war, the U.S. and Israel hit hundreds of military targets and killed top leaders of Iran, including Ayatollah Ali Khamenei.

The Iranian Health Ministry says 3,434 people have been killed since the war began, including 55 during the recent escalation. The latest U.S. strikes temporarily disrupted transportation and communications within Iran, and damaged water infrastructure used by thousands of people.

The U.S. military has said its recent barrages were aimed at degrading Iran’s ability to threaten vessels in the strait. But Iran hasn't backed down.

It has intensified strikes on ships in the strait and on Gulf countries housing U.S. bases, killing at least four American soldiers and damaging critical infrastructure. Israel has so far not been targeted in this latest round of fighting, and it has not joined the U.S. in launching attacks.

Here is a look at what the U.S. has been striking and what it may have achieved:

The first days focused on Iran’s coast

Not long after the countries had reached an interim ceasefire deal, Iran began striking ships in the Strait of Hormuz, triggering tit-for-tat attacks with the U.S. By July 12, the U.S. military intensified its bombing campaign, and a day later, President Donald Trump reimposed a U.S. blockade on Iranian ports.

In two days of bombardment, the U.S. military said it struck dozens of targets, including air-defense systems, coastal radar sites, missile and drone factories and launchers, and small boats. It used precision munitions, naval vessels and, for the first time, one-way attack sea drones.

The strikes focused on coastal provinces along the strait and Persian Gulf: Khuzestan, Bushehr and Hormozgan. The city and port of Bandar Abbas, which is on the strait and home to critical naval and trade infrastructure, bore the initial brunt. Strikes also hit key islands in the Gulf -- Qeshm, Abu Musa and Kish. Further east, naval and military bases in Sistan and Baluchistan province on the Gulf of Oman have been hit.

Strikes have aimed to take out roads, bridges and infrastructure

A flurry of strikes over two days damaged at least six bridges and a tunnel around Bandar Abbas, images on state TV showed. The goal appeared to be to sever the links of the Revolutionary Guard bases there with the rest of the country. Another strike hit a railway junction west of the port city.

Residents captured images of traffic jams on some roads following the strikes.

Over the past two weeks, other strikes in Bandar Abbas hit the offices of the radio and communications regulatory authority, which manages Iran’s radio-frequency spectrum. For three days, the U.S. hit a maritime communications tower in one of the city's ports, totally destroying it on July 17. Another communications tower was hit about 120 kilometers (75 miles) down the coast.

Strikes also disrupted communications temporarily between the mainland and the islands of Kharg and Qeshm, though by the 10th day of the campaign, Iranian authorities said they had restored connections. A fishmeal production factory was hit in Qeshm.

At the northern end of the Persian Gulf, power outages were reported in parts of Khuzestan province after strikes there.

Other infrastructure has also been hit, including an agricultural water pumping station in Khuzestan, killing one person, according to local officials. A reported strike on July 18 hit a water desalination plant in Jask, on a peninsula just outside the Strait of Hormuz, destroying the pumping stations and affecting water supply to 10,000 residents nearby, according to Iranian officials. That attack followed an Iranian strike on U.S. bases in Jordan, where at least three soldiers were killed and others were injured.

A U.S. strike on a border crossing with Iraq, where hundreds of pilgrims had gathered, killed two people, according to state media.

The American military has said it is hitting “logistics infrastructure.” Last week, Trump warned that for every Iranian attack on the strait, a power plant or bridge will be hit.

Iranian media have been quick to report that roads and tunnels hit by the Americans were under repair, or that alternative routes were established to connect the south with the rest of the country.

More strikes are targeting Iran's interior

By the third day of the reignited conflict, U.S. strikes moved to hit deeper inside Iran. Targets included Revolutionary Guard and military bases believed responsible for attacks on American bases in the Gulf, as well as reported missile production units, military installations and airports used by the Guard.

U.S. forces hit a military barracks in the city of Iranshahr in the far southeast of the country, killing seven soldiers and wounding a dozen others, according to Iranian officials. The Iranian military had recently claimed it conducted drone attacks against American bases in the region, including one in Jordan on July 15, according to a report by the Institute for the Study of War and the Critical Threats Project.

At least two strikes hit a Revolutionary Guard Aerospace Force installation in Khuzestan province, also believed to have been involved in attacks on U.S. bases.

So far, the Tehran area has only been hit twice, in contrast to the first round of the war, when the capital was pounded by hundreds of strikes, mainly by Israel. A July 19 strike hit the Khojir military complex near Tehran, one of Iran’s main missile factories. A missile site outside the capital was later hit.
