World.title: Japan Tops Global Waste Index 2025; U.S., Israel, and Chile Rank as Worst Polluters
World.content:
Japan has emerged as the world leader in waste management, while Israel, Chile, and the United States rank among the worst-performing countries, according to the Global Waste Index 2025 released by Slovak-based waste technology company Sensoneo.

The report, which ranks all 38 OECD member states based on their waste generation and disposal practices, highlights significant disparities in global waste management. Sensoneoâs index evaluates countries on per capita waste generation, recycling, incineration, and landfill use.

Israel and Chile ranked last and second-to-last, respectively, primarily due to their heavy reliance on environmentally damaging landfilling practices. Israel sends 524 of the 650 kilograms of waste it generates per person each year directly to landfills. Chile recycles just 1% of its waste and sends more than 95% to landfill.

The United States, which increased its per capita waste generation from 811 to 951 kilograms since 2022, remains the highest generator of municipal solid waste globally. The U.S. disposes of nearly half of that â 447 kilograms â in landfills annually. Neighboring Canada also performed poorly, landfilling 67% of its annual 694 kg per capita waste.

At the other end of the spectrum, Japan ranked No. 1, followed by South Korea and Estonia, all of which combine relatively low waste generation with efficient disposal methods. Japan sends only 3 kilograms per capita to landfill, relying heavily on incineration (245 kg) and maintaining a controlled recycling rate.

European countries dominated the top 10 rankings, with Austria, Germany, Finland, Belgium, Sweden, Norway, and Switzerland all demonstrating strong waste management systems. Austria topped the recycling chart with 334 kilograms of municipal waste recycled per person annually â accounting for 42% of its total waste.

Meanwhile, Spain fell four places to 27th despite minor improvements. The country reduced its landfill and incineration rates slightly while increasing recycling by 10 kilograms per capita. However, its overall waste generation rose by 10 kg compared to the 2022 index.

The index revealed that in 12 of the 38 countries, over half of all waste is still landfilled â including in developed nations like Australia, New Zealand, and Canada. By contrast, Switzerland was the only country to report zero landfill disposal, while Belgium, Finland, Estonia, and Japan landfilled less than 3 kg per person.

Other key findings include:

New Zealand , Finland , and Iceland posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita.

, , and posted the largest reductions in waste generation per capita. From an environmental standpoint, incineration is considered preferable to landfilling, but excessive reliance on either suggests a need for stronger waste reduction and recycling strategies.

About the Index and Sensoneo

First launched in 2019, the Global Waste Index is published every three years by Sensoneo, a company specializing in digital transformation for waste management systems. The 2025 edition is based on the latest available national data.

Sensoneo operates in 87 countries and provides waste monitoring solutions to cities, industries, and governments. It is the only company to have successfully implemented deposit return systems (DRS) IT infrastructure in nine countries, achieving recycling rates above 90%.

In Madrid, Sensoneo is deploying 11,100 smart sensors, marking the worldâs largest smart waste monitoring installation to date.

World.title: South Korean Model and Actor Kim Jong Suk Dies at 29, Family Urges Respect Amid Speculation
World.content:
South Korean model and television personality Kim Jong Suk has died at the age of 29, his family confirmed on June 6. The news has shocked fans and colleagues across the countryâs entertainment industry, where Kim rose to prominence following his appearance on tvNâs 2022 reality dating show Skip Dating.

Kim, who began his career in modeling before transitioning to television, had been steadily gaining popularity in recent years. His sudden death has prompted an outpouring of grief and speculation online.

While the exact cause of death remains unconfirmed, some media reports have linked Kimâs passing to an incident in Hanam involving a violent altercation between a young man and his girlfriend. According to the reports, law enforcement responded to the scene, after which the man allegedly died by suicide after jumping from a high-rise building.

Amid widespread online discussion and conjecture, Kimâs family issued a public plea for restraint, asking the public and media to refrain from spreading misinformation or making disrespectful assumptions.

Kimâs older sister posted on social media, expressing the family’s devastation and emotional exhaustion. âWe ask for privacy and understanding during this difficult time,â she wrote, emphasizing the familyâs wish to grieve in peace.

Details regarding funeral arrangements have not been made public.

World.title: Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications
World.content:
Uruguay faces a 12.5% US tariff as its foreign ministry weighs the implications

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:05 UTC Full article

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations”

Uruguay was placed in the highest band of the new US tariff scheme, with an additional 12.5% levy on its exports to the United States, for not having an explicit ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor. The measure, which took effect on Friday, raises the rate that had applied to the country since February, of 10%.

Sources at the Foreign Ministry confirmed the decision and said its implications are being analyzed, while noting that the outcome “was within expectations,” given that the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) had announced the start of the investigation in March and released its proposal in June. The Ministry of Economy and Finance confirmed the move from 10% to 12.5%.

The new scheme, applied under Section 301 of US trade law, covers 60 trading partners accounting for about 99% of US imports, and replaces the 10% universal tariff that expired on Friday. Under the USTR's determination, the 12.5% rate applies to economies that have not adopted a ban on the import of goods produced with forced labor, did not commit to implementing one through a reciprocal trade agreement, and are not part of the differentiated calculation group, which includes the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Taiwan, and Switzerland.

The breakdown leaves Uruguay at a disadvantage relative to several regional partners. Argentina, Ecuador, Mexico, Guatemala, Honduras, and El Salvador fell under the lower 10% rate, having adopted restrictions or committed to doing so. Costa Rica, Panama, and the Dominican Republic, by contrast, face 12.5%, as does Uruguay. Brazil, meanwhile, has since Wednesday been subject to 25% tariffs issued under the same legal instrument, following a separate investigation.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said US Trade Representative Jamieson Greer in announcing the measure.

The USTR said certain products are exempt, among them raw materials whose higher cost could cause supply shortages in the US market, though it did not publish a detailed list. China does not appear in this scheme, as it is subject to separate and higher tariffs.

The round is part of Donald Trump's administration's effort to rebuild its tariff structure after the Supreme Court struck down in February the tariffs issued under an emergency powers law, finding that the administration had exceeded its authority.

World.title: Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner
World.content:
Six candidates to lead the UN debate in the General Assembly with no clear front-runner

24th Friday, July 2026 - 07:00 UTC Full article

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts

The six contenders to succeed António Guterres at the head of the United Nations set out their proposals on Thursday in a debate held in the General Assembly Hall, a week before the formal start of the selection process. For nearly two hours they answered questions from diplomats, UN staff, and civil society representatives, in a publicly broadcast session.

The candidates are former Chilean president Michelle Bachelet, former Ecuadorian foreign minister María Fernanda Espinosa, Argentina's Rafael Grossi, currently director general of the International Atomic Energy Agency, Costa Rica's Rebeca Grynspan, secretary-general of the UN Conference on Trade and Development, former Guyanese foreign minister Carolyn Rodrigues-Birkett, and former Senegalese president Macky Sall. Five of the six come from Latin America and the Caribbean, in line with the regional rotation expectation that favors the region this cycle; Sall is the only African candidate. Guterres leaves office on December 31.

The common thread across the interventions was the need to restore the credibility of an organization facing financial strains and largely absent from negotiations over the world's major conflicts. “I would like no one to ask me again where the UN is. That will be my indicator,” Grynspan said when asked what achievements she would hope to show after five years. On Security Council paralysis, she argued that “the blockade of the Security Council is when the job of the secretary-general starts,” citing her role in the deal that allowed grain exports through the Black Sea as a precedent applicable to the Strait of Hormuz crisis.

Bachelet stressed the importance of the post's moral authority and said neutrality and independence are essential for all 193 member states to feel represented. Asked how he would act if a permanent Council member waged a war of aggression, Grossi replied that the secretary-general must “dialogue and listen” and approach conflicts realistically, examining their root causes and the situation of the party under attack. Espinosa said the organization is in crisis and must recover its capacity to prevent conflicts, while Sall focused on reforming the international financial architecture and Rodrigues-Birkett defended the scope for action despite the post's lack of executive power.

The format, with no direct exchange between participants, limited the contrast of ideas. According to analyst Richard Gowan, Grossi is the most frequently mentioned front-runner, though he has not locked up the race, and both Grynspan and Rodrigues-Birkett have significant backing. Several capitals have yet to define their positions. The decisive phase begins on July 30, when the fifteen members of the Security Council, five of them with veto power, start their closed-door voting.

World.title: Family of murdered journalist urges Paraguay to comply with Inter-American Court ruling
World.content:
Family of murdered journalist urges Paraguay to comply with Inter-American Court ruling

24th Friday, July 2026 - 06:48 UTC Full article

The family also said it had proposed holding the official act of acknowledgment of responsibility at the site of the killing, a proposal that was not accepted

The widow and children of Paraguayan journalist Santiago Leguizamón, murdered in 1991, have called on the state to fully comply with the ruling in which the Inter-American Court of Human Rights found Paraguay responsible for failing to properly investigate the crime. The demand was voiced on Monday at a ceremony beside the monument honoring the broadcaster in Pedro Juan Caballero, on the border with Brazil, convened by the family, the Paraguayan Journalists' Union, and the Human Rights Coordinating Body, with backing from the International Federation of Journalists.

Leguizamón, director of the Mburucuyá radio station, was shot on April 26, 1991, as he left the studio, after receiving threats over his investigations into organized crime along the border. In November 2022, the Inter-American Court declared Paraguay internationally responsible for violating his rights to life and to freedom of expression, as well as his relatives' judicial guarantees.

Among the reparation measures, the court ordered the reopening of the criminal investigation, the advancement of a law protecting journalists and human rights defenders, the strengthening and funding of the Journalists' Safety Roundtable, the creation of a fund for prevention and assistance programs, and the reinstatement for five years of the national journalism prize bearing the broadcaster's name.

“The most important part, the structural one, which concerns public policies to protect journalists, still has not advanced,” said Dante Leguizamón, the journalist's son and executive secretary of the Human Rights Coordinating Body. The family also said it had proposed holding the official act of acknowledgment of responsibility at the site of the killing, a proposal that was not accepted.

For its part, the vice-presidency has convened for July 27 the Public Act of Acknowledgment of International Responsibility in the journalist's memory, and maintains that compliance with the ruling is advancing through the interinstitutional commission that coordinates the implementation of international judgments, in whose meetings the family's representation has taken part.

The bill recommended by the court was submitted to Congress in 2023 by opposition lawmakers. An alternative proposal pushed in 2025 by governing-party legislators, which excludes human rights defenders and concentrates its implementation in the Interior Ministry, was rejected by journalists' unions and remains stalled in committee.

Since the end of Alfredo Stroessner's dictatorship in 1989, 22 journalists have been murdered in Paraguay, nine of them in the border department of Amambay. Only three of those cases have reached a final judicial resolution.

World.title: World Bank estimates $19.6 billion in earthquake damage in Venezuela
World.content:
World Bank estimates $19.6 billion in earthquake damage in Venezuela

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 22:37 UTC Full article

The disaster struck a country with a poverty rate above 76% and an economy that contracted sharply over the past decade, in a period marked by US sanctions

The twin earthquakes that struck northern Venezuela on June 24 caused an estimated $19.6 billion in direct physical damage, according to a preliminary assessment published on Thursday by the World Bank. The figure is equivalent to about 18% of the country's gross domestic product, based on International Monetary Fund data.

The report, produced using the institution's rapid damage estimation methodology, attributes 47% of the losses to residential buildings, 27% to infrastructure, and 26% to non-residential buildings. La Guaira state and the Capital District, which includes Caracas, account for roughly half of the total impact. In La Guaira, the hardest-hit area, the institution estimates that one in five homes was destroyed.

The estimate does not include the costs of rebuilding with structural improvements or of debris removal, which the World Bank says could amount to between two and two and a half times the replacement value, bringing the total bill to close to $50 billion. An early United Nations assessment, released a week after the quakes, had put direct damage at $37 billion.

“This assessment provides the Government of Venezuela and its partners with an early, objective basis for recovery planning,” said Susana Cordeiro Guerra, the institution's vice-president for Latin America and the Caribbean, adding that the earthquakes “have disrupted lives, damaged critical infrastructure, and created new challenges” for the country.

The earthquakes, of magnitudes 7.2 and 7.5, left 5,398 dead and 16,740 injured according to official figures, which authorities present as provisional, while unofficial estimates put the number of missing in the thousands. About 18,000 people remain without housing. It is the deadliest quake recorded in Venezuela since 1812. The United Nations estimates that more than a million people need immediate humanitarian assistance.

The disaster struck a country with a poverty rate above 76% and an economy that contracted sharply over the past decade, in a period marked by US sanctions. The World Bank warned that, at current levels of public and private investment, reconstruction would stretch beyond ten years, with lasting effects on economic activity, and called for a rapid increase in public funding.

The report was published after fourteen US Democratic lawmakers asked President Donald Trump to lift economic sanctions on Venezuela and facilitate the country's access to its frozen assets abroad. A hundred economists signed a request along the same lines. The institution said it is working with the Venezuelan government, the Inter-American Development Bank, and CAF to define additional technical and financial support.

World.title: US rebuilds its tariff wall with forced-labor levies on 60 economies
World.content:
US rebuilds its tariff wall with forced-labor levies on 60 economies

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 22:33 UTC Full article

The levies are applied under Section 301 of the 1974 trade law, which allows a response to unfair trade practices following an investigation

The United States imposed tariffs of between 10% and 12.5% on 60 trading partners, which together account for about 99% of its imports, over what the Office of the US Trade Representative (USTR) described as their failure to adopt and effectively enforce bans on the import of goods produced with forced labor. The measures, announced on Thursday, took effect at 12:01 a.m. on Friday, at the same moment the 10% universal tariff in place since February expired.

The levies are applied under Section 301 of the 1974 trade law, which allows a response to unfair trade practices following an investigation. The move is the biggest effort by Donald Trump's administration to rebuild its tariff framework after the Supreme Court struck down his “reciprocal” tariffs in February, finding that the administration had exceeded its authority by invoking an emergency powers law. The temporary tariff that replaced them, issued under Section 122, was valid for 150 days without congressional approval.

The final breakdown sets a 10% tariff for seventeen economies that adopted restrictions or committed to doing so — among them Canada, Mexico, the United Kingdom, and India — effective rates of 10% to 12.5% depending on the product for another five, and 12.5% for the remaining 38. Several countries changed their legislation after the proposal was made public in June and moved to the lower band; India, for instance, had initially been placed at 12.5%. Oil and gas, fertilizers, and goods qualifying as duty-free under the North American trade agreement are exempt, as are goods in transit.

“The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it; it's well past time for our trading partners to do the same,” said Trade Representative Jamieson Greer, who argued the action corrects “both a human rights abuse and distortive trade practice.” A senior official, speaking on condition of anonymity, described it as the most significant international labor-rights action undertaken by any country.

Several partners rejected the accusation. The European Union dismissed it explicitly even before the final determination. Tariffs are paid by US companies importing the products, which typically pass the cost on to consumer prices.

The measure adds to other recent actions under the same legal instrument: the 25% tariffs on most Brazilian products took effect on Wednesday, and this week Trump signed proclamations to apply additional 50% levies in 30 days on a range of Canadian goods. Several companies are expected to challenge the new round in court.

World.title: New York judge sets June 2027 for the start of Maduro and Cilia Flores's trial
World.content:
New York judge sets June 2027 for the start of Maduro and Cilia Flores's trial

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 07:34 UTC Full article

Maduro, 63, is charged with conspiracy to commit narcoterrorism, cocaine importation, and possession of machine guns and destructive devices

Federal Judge Alvin Hellerstein set June 1, 2027, as the preliminary start date for the trial of former Venezuelan president Nicolás Maduro and his wife, Cilia Flores, in the narcoterrorism case they face in the United States. The decision came on Wednesday during the case's third hearing before the US District Court for the Southern District of New York, which lasted only a few minutes.

Maduro, 63, is charged with conspiracy to commit narcoterrorism, cocaine importation, and possession of machine guns and destructive devices. Flores, 69, faces charges linked to drug importation and weapons possession. Both have pleaded not guilty to all counts and have been held at a federal prison in Brooklyn since January 3, when they were captured in Caracas during a US military operation.

The schedule, jointly proposed by prosecutors and the defense the previous day, contemplates two rounds of pretrial motions. The defense will file a first set before September 2 arguing Maduro's immunity as the head of a sovereign state, one of its central contentions. According to his lawyer, Barry Pollack, if that motion succeeds, the second round would not be necessary. Prosecutors expect to complete the handover of unclassified evidence by September 22 and of classified material by November 15. Hellerstein called a hearing for November 17 to debate those arguments.

“This is a realistic schedule, we don't think it will be delayed,” Pollack said, after the judge voiced doubts about the parties' ability to meet the deadlines set for submitting evidence, witnesses, and experts.

Demonstrators for and against the proceedings gathered near the courthouse, with police present to prevent incidents, as had happened at the March hearing. From Caracas, the former president's son and lawmaker for the governing PSUV, Nicolás Maduro Guerra, called the process “unjust” and demanded his parents' release.

The case earlier saw a dispute over funding for the defense: Maduro and Flores argued they could not pay private lawyers because of US sanctions and because they were barred from using Venezuelan state funds. In April, Washington authorized Venezuela to cover their legal representation.

Since the capture, Venezuela has been governed by former vice-president Delcy Rodríguez, under whose tenure the United States eased sanctions on the oil industry. The former president also faces other civil proceedings in the United States: last week, a Miami judge issued a default judgment ordering him, along with other officials, to pay $314 million to three US citizens.

World.title: Wes Streeting appointed UK Defence Secretary; ‘disappointment’ with removal of Dan Jarvis, responsible for DIP
World.content:
Wes Streeting appointed UK Defence Secretary; ‘disappointment’ with removal of Dan Jarvis, responsible for DIP

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 07:34 UTC Full article

“With John Healey now looking after the money, Wes Streeting can focus on the vital Defence Reforms necessary to deliver.”

Former Health and Social Care Secretary Wes Streeting has been appointed by Prime Minister Andy Burnham as the new UK Defense Secretary, replacing Dan Jarvis who has taken the job when John Healey resigned last June.

This means Jarvis was Defence Secretary for less than six weeks – but in that time he was responsible for publishing the long awaited Defense Investment Plan (DIP), and there was expectation across the forces whether PM Burnham would keep his in Defense..

However taking to social media after it was announced that Streeting would replace him in the role, Mr Jarvis said: “It’s been an immense honor to serve as Defense Secretary and again be amongst those who give everything to defend our nation.”

“We owe them a huge debt of gratitude — and they will always have my absolute support. I wish my successor every success in this vital role.”

Former conservative Defence Secretary Ben Wallace criticized Mr Burnham’s decision to replace Mr Jarvis .

“Removing Dan Jarvis to find a spot for Wes Streeting shows a contempt for Defense at a time they need continuity and someone who understands the new way of warfare and the men and women of the armed forces,” he posted on X.

But there was a more positive reaction to the news from retired Air Marshal Greg Bagwell, a former combat pilot and senior leader in the RAF, who said: “With John Healey now looking after the money, Wes Streeting can focus on the vital Defense Reforms necessary to deliver.”

Meanwhile, a former head of the British Army has also said he is “disappointed” that Wes Streeting has been made defense secretary but spoke more positively about the potential relationship between Mr Streeting and his predecessor in the Treasury.

Lord Dannatt told Times Radio: “A new defense secretary has a lot to learn – the defense portfolio is one of the more complicated ones in government and as far as I’m aware Wes Streeting has got no background in defense, no background in the military”. (Forces)

World.title: Stephen Doughty confirmed as Minister of State for Overseas Territories
World.content:
Stephen Doughty confirmed as Minister of State for Overseas Territories

23rd Thursday, July 2026 - 02:00 UTC Full article

Minister Doughty during a meeting in London with MLA Roger Spink

Stephen Doughty MP has been confirmed at Minister of State in the Foreign, Commonwealth & Development Office. Until 21 July 2026 and from 8 July 2024 he was previously Minister of State for Europe, North America and Overseas Territories in the FCDO.

Stephen was first elected as Welsh Labour and Co-operative Member of Parliament for Cardiff South and Penarth in November 2012.

Stephen studied at Lester B. Pearson UWC in Canada, Oxford University and St Andrews University. He later worked for the OSCE Parliamentary Assembly and for members of the then National Assembly for Wales.

Stephen spent a number of years working for humanitarian and international development NGOs World Vision UK, Oxfam GB, Oxfam International and Oxfam Cymru. During the previous Labour government he was Special Adviser to the Secretary of State for International Development.

Stephen served at the Wales, Home Affairs, Arms Export Controls and International Development Committees in Parliament. He was also an opposition Whip and a Shadow Minister for Trade and Industry. He chaired the All-Party Parliamentary Group for HIV and Aids, and was a member of the British-Irish Parliamentary Assembly.

Stephen completed the Armed Forces Parliamentary scheme, attending the Royal College of Defense Studies 2017 to 2018. He has also served as an Army Reservist. In 2020 he was appointed Shadow Foreign Affairs and International Development Minister and in 2021 he was appointed Shadow Minister for Europe, North America and the Overseas Territories.

Stephen Doughty as Minister for Europe last week signed the UK/EU treaty on Gibraltar, ensuring ministerial continuity at the FCDO. Gibraltar media reported his reappointment is significant in the implementation phase of the treaty and when the treaty comes to be ratified by the House of Commons under the process set out in the Constitutional Reform and Governance Act 2010.

As a UK Government minister, Mr Doughty was closely involved in the final phases of the negotiation on the treaty and has close knowledge of the matter. He is also well versed in Gibraltar issues, having visited the Rock on numerous occasions in recent years including for National Day celebrations.

“I’m delighted to see that Stephen has been reappointed to the post of Minister for Europe,” said Chief Minister Fabian Picardo, reacting to the news. “He has a deep knowledge of the issues affecting Gibraltar from his time in Opposition and in Government.”

World.title: Sheinbaum touts improved security perception amid 54% drop in Morelos homicides: Friday’s mañanera recapped
World.content:
Sheinbaum’s mañanera in 60 seconds

🎤 Cuernavaca cabinet meeting: Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos.

Sheinbaum held her Friday presser in Morelos, spotlighting a 54% murder-rate drop under Gov. Margarita González, credited to the federal Plan Morelos. 📊 Security perception improves: INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December.

INEGI’s Q2 survey showed 59.8% of respondents feel unsafe in their city, down from 61.5% in March and 63.8% in December. 🚨Temoac mayor murder: Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday.

Federal agents are aiding Morelos prosecutors probing the killing of Mayor Valentín Lavín Moreno, who had alleged ties to local crime groups; his in-laws were arrested Thursday. 📰 Oaxaca journalist killing: Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family.

Federal prosecutors took over the case of slain journalist Alejandro Leyva at Oaxaca’s request; Sheinbaum tasked the AG with meeting Leyva’s family. ⚖️ Ruffo arrest not political: Sheinbaum denied persecution claims over ex-Baja California governor Ernesto Ruffo’s arrest, tying it to a 12-month fuel theft probe involving his company, Ingemar.

Why today’s mañanera matters

President Claudia Sheinbaum held her Friday morning press conference in Cuernavaca, the capital of the state of Morelos, continuing a practice begun in January of holding regional Security Cabinet meetings on the road to highlight local challenges.

Located just south of Mexico City, Morelos is the third-smallest entity in the republic, with a population of just under 2 million residents.

Morelos is grappling with corruption and organized crime challenges, though murder rates have dropped by 54% since Governor Margarita González was sworn in on Oct. 1, 2024 (the same day Sheinbaum took office).

Officials credited Plan Morelos — a joint federal-state security strategy implemented in April — and state-level efforts for reducing high-impact crimes across the state.

President touts improving public perception of security

Sheinbaum highlighted improvement in the public perception of security as reflected in the quarterly survey conducted by the national statistics agency INEGI, saying the results indicate that the public is noticing the advancements her government is making.

So far this year, Mexicans’ perception of insecurity dropped in both the first and the second quarter.

INEGI reported that 63.8% of those surveyed felt unsafe in their city in December, while 61.5% said they felt unsafe in March. That number fell to 59.8% in the latest survey.

The president acknowledged that perception sometimes changes gradually, often depending on whether one or one’s family have been victims of a crime.

“But it also depends on what you hear or read,” she said. “The important thing is that we are delivering results … and the population sees that.”

Federal authorities take over two high-profile murder cases

In stark juxtaposition to the public perception survey, Sheinbaum and Security Minister Omar García Harfuch offered updates on the investigations into Wednesday’s shocking murders.

With regard to the murder of Valentín Lavín Moreno, the mayor of Temoac (just 80 kilometers east of Cuernavaca), Harfuch said federal agents are working closely with Morelos prosecutors “to clarify the events and apprehend those responsible.”

Harfuch added that Lavín, who was shot to death in his City Hall office, was under investigation for possible links to two local crime groups. Lavín’s in-laws were arrested on Thursday, accused of having ties to organized crime.

A few hours before the tragic events in Temoac, journalist Alejandro Leyva was shot to death in the state of Oaxaca.

Federal prosecutors have taken over the case at the request of the Oaxaca authorities, Harfuch said, declining to elaborate further.

Sheinbaum has directed Attorney General Rosa Icela Rodríguez to meet with Leyva’s family and will also consult with journalists. “We have committed to several meetings in hopes of reassuring them that impunity will not be permitted,” Rodríguez said.

Sheinbaum denies Ruffo arrest linked to politics

In response to a question regarding opposition figures accusing the Sheinbaum administration of political persecution, the president denied that federal prosecutors are targeting political opponents.

Addressing the recent arrest of former Baja California Governor Ernesto Ruffo — a member of the National Action Party (PAN) — Sheinbaum said Ruffo was ensnared in a 12-month fuel theft investigation in which eight others were arrested.

“[Ruffo] is the primary shareholder [of Ingemar, the company accused of criminal activity], but he was not the ‘target’ … and the investigation is ongoing,” she said, adding that any others found to be involved will be pursued equally.

Sheinbaum said the investigation seeks to prove that Ingemar was illegally importing fuel (and evading taxes) and was fraudulently distributing it. “This has nothing to do with politics,” she said.

With reports from Milenio and Infobae

World.title: Michoacán priest douses crowd with pressurized holy water, sparking online debate
World.content:
A Catholic priest in the western Mexican state of Michoacán has gone viral after a video showed him using a pressure washer to spray holy water over a crowd during a patron saint festival.

The footage, widely shared across TikTok, Facebook and Instagram, shows Father Rubén Pérez Rubio standing in the bed of a white pickup truck during celebrations honoring Saint James the Apostle in Contepec, a Michoacán municipality of about 35,000 near the Querétaro border.

Holding a pressure washer (hidrolavadora in Spanish) he directs a stream of holy water (agua bendita) toward dozens of parishioners gathered outside the church on Wednesday.

The unusual method allowed the priest to reach a large crowd at once, with attendees — including women, children and elderly worshippers — reacting with laughter, raised hands and applause as they received the blessing.

“May my magnanimous mercy pour out its grace upon you all,” the priest says in Spanish in the video.

Local accounts cited by El Universal and other media outlets say the approach was intended to ensure no one was left without holy water during one of the municipality’s most important annual religious celebrations, which draws large numbers of residents and visitors.

The video quickly went viral, generating thousands of comments and sparking debate about the balance between tradition and innovation in religious practice.

Some social media users praised the priest’s creativity and practicality, saying the method helped engage the community and adapt to large crowds.

Others questioned whether using a pressure washer diminished the solemnity of a ritual typically performed with a traditional aspergillum.

Additional criticism focused on what some described as a waste of holy water and a lack of reverence.

Still, many commenters framed the act as a lighthearted moment that reflected a more accessible and modern approach to religion.

As of Friday, Pérez Rubio had not publicly commented on the viral video.

Saint James the Apostle, or Santiago Apóstol in Spanish, is honored across Latin America and Spain as a patron of pilgrims and towns whose July 25 feast day blends Catholic ritual with local tradition.

In Michoacán, patron saint festivals for him typically feature special Masses, processions through the streets, music and cultural activities.

With reports from El Universal, El Heraldo de México, Luz Noticias and N+

World.title: The Mexican historical figures behind San Miguel de Allende’s iconic landmarks
World.content:
San Miguel de Allende’s colonial streets and centuries-old architecture bear the names of some of Mexico’s most prominent historical figures. From leaders of the revolution to artists and architects, San Miguel is a living history lesson around every turn. So when you are strolling the gardens in San Miguel’s parks or walking down some of its most historic streets, here are the prominent figures that give their names to San Miguel’s most iconic sites.

Ignacio Allende

Ignacio Allende, a leader of the Mexican Revolution against Spain and the namesake of San Miguel de Allende, is the most prominent Mexican historical figure born in San Miguel.

The son of wealthy Spanish colonists, Allende enlisted with the Spanish army in Mexico before joining the underground independence movement. Eventually, Allende was named lieutenant general of the Revolutionary Army with Miguel Hidalgo y Castillo serving as Captain General.

The two succeeded in winning early victories, but were pushed back towards Guadalajara after failing to march on Mexico City. Hidalgo and Allende, despite greatly outnumbering the royalist forces, were defeated at the Battle of Calderon Bridge in Jalisco. This caused the insurgent troops to oust Hidalgo as their leader and install Allende as the head of the revolution.

Allende attempted to move north towards the United States in the hope of making powerful allies with the Americans. However, he was ambushed by royalist forces and taken to Chihuahua, where he was tried and executed by firing squad on June 26, 1811.

San Miguel de Allende was named after him when it became a city in 1826. The Plaza Ignacio Allende in Centro and the Instituto Allende on Salida a Celaya bear his name. Municipalities in six other Mexican states, including Chihuahua, Nuevo León and Jalisco are named after him.

Benito Juárez

Benito Juárez is one of the most famous historical figures in Mexican history, becoming the first Indigenous president after winning the Reform War and helping to fight off monarchist troops during the French invasion. Benito Juárez Park, about two blocks south of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel, is named after him.

Juárez walked nearly 30 miles to Oaxaca City when he was young to find work, eventually becoming a lawyer. He became the governor of Oaxaca in 1847, but was later exiled by the dictator Antonio López de Santa Anna and he fled to New Orleans, Louisiana.

Juárez later returned as a member of the Reform Party, but was imprisoned as Mexico began to fracture in civil war. After the conservatives won early battles, the liberals regrouped and were able to triumph. Juárez then became the first Indigenous president after assuming the role in 1861.

His problems were far from over, however, as the French — at the invitation of Mexican monarchists — invaded central Mexico and installed Austrian royal Maximilian as emperor. After fleeing north and narrowly escaping death, Juárez received a massive loan from the United States that reinvigorated the Republican troops, eventually forcing the French to flee.

Juárez once again assumed the role as the leader of Mexico, and executed Maximilian despite pleas for clemency. Juárez served for over 14 years as president before dying of a heart attack while still in office in 1872.

Zeferino Gutiérrez

The towering pink facade of the Parroquia de San Miguel Arcángel is, by far, the most iconic landmark in San Miguel. It was designed by iconic stonemason Zeferino Gutiérrez, a highly respected master of his craft despite never being trained as an architect.

Gutiérrez, whose previous work only involved steps and altars of local churches, used postcards of iconic European castles to design the iconic facade. He used pink lava stone, which has retained its color to this day and helped transform San Miguel into a world-renowned tourist destination.

Gutiérrez was given a home in San Miguel for his work on the church and continued to design and build places of worship. He designed the original Mercado Ignacio Ramírez on the town’s Civic Plaza, which was later replaced with the iconic statue of Ignacio Allende on a horse.

The typhus epidemic swept through San Miguel during the height of the Mexican Revolution, killing Gutiérrez in 1916. In January 2020, Zeferino Gutiérrez Park opened in San Miguel just north of the Fabrica la Aurora art center, becoming the largest park in the municipality.

Ignacio Ramírez

Ignacio Ramírez was one of the most prominent liberals of the La Reforma movement, which aimed to create a liberal democracy in Mexico and advocated for the separation of church and state.

The Ignacio Ramírez Cultural Center in the Centro neighborhood bears his name, along with the Mercado Ignacio Ramírez just north of the Civic Plaza.

Ramírez was born in San Miguel de Allende and was raised on liberal values before studying at university in Querétaro. He began publishing liberal newspapers and worked a slew of governmental positions before participating in the reform movement.

When the government of Benito Juárez eventually won power, Ramírez was given a spot in the cabinet where he continued to push for liberal reforms. He was forced out of the capital when the French marched into Mexico City, but continued to publish liberal ideals in hiding. Ramírez was imprisoned by the monarchist government upon his return to Mexico City, but was freed when the empire fell in 1867.

Under President Porfirio Díaz, who seized power in a military coup, Ramírez was named Minister of Justice and was elected to the Supreme Court. He died in 1879 at 60 years old.

Ángela Peralta

Located in the heart of Centro near the Ignacio Ramirez Cultural Center stands the Ángela Peralta Theater, one of the cultural icons of San Miguel.

Peralta, one of the greatest operatic singers in Mexican history, made her debut at just 15 years old in Mexico City before relocating to study in Italy under the bank of a wealthy financier. She made 32 curtain calls in Europe and North Africa, where she was dubbed the “Mexican Nightingale,” before returning to perform in Mexico at the invitation of Maximilian.

After another stint in Europe, Peralta returned to Mexico City, but was involved with an affair with a local entrepreneur, causing many in the city to boycott her performances. She left the city and recovered her reputation before embarking on a tour of northern Mexico. The tour was a success, but on an elaborate visit to Mazatlán, Peralta — along with most of her troupe — contacted yellow fever. Perlata died on Aug. 30, 1883 at the age of 38.

On top of her singing, Peralta was a composer, pianist and harpist. Amphitheaters and theaters across the country are named after her in tribute.

Pedro Vargas

Pedro Vargas, an actor and singer born in San Miguel de Allende, was one of the key figures of the golden age of Mexican cinema from 1936-1956. His former home and his statue sits on the street Salida Real a Querétaro. The house is now a luxury estate, next to the popular lookout of the Parroquia.

Vargas, nicknamed “The Nightingale of the Americas,” left San Miguel at just 14 years old for Mexico City, where he studied at the National Conservatory of Music. Although his career began in the opera, he transitioned into popular song and appeared in over 70 films, eventually performing for U.S. President Franklin D. Roosevelt at the White House in 1942. Vargas also performed extensively throughout Mexico and at major venues in the United States, including Carnegie Hall and Madison Square Garden.

Throughout his career, Vargas performed lyrical pieces, boleros and ranchera ballads written by some of Mexico’s most celebrated composers, including Agustín Lara. Vargas died in 1989 at the age of 83 in Mexico City.

Jared Tucker is a summer intern at Mexico News Daily in San Miguel de Allende and a rising senior at the University of Washington in Seattle, where he is the sports editor for The Daily UW. He was previously a fellow at TheFulcrum.us, where he covered public participation in American democracy.

World.title: Feelings you can only experience in Mexican Spanish
World.content:
I was raised in a bicultural environment. Not because either of my parents was from abroad, but because I went to a bilingual school my entire life. Most of my teachers were either from the United States or the United Kingdom — so yes, growing up, I learned how to count pennies and quarters, as well as Mexican pesos.

However, I was often curious as to how to translate the use of usted, for example, which in English does not exist. At a very early age, I remember being unable to express in English some of the feelings I spoke about at home, which were inherently of a Mexican traditional upbringing. Culturally, there were literally no words that could transmit the warmth of an apapacho or the joy of cotorreo in English. As the editors probably know, I often misuse prepositions (I hope it brings them some relief to know I also experience this in Spanish).

Beyond my grammatical imperfections and translation confusions, here’s a handpicked guide to some of my favorite feelings you can only experience in Mexican Spanish — from an imperfect Mexican writer to an ever-supportive readership.

Cotorrear

Cotorrear comes from the word cotorro, meaning parakeets, which are widely known for being talkative and outspoken animals. Cotorrear, thus, implies a noisy conversation in which friends and family members talk over one another excitedly, about anything and everything, all at once.

People, however, do not cotorrean with their bosses or the police (that would be, to say the least, suspicious). You do so with your close inner circle, because although it is a leisurely talk, it’s usually not just small talk. People cotorrean about their issues, about politics and about how their car landed again at the mechanic.

Apapachar

As happens with most Mexicanisms, apapachar comes from Náhuatl, the official language of the Mexica Empire. It translates as people allowing others to care for them with tender displays of affection, such as Grandma’s hug, a nice, warm soup made by Mom, or even just going to a dear friend’s house to talk about a recent loss. “Ser apapachada, apapachado” implies allowing oneself to be vulnerable to a loved one, especially when you’re feeling ill or down emotionally.

Chacharear

Chacharar is just fun. It’s what you do when you’re on vacation and land in the Pueblo Mágico’s wondrous mercado de artesanías, or go on a Sunday stroll to La Lagunilla market. The word comes from cháchara: “something small, unimportant and of little value,” as defined by the Dictionary of Mexican Spanish. I think the best translation is simply “a trinket.”

Chacharear, however, is not like window shopping. You actually get to feel and touch the trinkets in the market, and even get to discuss a lower price with your vendor (oh, the glorious thrill of regateo!). Also, when you’re chachareando, it doesn’t mean you will actually buy any of the things that caught your eye! Actually, you probably won’t — you just do it for the joy of contemplating useless things you don’t need, but you somehow find interesting or amusing.

Achicopalarse

You know when someone is so sad, they actually round their back in a crestfallen way? They’re probably achicopalada, achicopalado. The term comes, again, from Náhuatl achikopa, which has been translated as “feeling inferior.” However, in contemporary Mexican Spanish, the term is used as simply “feeling down.”

You’ll probably feel achicopalada when your boyfriend just dumped you, or when you failed the test you studied so hard for. Or even when your parents unfairly grounded you. People can even feel achicopalados when the sky is heavy with dark clouds, or the weather isn’t that nice, too.

Desconchinflarse

When the blender breaks down, the air conditioner doesn’t work, or the TV screen refuses to turn on, that’s when you know your appliances are desconchinfladas. And it’s sad. Because they’re not beyond repair, they’re simply waiting for you to take them to the shop to be fixed — and maybe you’re just too busy (or lazy) to go.

However, desconchinflarse does not only apply to hardware. Whenever you hurt your leg or possibly strain an ankle, you can also say your foot is desconchinflado. You don’t get to go to the hardware store to repair one of those, though (please, go see a doctor).

Petatearse

Petatearse is possibly the only feeling in Mexican Spanish that every person on planet Earth (and beyond) will eventually face. It comes from the Náhuatl word petate, a rug, and it translates literally as dying. When people in the ancient Mexica Empire died, they were wrapped in a handmade ritual mat before their funeral ceremonies. So whenever you hear someone “se petateó,” it literally means they passed.

However, you would never hear anyone say their grandmother “se petateó.” That would just be disrespectful and rude. Petatearse is a verb people use as slang when referring to someone they don’t know in a mischievous Mexican way. So no, if you receive the news of a dear friend who just lost a family member, do not say “se petatearon.” Please. Ever.

Andrea Fischer contributes to the features desk at Mexico News Daily. She has edited and written for National Geographic en Español and Muy Interesante México, and continues to be an advocate for anything that screams science. Or yoga. Or both.

World.title: El Jalapeño: ‘El Mayo’ urges Mexican kids not to do all the things he did for 68 years
World.content:
All stories in El Jalapeño are satire and not real news. Check out the original article here.

Following a federal courtroom speech in which he urged young people to avoid his life path, former Sinaloa Cartel leader Ismael “El Mayo” Zambada announced Thursday the launch of a new youth mentorship initiative aimed at breaking down, in meticulous detail, the exact operational blueprint that allowed him to evade law enforcement for nearly seven decades.

Titled “Don’t Do What I Did: A 68-Year Step-by-Step Case Study,” the initiative is designed to steer teenagers away from organized crime by offering an exhaustive, multi-volume curriculum detailing logistics, supply chain management, high-level corruption strategies and long-term asset diversification, so that young attendees know precisely which sophisticated mechanisms to avoid.

“Violence only leads to two places: prison or death,” Zambada said in a statement released through his legal team, emphasizing that his life serves as a stark warning. “To ensure our youth do not make the same mistakes, my curriculum will thoroughly examine how to build a transnational logistics network across four continents without using a cell phone until approximately 2018. It is vital that kids understand the terrifying burden of managing thousands of decentralized distribution nodes, so they never feel tempted to attempt it themselves.”

Organizers confirmed the seminar series will feature interactive workshops where participants are shown maps of remote airstrips and hidden mountain labs, accompanied by stern lectures on why establishing such complex infrastructure represents a tragic waste of potential. Attendees will also receive a 400-page workbook outlining the specific, highly effective techniques used to maintain regional monopolies, accompanied by large red text reading “DO NOT ATTEMPT” across every page.

Policy analysts have noted the uniquely thorough approach of the cautionary campaign, which treats 68 years of criminal supremacy not as a heroic narrative, but as an overwhelming administrative nightmare that no teenager should ever want to inherit.

“It is a powerful message,” said Dr. Fernando Reyes, a senior researcher in public safety policy. “By spending eight hours a day explaining the exact mechanics of money laundering through agricultural front companies and international trade finance, Zambada is sending a clear signal: running an illicit global conglomerate involves far too much paperwork, supply chain volatility and court-mandated restitution to ever be considered a viable career path.”

At press time, federal officials confirmed that while the curriculum’s moral message was universally praised, the accompanying 12-disc masterclass video set had already been flagged for containing far too many practical tips on customs evasion.

World.title: Mexico intercepts a trafficking scheme smuggling native ants to SE Asia
World.content:
Mexican authorities have intercepted Amazon parrots, peacock turtles, howler monkeys and even baby crocodiles in recent years, but the country’s latest case of illegal wildlife trafficking centers on a far smaller animal: queen ants.

Earlier this month, environmental officials in the west-central state of Jalisco seized 105 queen ants hidden inside plastic toys and labeled as “collectible figures” in a shipment bound for Southeast Asia, the Federal Attorney for Environmental Protection (Profepa) said.

The discovery was made July 9 after a parcel company flagged a suspicious package in El Salto, Jalisco, outside Guadalajara. The package was addressed to Laos, a landlocked country between Vietnam and Thailand.

Inside, inspectors found the insects sealed in individual test tubes and concealed within toy figures, including one containing 22 tubes and another with 83. Each small tube appeared to contain cotton and moisture, the standard way to house queen ants in test tubes.

Experts determined that it was not feasible to keep so many ants alive in that manner because of their biological needs.

According to a Profepa press release, 87 ants survived and were later released into the Cerro Viejo Protected Natural Area, while 18 died.

The seized ants belong to the genus Pogonomyrmex and are commonly known as harvester ants. They are native to Mexico and play a role in seed dispersal and soil health in arid ecosystems.

The seized ants fit into a growing niche hobby in Europe and Asia, where buyers use queen ants to stock formicariums, specialized terrariums that house and display ant colonies. Owners watch the ants build tunnels, haul seeds and care for larvae.

The ant farms are promoted as do-it-yourself ecosystems built around a single fertilized queen, which can eventually produce thousands of workers.

Collectors and hobbyists sometimes pay 200 to 400 pesos (US $11 to $22) for a queen ant online, while more exotic ants can fetch up to 1,200 pesos (US $68), according to the newspaper El Sol de México.

Illegal wildlife trafficking remains a major issue in Mexico. Authorities have seized hundreds of turtles on highways and at airports, along with parrots, reptiles and other species trafficked through parcel services and border crossings.

The numbers especially surged during the coronavirus pandemic, according to Profepa.

Globally, illegal wildlife trafficking affects more than 4,000 plant and animal species in at least 162 countries and territories, according to the United Nations Office on Drugs and Crime. Some assessments have valued the illegal wildlife trade at up to US $23 billion a year.

Despite the enforcement action in Jalisco, no arrests have been reported so far.

“Profepa will follow up on the corresponding administrative procedure,” the agency stated, adding that it will continue to fight illegal wildlife trafficking through surveillance and other means.

With reports from El Sol de México and Milenio

World.title: Oaxaca journalist, known for criticizing governor, shot dead; Feds takes over the case
World.content:
Journalist Francisco Alejandro Leyva was shot and killed Wednesday in San Pablo Etla, a suburb of Oaxaca city, the second media figure slain in Mexico in less than a week.

Leyva, a former executive producer of the Oaxacan Radio and Television Corporation, was attacked while eating breakfast at a street food stand. The gunmen escaped on a motorcycle.

The 60-year-old was well-known for his column “El zumbido de moscardón” (“The buzzing of a bumblebee”), in which he critically analyzed political life and corruption in the state of Oaxaca.

Hours after his murder, state prosecutors said video intelligence had already been uncovered from local CCTV. On Thursday, the Federal Attorney General’s Office said it would take over the investigation at the request of Oaxaca authorities, assigning it to the Specialized Prosecutor’s Office for Human Rights.

As of noon Thursday, authorities had not cited a motive for the murder nor reported any arrests.

Leyva published his final article on Tuesday night, addressing insecurity in the state and the alleged interference of organized crime in local economies and politics.

In this text, he discussed the violence in Oaxaca in the context of the Guelaguetza, calling the annual Indigenous cultural festival a failure due to government mismanagement and security issues.

Just over a year ago, Leyva filed a formal complaint with the state Human Rights Ombudsman’s Office about receiving death threats. He linked these threats to the public smear campaign he faced from regular criticism lobbed at him by Oaxaca Governor Salomón Jara during the latter’s daily press conferences.

For his part, Governor Jara condemned Wednesday’s attack, saying “[Leyva] was a journalist critical of our government (…) but no difference with the practice of journalism can ever justify an act of violence.”

International press associations also condemned the murder. Reporters without Borders said “The murder of seven journalists in just over six months is evidence of a serious and sustained failure of the Mexican state,” while calling on the federal government to present “a national emergency plan.”

📣 ARTICLE 19 condena el asesinato del periodista Alejandro Leyva Aguilar, exdirector de la Corporación Oaxaqueña de Radio y Televisión (CORTV), autor de la columna El Zumbido del Moscardón, ocurrido esta mañana, en el municipio de San Pablo Etlan, #OaxacaDeJuárez 🧵 pic.twitter.com/Z3gDePuLTY — ARTICLE 19 México y Centroamérica (@article19mxca) July 22, 2026

More than half a dozen journalists have been killed in Mexico this year, five of them since June 11. Josué Martínez, executive producer of Noticias San Martín Texmelucan, was gunned down in the state of Puebla on July 16.

Reuters news agency described Mexico as “one of the ​most dangerous countries in the world for journalists outside active war zones,” adding that “the vast majority of crimes against journalists go unpunished.”

With reports from El País, El Universal, Latinus, Aristegui Noticias and Milenio

World.title: Conservation advocates celebrate a ‘Night of the Bats’ in Oaxaca
World.content:
On June 20, as Pride parades filled the streets, the team at Proyecto LAM was preparing for their annual “Noche de los Murciélagos” (“Night of the Bats”).

Proyecto LAM is a vibrant plant nursery in Santa Catarina Minas, Oaxaca, founded in 2018 by Graciela Ángeles and her family, who produce Real Minero. Graciela explains that originally, the project focused on studying the agave plant; then “as a side effect, the need arose to study its pollinators, especially the bats.”

View this post on Instagram A post shared by Real Minero (@realminerooficial)

Guests are invited for a sunset walk through the garden before a series of presentations, dinner and mezcal.

The underrated importance of bats

Each year, they invite specialists to speak on the garden’s themes: its plants, pests and pollinators. This year, Irene Martínez Velasco spoke about the genetics of agave before Rosario Aceves Íñiguez, a biologist from Guadalajara, led an introduction to bats. She discussed the ecological significance and diversity of bats before emphasizing some of the challenges faced by bat populations.

Rosario says she considers bats to be one of the most misunderstood groups of mammals, “despite also being among the most fascinating, interesting and wonderful.”

Bats play a fundamental ecological role in the maintenance and functioning of ecosystems, yet they remain one of the most undervalued groups of mammals. In Mexico, where agave plays an iconic role, bats are invaluable. Nectar-feeding bats and agaves share a close ecological relationship where bats act as primary pollinators. Preserving this bond is vital for agave biodiversity and the survival of endangered bat species.

Bats’ role in agave propagation

Graciela says that “declines in bat populations threaten the survival of the agaves, particularly those propagated solely through seeds.” Agave spirits producers can support bat populations by allowing a percentage of agaves to flower and go to seed to support nectar-feeding bats. “Bat Friendly” is a certification that promotes conservation and encourages consumer participation in tequila and mezcal, while initiatives such as the one noted above encourage the producers of these liquors to adopt sustainable practices.

However, fear surrounding bats follows this unfairly maligned mammal. Myths of blood-sucking vampires and perceptions like dirty “flying rats” plague bats and those trying to help them. Ongoing stigma and their nocturnal behaviors make bats difficult to study.

Studying bats also has significant challenges. Rosario explains that “national insecurity and forced disappearances hinder field research.” She says fieldwork using capture methods has become more complicated because work is done at night, which implies greater risk. “There has been a shift towards other techniques that do not require capture, but in projects where it is possible to record or work with bats, many studies and research projects require having the specimens in hand.”

Habitat loss and other challenges for bat populations

A major concern is habitat loss. Rosario described how this reduces the number of places where bats can roost and limits food sources. Monocrops, like the agave plants used for tequila, with significant levels of pesticides, are also hurting bat populations.

Disease is also having a significant impact, in particular “white-nose syndrome,” a fungal disease that primarily affects cave-dwelling bats. According to Rosario, “over the last decade, this has led to the deaths of millions of individuals in various regions of the world.” In Oaxaca alone, it is suspected of causing a drastic decline in bat populations.

Rosario’s concerns about bat populations were echoed by Graciela. She informed the group that over the past three years, the number of bats they have found during these activities has plummeted. “During the first capture in 2018, there were several hundred bats. Last year, we only managed to capture three bats. This year, 15 were captured.”

Fortunately, there are endeavors to conserve bat populations. Conservation efforts prioritize what Graciela describes as “citizen science,” which involves making scientific data accessible to the public and facilitating knowledge sharing between farmers, producers and academics. Events like the “Noche de los Murciélagos” bring the public closer to science through workshops, talks and bat-monitoring demonstrations. These efforts help to foster awareness of the bat-agave connection.

Teaching kids (and adults) about the beauty of bats

This year, they held a contest with students from the middle school in Santa Catarina Minas to make artwork about bats. They awarded certificates and sketchbooks to the winners. For Graciela, this is a way to “influence these young people to develop their creative skills, whether through writing or drawing, and at the same time bring them into a scientific activity.” She says, “I think one of the most important things is that this year we had so many children visit. It’s something beautiful that young people are interested in science.”

Rosario says that the public can contribute by “learning about the ecological importance of bats, avoiding the destruction of their roosts, promoting their conservation and supporting initiatives and products that encourage practices friendly to these species.”

During the evening, Rosario and the team from Proyecto LAM used techniques like “mist-netting” to capture and identify species. They recorded data on the bat’s weight, sex and size, which helps document the health and presence of local populations over time. It was fascinating to watch them at work.

‘Intrepid pollinators’ released into the night

Once they had made their assessments, the bats were fed some sugar water before being released back into the wild. Rosario held each bat, and there was a brief pause before they took off into the night. It was surprisingly moving to see these fragile animals spread their wings as they realized they were free again.

Hopefully, events like “Noche de los Murciélagos” will continue to inspire people to learn about bats. Not as stigmatized creatures of the night, but as the intrepid pollinators that help maintain our diverse and beautiful ecosystem. As Graciela warns, without bats, we won’t have agave — or mezcal!

World.title: Inter&Co Stadium Orlando in $55 Million Naming Deal
World.content:
Brazilian Fintech Goes Global

Key Facts —The Rebrand. Banco Inter now operates globally as Inter&Co, with a new logo reflecting seven business verticals. —The Stadium. Orlando’s 25,000-seat soccer venue is now Inter&Co Stadium under a 10-year deal. —The Price Tag. The naming-rights agreement is valued at over $55 million (roughly R$275 million). —The First. Inter&Co is the first Latin American-rooted financial institution to name a major U.S. stadium. —The Audience. The group serves over 30 million clients across Brazil and the United States.

Brazilian digital bank Inter&Co has completed a sweeping global rebrand and secured the naming rights to Orlando’s major soccer stadium, planting its flag firmly in the U.S. market.

From Banco Inter to a Global Super App

The institution Brazilians knew as Banco Inter has formally stepped onto the world stage as Inter&Co. The holding company, listed on Nasdaq, launched a new visual identity in December 2023 that it describes as a reflection of its evolution into a global financial super app.

The refreshed logo features a symbol with seven distinct elements. Each element represents one of the group’s core verticals: banking, shopping, investments, credit, insurance, global services, and loyalty.

The rebrand is not cosmetic. It signals a structural shift that began in 2022, when the group reorganised under the Inter&Co umbrella to accommodate its growing U.S. operations, including the cross-border payments platform USEND.

Inter&Co Stadium Orlando Becomes a Reality

The centrepiece of this international push is a long-term naming-rights agreement for the 25,000-seat downtown Orlando stadium. The venue, home to Orlando City SC of Major League Soccer and the Orlando Pride of the National Women’s Soccer League, is now officially called Inter&Co Stadium.

The deal, announced in January 2024, spans ten years and is valued at over $55 million. It marks the first time a financial institution with Latin American roots has held the naming rights to a major stadium in the United States.

The stadium, which opened in 2017, was previously known as Exploria Stadium. The rebranding places the Inter&Co name in front of a large, engaged American sports audience week after week.

A Calculated Bet on U.S. Brand Awareness

The Orlando deal is not a standalone marketing stunt. It is the logical next step in a sports-sponsorship strategy Inter&Co has already tested extensively in its home market.

In Brazil, the group has partnerships with clubs including Athletico Paranaense, Fortaleza, and Atlético Mineiro, where it holds naming rights to the MRV Arena. The Orlando move extends that playbook to a strategic U.S. market.

The company first became the official financial institution of Orlando City and Orlando Pride in September 2023. Escalating that relationship to full stadium naming rights shows a clear commitment to building brand equity among American consumers.

What the Inter&Co Stadium Deal Means for Investors

For investors watching Latin American fintech, the Orlando stadium deal is a tangible signal of international ambition. Inter&Co is not content to be a dominant digital bank in Brazil; it wants to be a recognised brand in the world’s largest consumer market.

The Nasdaq listing already gave the group access to global capital. The stadium naming rights give it something harder to buy: everyday visibility among a qualified U.S. audience in a fast-growing Florida market.

The $55 million price tag, spread over a decade, represents a manageable marketing expense for a group serving over 30 million clients. The real test will be whether that visibility translates into customer acquisition for its U.S. products.

The Broader Latin America Read-Through

Inter&Co’s move fits a broader pattern of Latin American companies seeking growth beyond their home markets. Brazil’s large consumer base has produced several fintech champions, but domestic competition is fierce.

Expanding into the United States offers a path to diversify revenue and build a moat against rivals at home. The stadium deal gives Inter&Co a physical, high-profile anchor for that expansion.

For expats and internationally minded professionals, the rebrand also simplifies the story. The Inter&Co name now unifies what were once separate domestic and international operations under a single, modern identity.

What to Watch Next

The stadium deal runs for a decade, so the brand presence in Orlando is locked in. The key metric to track will be user growth for Inter&Co’s U.S. products, particularly USEND, its cross-border payments platform.

Any further sports or entertainment partnerships in the United States would confirm that the Orlando deal is a template, not a one-off. For now, Inter&Co has achieved something no other Latin American financial group has managed: putting its name on a major American stadium.

Frequently Asked Questions

What is Inter&Co Stadium in Orlando?

Inter&Co Stadium is the new name for the 25,000-seat downtown Orlando soccer venue that hosts Orlando City SC and Orlando Pride matches. The name comes from a ten-year, $55 million naming-rights deal with Brazilian financial group Inter&Co, the first Latin American-rooted bank to name a major U.S. stadium.

Why did Banco Inter rebrand to Inter&Co?

Banco Inter rebranded to Inter&Co as part of a global strategy to unify its Brazilian digital bank, U.S. operations, and multiple service verticals under one identity. The new brand, launched alongside a Nasdaq listing, reflects the group’s ambition to be a cross-border financial super app serving over 30 million clients.

How much did the Inter&Co Stadium naming-rights deal cost?

The naming-rights agreement for Inter&Co Stadium is a ten-year deal valued at over $55 million, equivalent to roughly R$275 million at current exchange rates. The deal covers the home stadium of Orlando City SC and Orlando Pride in downtown Orlando, Florida.

World.title: Argentina’s Aerolíneas Orders 20 Jets in Self-Funded Renewal
World.content:
Argentina Aviation

Key Facts —The order. Aerolíneas Argentinas will incorporate 20 new-generation aircraft between 2027 and 2031. —The mix. The plan includes 6 Airbus A330neo, 8 Boeing 737 MAX 10, and 6 Boeing 737 MAX 8 jets. —The financing. The entire programme is funded from the airline’s own operating surpluses, without government subsidies. —The structure. Aircraft will arrive via operating leases with lessors including Avolon and Aviation Capital Group. —The scale. The renewal covers roughly 25% of the total fleet and replaces about 60% of long-haul aircraft.

Aerolíneas Argentinas has unveiled its largest fleet renewal in a decade, ordering 20 Airbus and Boeing jets and financing the entire programme from its own operations for the first time since re-nationalisation.

A historic shift away from state dependence

Argentina’s flag carrier will take delivery of the 20 aircraft between 2027 and 2031. The airline confirmed the plan is backed entirely by operating surpluses and audited positive results, not by transfers from the national treasury.

This marks a structural break with the carrier’s post-renationalisation history. For years Aerolíneas relied on state subsidies to cover operational gaps and fleet investments, making this self-funded programme a significant financial milestone.

For a foreign reader, it helps to understand that Argentina re-nationalised the airline in 2008, bringing it back under full state control. In the years that followed, the carrier consistently required injections of public money to keep flying and to renew ageing aircraft.

Breaking that pattern is therefore about more than just balance-sheet arithmetic. It suggests that internal restructuring efforts are producing genuine, measurable change in how the company operates day to day.

Inside the Aerolíneas Argentinas fleet renewal: the aircraft mix

The order splits across three types. Six Airbus A330-900neo aircraft will serve long-haul routes, replacing older wide-body jets with more fuel-efficient models featuring new cabins and a three-class layout.

For domestic and regional operations, the airline selected eight high-density Boeing 737 MAX 10 jets and six smaller 737 MAX 8 aircraft. Together the new planes will renew about a quarter of the total fleet and roughly 60% of the long-haul segment.

In plain terms, the A330neo is a wide-body, twin-aisle aircraft built for flights of eight hours or more, such as Buenos Aires to Madrid or Miami. The “neo” stands for “new engine option,” which delivers a substantial reduction in fuel burn compared to the previous generation.

The 737 MAX family, meanwhile, is Boeing’s latest narrow-body workhorse, designed for shorter routes with lower per-seat costs. The MAX 10 is the largest variant of that family, seating more passengers, while the MAX 8 is a mid-size model suited to thinner domestic and regional corridors.

How the deal is structured and financed

The aircraft will arrive through operating lease agreements rather than outright purchases. Avolon will supply the A330neo jets, while Aviation Capital Group is providing part of the 737 MAX 10 fleet.

Contracts for 14 of the 20 aircraft were formally signed at the Farnborough Airshow in the United Kingdom. The remaining six MAX 8 and some MAX 10 units are still in the final contracting phase, though the full programme is confirmed as self-financed.

An operating lease works much like a long-term rental: the airline pays a monthly fee to use the aircraft for a set number of years, but the asset itself stays on the lessor’s books. This approach keeps upfront capital costs low and transfers the residual-value risk to the leasing company.

Avolon and Aviation Capital Group are two of the world’s largest aircraft lessors, and their willingness to place new-technology jets with Aerolíneas is itself a signal of confidence in the carrier’s credit profile.

Delivery timeline stretches to 2031

The first aircraft to arrive will be a Boeing 737 MAX 8, expected in the first quarter of 2027. Airbus A330neo deliveries begin in the first half of 2028 and continue through 2029 and 2030.

The largest delivery wave is concentrated around 2030, when multiple A330neo and 737 MAX 10 aircraft are scheduled to arrive. The final MAX 8 units will complete the programme around 2031.

A timeline this long is normal for new-generation aircraft orders. Global backlogs at both Airbus and Boeing mean that airlines placing firm orders today often wait several years for delivery slots.

The staggered arrival also gives Aerolíneas time to train crews, adjust maintenance programmes, and phase out older jets without disrupting its schedule.

What the Aerolíneas Argentinas fleet renewal means for investors and the region

For investors watching Argentina’s state-owned enterprises, the self-funded structure is the headline. It signals that operational restructuring is generating real cash flow, reducing contingent liabilities on the sovereign balance sheet.

The airline expects the new aircraft to cut unit costs, measured by cost per available seat kilometre, and increase total seat capacity by about 10%. Improved long-haul economics could strengthen Buenos Aires as a connecting hub for South American traffic.

For expats and frequent travellers, the renewal promises upgraded cabins, Wi-Fi connectivity, and a more consistent product across the network. The A330neo’s three-class configuration also suggests a renewed push for premium long-haul revenue.

Cost per available seat kilometre, or CASK, is the industry’s standard yardstick for efficiency. It simply divides total operating cost by the number of seats flown one kilometre.

A lower CASK means the airline can either price tickets more competitively or improve margins on existing fares. The projected 10% capacity increase, meanwhile, matters because it implies the new jets will not just replace old metal but also allow the airline to grow where demand supports it.

From an 18-jet plan to a 20-jet programme

The current announcement builds on an earlier self-funded plan for 18 aircraft with deliveries concentrated between 2026 and 2029. That earlier blueprint included four A330neo and fourteen 737 MAX variants.

The expanded 20-aircraft programme extends the timeline to 2031 and adds two more A330neo jets while adjusting the narrow-body mix. The core principle remains unchanged: no government money, no Treasury guarantees, just operating leases backed by the airline’s own results.

What to watch next is whether the airline can sustain the operating surpluses that underpin this plan through an Argentine economic cycle that has historically been volatile. Another open question is how the arrival of more fuel-efficient long-haul jets will affect route decisions, particularly whether Aerolíneas will open new destinations or deepen frequencies on existing trunk routes to Europe and North America.

Finally, the leasing structure raises a practical question: if market conditions shift, how much flexibility do the lease terms provide to adjust delivery pace without incurring penalties?

Frequently Asked Questions

Is the Argentine government paying for the new Aerolíneas Argentinas aircraft?

No. The airline has stated repeatedly that the entire 20-jet programme is financed from its own operating surpluses and audited positive results.

No transfers or subsidies from the Argentine government are being used, which represents a first for the carrier since it was re-nationalised.

When will the first new Aerolíneas Argentinas aircraft enter service?

The first delivery is a Boeing 737 MAX 8 scheduled for the first quarter of 2027. The Airbus A330neo jets will begin arriving in the first half of 2028, with deliveries continuing through 2031.

How much of the Aerolíneas Argentinas fleet is being replaced?

The 20 new aircraft will renew approximately 25% of the airline’s total fleet. On the long-haul side, the six A330neo jets will replace roughly 60% of the existing wide-body capacity, significantly modernising the carrier’s international product.
