Zaal Andronikashvili: “It is important to find the right name for what is happening in Georgia. The situation is new, and historical parallels apply only in part.

Since at least 2019, during the ‘Gavrilov Night’ protests, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have done everything possible to prevent a peaceful transfer of power. Some scholars describe this as a ‘coup from above’.”

This “coup from above” is not peaceful.

Anyone who believes that Georgia is at peace today is deeply mistaken. Beyond dragging Georgia into a geopolitical confrontation on Russia’s side — at an enormous cost to the country — Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are waging an asymmetric, hybrid civil war against the overwhelming majority of the Georgian population.

Part of this hybrid civil war consists of unlawful restrictive legislation enforced only against certain groups of citizens and against civil society as a whole.

There is also financial repression aimed at depriving opponents of the regime of their livelihoods, as well as the deliberate destruction of education and culture. Alongside this come aggression, hopelessness, and an absence of love and empathy elevated to the level of state policy.

There is micro-level violence — encouraging crime and fostering a culture of impunity that ultimately erodes trust in the law, the justice system, and the very idea of justice. There is macro-level violence carried out by the police and special forces, along with many other elements.

“I repeat: this is not peace.

It is a hybrid civil war waged by a regime that controls the police, the legislature and the country’s financial resources against the majority of Georgia’s population, especially its most active citizens. Its goal is to suppress, subjugate and ultimately enslave them.

The other side has nothing but the truth and peaceful resistance. But the truth is a powerful, almost invincible weapon — and it can never truly be defeated.

Despite this asymmetric civil war, whose domestic objective is to cement the regime permanently in power and make the current government irreplaceable, while its foreign policy goal is to sever Georgia once and for all from the European values-based community and turn it into a banana republic under a quasi-colonial regime, Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party have failed to win this unequal conflict.

Peaceful resistance is alive. The people have not been broken. They have not been intimidated.

Those who support the regime today, or choose silent complicity, should look at Russia.

People there also believed that if they kept quiet and buried their heads in a bowl of caviar, none of it would affect them. Other people’s children would die, someone else would go to prison, someone else’s life would be ruined. Perhaps someone would stop greeting them, but they could live with that.

In reality, supporting injustice always comes at a price. Injustice and lawlessness may begin by targeting only selected groups, but they very quickly spread to everyone.

By supporting injustice, you create an environment in which that injustice will inevitably reach you in one form or another.

But people are willing to ignore it until it affects them personally. There is a powerful metaphor in the Gospel of Matthew (26:52): ‘All who draw the sword will die by the sword.’ This is not really about the sword itself, but more broadly about the laws of social reality and their universal nature.

There is no peace in Georgia. Bidzina Ivanishvili and the Georgian Dream party are responsible for that.”

Opinion on the latest events in Georgia

World.title: Russia’s state Duma passes law targeting citizens abroad, restricting property rights and passport renewals
World.content:
Russia Passes Law Targeting Citizens Who Left the Country

Russian Embassy in Lisbon, Portugal. Photo: Antonio Pedro Santos / EPA

On July 22, Russia’s State Duma approved, in its second and third readings, a bill introducing what it calls “temporary restrictive measures.” The legislation targets people living outside Russia who are deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties.

The restrictions will apply to anyone convicted under any article of Russia’s Criminal Code. They will also affect people facing a range of administrative charges — many of them based on provisions that Russian authorities have increasingly used to prosecute political opponents and dissenters.

The law will take effect once it is officially published.

This article is based on reporting by Novaya Gazeta Europe.

What restrictions would the law introduce?

Authorities would be able to impose the following measures on people entered into the special registry:

freeze bank accounts and other assets;

block access to banking apps and online accounts;

redirect a person’s income into a special ruble-denominated account;

prohibit the sale of real estate and vehicles;

block the registration of property and automobiles;

suspend licenses, permits and accreditations;

bar individuals from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers;

restrict driving privileges;

deny access to government and consular services;

prohibit notarial services and transactions carried out through a power of attorney.

Before the vote, State Duma Speaker Vyacheslav Volodin said that Russians living abroad should be thinking about how to appear before a court.

“We are talking about people who are harming our country — extremists, traitors to our homeland. People who have spent years trying to do everything possible to destroy our state,” Volodin said.

How the registry will work

The government will create a state registry of people who are outside Russia and deemed to be evading criminal or administrative penalties. The registry will be maintained by the Justice Ministry, which already administers the country’s lists of “foreign agents” and “extremists.”

Information will be supplied to the Justice Ministry by the Interior Ministry, the Federal Security Service (FSB), the Prosecutor General’s Office, the Federal Bailiff Service and other government agencies.

To be entered into the registry, a person must meet three criteria:

have a criminal conviction or administrative penalty that has entered into legal force;

be officially deemed to be “evading” enforcement of that sentence or penalty;

be outside Russia.

The law, however, does not specify how authorities will determine whether someone is “evading” enforcement.

An interagency commission will be established to coordinate information sharing between the Justice Ministry and law enforcement bodies. It will also decide whether to impose the restrictions.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov said he expects the registry to expand regularly, much like Russia’s list of “foreign agents.”

“I believe the mechanism will closely resemble the weekly expansion of the ‘foreign agents’ register. It will become a show of intimidation through the constant addition of new names,” he told Novaya Gazeta Europe.

Who could be affected?

Formally, the law applies to anyone outside Russia who has been convicted of a crime or an administrative offense and is deemed to be evading enforcement of the resulting sentence or penalty. The specific article under which a person was convicted does not matter.

In practice, however, those most at risk are people prosecuted for political reasons. According to lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov, this primarily includes journalists, politicians, human rights defenders and civic activists.

The law also applies to people facing administrative charges under six specific provisions:

failure to comply with Russia’s “foreign agents” law;

violations of regulations governing the activities of a “foreign agent”;

calls to violate Russia’s territorial integrity;

“discrediting” the Russian Armed Forces;

calls for sanctions against Russia;

participation in the activities of an “undesirable organization.”

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova said the legislation is primarily intended to intimidate Russians living abroad. Since the state cannot physically detain them, she argued, it is instead restricting their civil and property rights.

In her view, the authorities also aim to silence opponents of the war and spread fear among Russians who have left the country.

What happens to a person’s money and property?

The law allows authorities to freeze a person’s funds and other assets. Formally, this does not amount to confiscation, since ownership does not transfer to the state. In practice, however, it would make it much more difficult for people to manage or dispose of their property.

All payments, including pensions, would be redirected to a special ruble-denominated account. The rules governing access to and use of those funds will be determined later by the Central Bank of Russia. Court costs and other financial penalties could also be deducted directly from the same account.

People included in the registry would be barred from selling real estate or vehicles. They would also be unable to register ownership of newly acquired property or register a vehicle.

In addition, banks would block their access to mobile banking apps and online accounts, making routine bank transfers impossible. Banks would also be allowed to deny them loans and other forms of credit.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina described the measures as a tool of financial pressure.

“It creates a paradoxical situation. A person is deprived of access to the very financial tools needed to fulfill the obligations that led to their inclusion in the registry,” she said.

Restrictions on business and employment

People included in the registry would be barred from registering as sole proprietors or self-employed workers.

If their profession requires a license, authorities would refuse to issue a new one. Existing licenses could also be suspended until the individual is removed from the registry.

The government would also be able to suspend permits and accreditations that have already been granted.

Driver’s licenses would not be revoked outright. However, the right to drive would be suspended until the person is removed from the registry.

Ban on powers of attorney and access to government services

People included in the registry would no longer be able to use an enhanced qualified electronic signature. Existing certificates could be revoked, and new ones would not be issued.

They would also lose access to Russia’s Gosuslugi online government services portal, making it impossible to submit applications, process official documents, or access federal and regional public services online.

Before carrying out any notarial act, Russian notaries would be required to check the registry. If a person’s name appears on the list, the notary would be obligated to refuse service.

The law would also prohibit anyone from carrying out transactions on behalf of a listed individual under a power of attorney. In practice, this would deprive Russians living abroad of one of the main ways to manage their property and handle legal matters in Russia remotely.

Which consular services would be denied?

One of the law’s most significant restrictions concerns Russian consulates abroad. People included in the registry would lose access to nearly all consular services.

They would no longer be able to:

obtain a new international passport;

notarize a power of attorney;

certify copies of documents or authenticate signatures;

obtain notarized consent required for legal transactions;

register a marriage or a legal name change through a consulate;

receive consular assistance if detained abroad;

rely on Russia for emergency consular assistance while overseas.

Lawyer Valeria Vetoshkina said the most consequential provisions are the ban on representation through a power of attorney and the restrictions on consular services. Those are the mechanisms that allow Russians living abroad to handle most legal matters remotely.

At present, even people held administratively liable can still obtain a new international passport through a Russian consulate. Those charged with or convicted of criminal offenses also retain access to some consular services.

Once the law takes effect, however, obtaining official documents without returning to Russia will become significantly more difficult.

Lawyer Yevgeny Smirnov described the initiative as a form of de facto deprivation of citizenship.

“Citizenship technically remains, but a person is no longer able to exercise the rights that come with being a citizen,” he said.

Lawyer Anastasia Burakova agreed with that assessment. In her view, the law would leave affected individuals in a situation approaching statelessness, as the Russian state would effectively cease providing them with documentation and legal assistance.

What is the “humanitarian allowance”?

The law provides for what it calls a humanitarian allowance. The payment may be granted if a person included in the registry has close relatives who are financially dependent on them.

Eligible relatives include parents, a spouse, or children who have no independent source of income. The allowance would be paid monthly using the person’s own frozen funds.

The decision to grant the payment would be made by the interagency commission, while the amount would be set by the Russian government in coordination with the Central Bank.

When would the restrictions take effect?

The restrictions would come into force the day after a person’s name is added to the registry.

In theory, a person could be removed from the registry in several circumstances:

if a court overturns or revises the underlying decision;

if the person begins serving their sentence or complies with the penalty;

if the person returns to Russia;

if the person dies.

If the Justice Ministry fails to remove someone from the registry without justification, that person may file a request for review. The ministry must issue a decision within 20 working days, and its refusal can be challenged in court.

In practice, however, not all penalties can be served remotely. For example, a prison sentence cannot be served from abroad. As a result, anyone convicted and sentenced to imprisonment would have no realistic way to be removed from the registry without returning to Russia.

Administrative penalties present a different paradox. A person on the registry would face restrictions on banking services while also being barred from appointing a representative under a power of attorney. It therefore remains unclear how they would be able to pay an administrative fine and secure their removal from the registry.

What do lawyers recommend for those at risk?

The law will take effect once it is officially published. Lawyers advise people who could potentially be affected to resolve key property and documentation issues before it comes into force.

In particular, they recommend:

settling matters related to real estate and vehicles in Russia in advance;

obtaining notarized copies of Russian documents;

securing apostilles for school certificates, university diplomas, and civil status documents;

renewing international passports while they can still obtain long-validity documents;

withdrawing funds from Russian bank accounts and deposits;

obtaining apostilled certificates confirming the absence of a criminal record and their driving history.

Once a person is added to the registry, many of these steps would no longer be possible.

exchange

World.title: ‘Unsolved crimes are being passed off as suicides’: Armenian soldier’s death sparks questions
World.content:
Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

A serviceman has died at an Armenian military base. Investigators found the body of 20-year-old conscript Narek Torosyan on July 21. The Investigative Committee released only limited information after the incident. It said authorities had opened a criminal case and launched an investigation.

The committee later charged two of Torosyan’s fellow servicemen with driving him to suicide through negligence. One is a junior sergeant and the other a private. Authorities have placed both men under arrest.

The Ministry of Defence has made no public statement about the soldier’s death. Human rights activists and politicians have condemned the ministry’s silence.

Among them was human rights defender Zhanna Aleksanyan, who regularly raises concerns about human rights violations in the armed forces. She wrote on social media that Defence Minister Suren Papikyan ultimately bears responsibility for the lives of servicemen.

“The minister remains strikingly detached when soldiers die. At the end of each year, he tries to downplay the numbers, but no genuine effort exists to reduce the death toll,” she said.

According to official figures, eight servicemen have died since the beginning of 2026.

What we know so far

Armenian media report that Narek came from the town of Charentsavan and was a fourth-year student at the Russian-Armenian University. He hoped to become a sports journalist. The army drafted him in January 2026. Shortly before the incident, he had gone home on leave and visited his family. Reports also identify Chambarak as his duty station.

Authorities have not disclosed where the incident took place or what exactly happened.

According to a version published by several local media outlets, other servicemen severely beat the soldier before he took his own life.

Charentsavan Mayor Hakob Shahgeldyan also told reporters that, according to the information available to him, Narek had died by suicide. However, the mayor provided no further details.

Comments

Human rights activist Zhanna Aleksanyan wrote:

“The Ministry of Defence remains silent about the death of 20-year-old serviceman Narek Torosyan.

The minister has still offered no explanation or clarification. Did he visit the military unit to find out what happened and why? I am certain he did not. He bears responsibility for the life of every serviceman, and he is accountable to both their families and society.

I cannot accept the ‘suicide’ version circulating in the media. Journalists may learn that a serviceman has died, but they cannot know the circumstances of his death. Law enforcement agencies often leak such versions to the press. They later use those same reports to support their own conclusion that it was ‘suicide.’

And in the army, most ‘suicides’ are in fact unsolved murders.”

Tigran Abrahamyan, an opposition MP from the I Have Honour alliance, wrote on social media:

“Soldier Narek Torosyan, who died following the incident at the Chambarak military base, was my student. […]

Narek was a kind, gentle person with outstanding personal qualities. Both students and lecturers respected and cared for him.

Given the sensitivity of the case, I do not want to comment on the different versions or discuss the information available to me.

One thing is clear, however. The state has failed to ensure proper discipline, maintain a healthy psychological environment in military units, and provide effective oversight. That failure ultimately leads to incidents like this.

The authorities must carry out an objective and comprehensive investigation and take steps to prevent similar tragedies in the future.”

Mané Tandilyan, founder of the Country to Live party, said:

“Do not say that incidents like this are inevitable in the army. We must not accept such an attitude. After so many losses, it is unacceptable that we continue to lose our young people in peacetime.

How do officers demonstrate accountability? How has violence and cruelty become so deeply rooted among 18- to 20-year-olds that it repeatedly leads to deaths? What is the army doing to foster mutual respect, discipline and responsibility?

What is especially alarming is that intolerance and aggression are becoming increasingly visible in society. And yes, much of the responsibility lies with the country’s top leadership, which speaks to society in a language that fuels division, hostility and hatred. That atmosphere eventually seeps into people’s everyday relationships.

We must overcome this nightmare. Let us each begin with the people around us.”

Death of soldier in the Armenian Armed Forces

World.title: Four regional RSLs merge to keep veterans' services going
World.content:
When Peter Fleming first joined the Red Cliffs RSL in the 1990s, the service was a thriving part of the community.

While its importance has not lessened in the years since, the number of people reaching out and getting involved in the far north-west Victorian town's RSL has declined.

It is the experience of many sub-branches across the state, which are balancing aging committees, increasing costs and high administration loads.

"Those [volunteer] numbers are falling away," Mr Fleming, who is now the president of the Red Cliffs-Irymple RSL, said.

"My committee's age ranges from 75 to 92, and a lot of the younger blokes that are coming through now tend to be going through Mildura rather than out to the traditional sub-branches.

"We're just not getting the numbers there to keep us viable."

To address the problem, Mr Fleming stepped forward with an idea to merge his sub-branch, along with those in Merbein and Robinvale, into the larger and more central Mildura RSL.

Members of the four Sunraysia RSL sub-branches and Mildura Veteran Services Manager Paul Mensch, who is running the veteran support pilot. (Supplied: RSL Victoria)

The merger, believed to be the largest in the state service's history, will create a new model of veteran support and commemoration, while maintaining a local presence in each community.

"We moved now while we're still capable of doing it. If we left it any longer then it would have been a major problem for us," Mr Fleming said.

"We could have ended up losing all our buildings,

" Doing what we're doing now, it secures our presence in the district. "

Concern across Victoria

In April, RSL Victoria CEO Sue Cattermole told the ABC the head organisation was reviewing its governance structures in order to ease the administrative burden on struggling sub-branches.

There are more than 250 RSL sub-branches in Victoria.

Paul Mensch says the merger was created with administration challenges in mind. (ABC Mildura-Swan Hill: Wade Stephens)

Mildura RSL manager of veterans services Paul Mensch said administration was an issue for smaller groups.

"Being a not-for-profit charity organisation, each sub-branch has a massive amount of compliance to go through," he said.

"With smaller numbers and less volunteers, that compliance is becoming harder and harder.

" We really hope that other regions will take this blueprint and run with it. "

Sue Cattermole says Mildura's merger may be a blueprint for other areas. (Supplied: RSL Victoria)

Ms Cattermole said the veteran community was gravitating towards larger regional centres.

"What is happening in Mildura may be a blueprint for other areas to use to find a model that suits their veteran community best," she said.

No change for community

The Red Cliffs-Irymple, Merbein and Robinvale sub-branches all have long histories in Sunraysia.

Robinvale's RSL began as a branch of the Returned Soldiers' Sailors' and Airmens' Imperial League Australia in 1944. Merbein's branch was officially opened in 1922, and Red Cliffs was established in 1925.

The 1953 official opening of the Red Cliffs RSL's Memorial Club Rooms, which now house the sub-branch's Red Cliffs Military Muesum. (Supplied: Red Cliffs & District Historical Society)

As a part of the merger, the sub-branches will now fall under the Mildura RSL name, but are expected to keep their own names when managing town-based activities, such as ANZAC Day services.

All buildings and memorabilia will be retained, while financials will be handled by Mildura.

"All it means is that each of the sub-branches will no longer have a president, treasurer, secretary … that will be all handled in Mildura," Mr Fleming said.

Red Cliffs-Irymple RSL president Peter Fleming, Merbein RSL president Brian Munro, Robinvale RSL vice president John Keating and Mildura RSL president Bradley McGlashan. (Supplied: RSL Victoria)

Mildura RSL Sub-Branch president Brad McGlashan said the small sub-branches were "valued pillars of our community" and the Mildura RSL had the financial and operational capacity to ensure the merger's success into the future.

"This is a sensible and proactive solution that strengthens veteran support while preserving the unique identity and heritage of our soldier settlement communities," he said.

RSL Victoria said a coordinated veteran support pilot had started under the direction of Mr Mensch and had already displayed encouraging outcomes.

The model will continue to be refined before being formalised at the end of the year.

World.title: Guerilla garden removed from Sydney intersection dubbed 'triangle of shame'
World.content:
Transport for NSW says it removed a guerilla garden on a concrete island in a busy inner west Sydney intersection due to safety concerns for pedestrians and motorists.

A collection of small trees in bathtubs, pot plants and a park bench had recently popped up in the intersection of King Street and Enmore Road in Newtown, dubbed by locals as "Newtown Forest".

Newtown resident Nic Lowe was among the group that set up the short-lived refuge and described it as an "imagination exercise" for beautifying the traffic island.

A community group attempted to beautify the concrete traffic island. (Supplied: Nic Lowe)

"We call it the triangle of shame," Mr Lowe, who is part of the community group K Shift, told 702 ABC Sydney.

"It was a place of natural sanctuary in the middle of an urban jungle.

"We had about eight pots there, about eight bathtubs. We had about 50 aloe veras."

Loading...

A spokesperson for Transport for NSW said it created safety risks because it reduced the line of sight for drivers and the items could become projectile risks if they were hit by vehicles.

"The installation also encouraged people to remain on or walk around the concrete island, which was not designed or intended for pedestrian access," the spokesperson said.

"The decision to remove the installation was made solely on safety grounds, with the safety of pedestrians, cyclists, and motorists our highest priority.

"We appreciate the community spirit and positive intentions behind the project and encourage residents interested in greening or beautification initiatives to work with the relevant authority to identify suitable locations where these activities can be delivered safely and compliantly."

Nic Lowe describes the concrete island as a "triangle of shame". (Supplied: Nic Lowe)

The concrete island, which covers about 60 square metres, separates north and southbound traffic in one of Sydney's key traffic arteries and runs through one of the city's busiest nightlife districts.

The island is home to traffic signals for the three-way intersection.

Mr Lowe said it was not in a dangerous position as the roads had a 40 kilometre an hour speed limit.

"It is, in fact, a pedestrian refuge anyway," Mr Lowe said.

"So if it's unsafe to sit there, then it's unsafe to stand there."

He compared the situation to median traffic islands in the neighbouring suburb Erskineville, where speed limits were 40km/h and featured trees and hedge plantings.

702 ABC Sydney understands while NSW Police were present during the garden's removal, no arrests or move-on orders were given.

World.title: Brewery uses solar bitcoin rig to make beer and cover power bills
World.content:
In the back corner of a busy brewery at Lisarow, on the NSW Central Coast, a set of computers is generating all the heat needed to make beer.

The computers are bitcoin miners that run huge numbers of calculations every second, and receive cryptocurrency for doing so.

The process consumes lots of energy, but the machines, run on solar power, actually help the brewers cut power costs.

"We don't always do things the traditional way," Hawkesbury Brewing Co operations manager Adam Neale said.

" We wanted to be on the cutting edge of doing something different. "

Adam Neale uses excess solar energy to operate a bitcoin mine. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

The machines earn Hawkesbury Brewing Co about $2,000 a month, which almost covers its power bills.

The bitcoin mine only runs when the brewery has too much solar energy, which means it costs nothing to run.

"We hit a crossroads where we knew we couldn't save any more energy anywhere else," Mr Neale said.

How does it work?

Sean Foley, a professor of applied finance at Macquarie University, said mining cryptocurrency was a very energy-intensive process.

Hot water generated by the bitcoin mine is used to clean bottles as well as produce beer. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

"[The computers] get really, really hot … because you're pumping so much power through these systems," Professor Foley said.

"You might be using in the order of 20 or 30 times what a regular PC would [use]."

Professor Foley said the heat could be harnessed as a useful by-product.

"It's a waste product, effectively, of the bitcoin mining process," he said.

"If you can utilise that heat for some sort of purpose … for heating, that's fantastic."

The bitcoin heating process is reflected in the name of some products. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

While cryptocurrency mining is banned in some parts of the world because of the amount of energy it uses, the brewery only uses renewable energy, leaving no carbon footprint.

Mr Neale began exploring the idea to avoid the fees that were charged for sending excess solar energy back into the grid.

"It'd be nice to give it back to the grid and get paid handsomely for it but it doesn't happen so we need to be able to use that power to then power the factory for the rest of the day," he said.

Storing the solar energy in a battery was not an option.

Solar panels on the roof of the brewery generate electricity to run the bitcoin mine. (Supplied: Hawkesbury Brewing Co)

"The big problem for us with having batteries is that there is alcohol on site. Flammability's always a problem. Insurance companies just don't like the fact that you're storing electricity," Mr Neale said.

Instead of batteries, the brewery installed 16 bitcoin miners into a tub filled with a non-conductive liquid that looks like water.

The liquid cools the computers, and in turn heats up to about 90 degrees.

A heat exchange process uses that liquid to heat the water used in the beer-making process.

"We found there was enough heat coming off those miners to heat our incoming town water supply," Mr Neale said.

"We can heat our water up and store it for days on end.

"Everything that we need to do with hot water is done via that process."

The bitcoin mine generates enough heat to produce 100,000 litres of beer a month. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

More potential uses

Mr Neale believes the technique could be applied in other ways.

"We can see the potential for this for public swimming pools, recirculation of hot water in apartment buildings [and] manufacturing," he said.

"If you need hot water on site and lots of it, it's a way of being able to produce that hot water for the day."

Beverages are produced with the assistance of the bitcoin mine. (ABC Central Coast: Sarah Forster)

Professor Foley cautiously agreed.

"I can't see anything particularly wrong with it, I'm just sceptical as to whether the economics are going to stack up," Dr Foley said.

"If they're able to earn some small amounts of bitcoin each day and then sell them and they can see that that's profitable, then I wouldn't see any restriction for other activities.

"Whether it were other brewers or other people who need to generate heat through the day, utilising bitcoin miners to do so."

World.title: Iran's attacks on US bases in the Middle East mark 'end of an era'
World.content:
Five months into a war Donald Trump said would last only weeks, the Iran conflict has so far cost the United States tens of billions of dollars and brought about "the end of an era" in American military strategy.

After a short-lived ceasefire, heavy bombings resumed earlier this month, with the US hitting Iranian targets and retaliatory strikes causing chaos across the Gulf.

The war has so far cost the US $US37.5 billion ($53.6 billion), according to the Pentagon's figures, and US politicians have approved even more funding.

An unprecedented $US1.15 trillion military spending package that will help fund the war this week advanced through the House of Representatives despite fierce pushback from Democrats concerned about spiralling costs. The bill now goes to the Senate.

And if the US is planning for a wider war, as the Washington Post reports, there could be more severe losses to US equipment and munition stocks to come.

Over the last five months, the US defence force has suffered heavy blows to its personnel, military bases and hardware, and analysts warn American war strategy long-term has been weakened.

This is what it's lost and what the impacts could be.

The damage on US bases

The US military footprint in the Middle East has sustained heavy damage during the war, as Iran struck US bases and outposts across the Gulf.

There are at least 19 US military facilities across the Middle East, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

Early in the war, sustained attacks on US bases in Saudi Arabia, Kuwait and Jordan left some of those bases "all but uninhabitable", the New York Times reported.

Among them was Camp Buehring, a post in north-western Kuwait. In March, two Iranian F-5 planes dropped eight bombs on the facility, striking the dining area, gym and garage, according to an analysis of Iran-released images by Mark Cancian and Chris Park of the Center for Strategic and International Studies (CSIS).

US military base Camp Buehring in Kuwait was attacked during the opening days of the war. (Supplied: Center for Strategic and International Studies/ABC News)

At a Jordanian base, in the opening days of the war, a powerful missile defence radar, which is part of the Terminal High-Altitude Area Defense (THAAD) system, was destroyed by Iran. It costs just shy of $US500,000.

In the latest escalation, the same base was targeted by a barrage of strikes, killing three American soldiers.

The US Ali Al Salem base in Kuwait has been repeatedly hit by Iran, including again this week. At least 20 American personnel have been injured in the attacks.

A naval base in Bahrain was also struck in late February, reportedly destroying two satellite communication terminals and other buildings. It was hit again in June.

Satellite images show Iranian attacks on warehouses (lower left) and headquarters (centre) at the Naval Support Activity (NSA) naval base in Bahrain. (Supplied: Center for Strategic and International Studies)

It could cost between $US4 billion and $US9 billion to rebuild these damaged bases, according to Mr Cancian.

But the attacks will have a deeper impact than just physical destruction, says Kelly Grieco, a defence policy expert at the Stimson Center.

"US bases … were to a large extent, sanctuaries," she said.

"The fact that this has been exposed as such a vulnerability and that the adversary is able to reach far deeper and to attack the bases has a psychological impact.

"Certainly, it marks … an end of an era. An era when the United States was just so dominant relative to others in controlling airspace."

A satellite view from March shows the Ali Al Salem Base in Kuwait after Iranian strikes. (Reuters: Planet Labs)

Along with well-known locations of US assets, Iranians have reportedly been targeting covert outposts as well.

The regime recently struck CIA facilities in the Gulf. One was located in the US embassy in Riyadh and another located in eastern Iraq, Reuters reported. The hits, according to the news service, prompted US intelligence analysts to investigate whether Russia assisted by providing targeting information or advanced drone technology.

Mr Cancian, a senior defence advisor at the CSIS, said Iranian strikes on US infrastructure had been "precise".

"There were no random craters … some of them were aimed at military facilities, but others were clearly intended to cause casualties [such as] attacks on barracks and dining facilities and gyms."

Loss of personnel

The greatest cost to the US so far, though, has been in the military personnel lost to this war.

All up, the Pentagon has said 18 service members have been killed since the war began.

Four died in the latest phase of the war, according to the Pentagon, including one killed in northern Iraq while carrying out a controlled detonation of unexploded ordnance from a downed Iranian drone.

Trump says Iran will 'pay' for soldiers' deaths The United States launches a new wave of strikes on Iran after identifying two soldiers killed while defending against Iranian missile and drone attacks in Jordan.

Six soldiers were killed in Kuwait during the first few days of the war, with another dying from injuries from a missile attack on Prince Sultan Air Base in Saudi Arabia.

Another six service members were killed in March when a KC-135 refuelling aircraft supporting operations against Iran crashed in Iraq.

Separately, the US military said a navy pilot died after a helicopter crashed into the Arabian Sea earlier this month during what it described as an emergency landing not caused by hostile action.

The Pentagon has been accused of withholding information about US casualties, with officials telling the New York Times that dozens of military personnel had been injured in the latest wave of Iranian attacks against US forces.

Dr Grieco said she was concerned the number of US casualties would rise.

"[People are] questioning why we are still fighting this war and are those lives worth it to be lost."

Weapons depleted

The US has worn down its weapons supply in a way that defence experts had not anticipated.

In Dr Grieco's words, the military has been "eating up" munitions at a rate it cannot afford.

"Things like missile defence systems, long-range strike weapons, Tomahawk missiles. We've been going through these at a high expenditure rate," she said.

She said the military had also used a large proportion of its "high-value critical systems", or military assets that it did not have in large numbers.

One example is the THAAD mobile system, which is specifically designed for ballistic missile defence and can hit targets at ranges of 150 to 200 kilometres.

"We were already in a hole before this war started … and now, because of this war, we've dug ourselves a much bigger hole that we need to get out of," Dr Grieco said.

"It's going to take years for us to be able to recover the numbers that we've lost."

A report to the US Congress in May found at least 42 American aircraft, including F-15 and F-35 fighter jets, 24 MQ-9 Reaper drones and an A-10 attack plane, had been destroyed or damaged since February.

Despite US Central Command claiming attacks on more than 10,000 targets, Iran had still retained roughly 70 per cent of its pre-war missile stockpile, according to a New York Times report in May.

Iran launches longest-ever ballistic missile reaching beyond Middle East An attempted attack on a US-UK military base in the Indian Ocean by Iran shows Tehran can launch missiles as far as 4,000km, raising concerns European cities are in reach.

The US has not made the current state of its military stockpile known, but Dr Grieco said that in recent months it had likely gotten worse. Meanwhile, she said, the Iranians' weapons supply may have grown.

The Iranian military may have used the ceasefire to excavate and reopen buried underground "missile cities" that had their entrances blocked by US and Israeli attacks, she added.

In contrast, half of America's stockpile of hard-to-make air defence interceptors had been depleted, while up to a third of expensive missiles had been used, a Center for Strategic and International Studies report said.

Compared to Iran, Dr Grieco said the US was in a "lopsided" position.

"[The] math already favoured Iran at the start of the war. It now looks worse," she said.

Some weapons could take five to six years to replace, which will weaken the US's deterrence capabilities, analysts say.

"There's going to be this gap, this window of vulnerability, until they can rebuild those inventories," Mr Cancian said.

"It's a problem for the Western Pacific. If a conflict were to break out with China, we would be way below where most analysts and the war planners want the inventories to be."

Learning military lessons the 'hard way'

Despite the persistent fighting words from Washington, analysts say there are signs the US is shifting its strategy in the Middle East.

One of them is that the US this month relocated dozens of aircraft to Ben Gurion Airport and Ramon Air Base in Israel, signalling Washington knows it has a problem, according to the Council on Foreign Relations.

The war has made the realities of the geography much more apparent as Iran has exploited the fact US military assets sit well within striking distance.

Dr Grieco said this conflict and Iran's role in it had cast a shadow across the future of US military presence in the Gulf.

"I don't know if we'll see these kinds of basing changes happening overnight," she said. "But I think long-term there's good reasons for these Gulf countries to really re-think whether they want these bases."

The US 'signal' hidden in a nuclear deal Analysts warn the US and Saudi Arabia's landmark deal could set off a "nuclear arms race in the Middle East".

The dwindling stockpiles of weapons also mean the US is constrained in its ability to help its allies.

Charles Kupchan, a professor at Georgetown University and senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations, pointed to Ukraine's desperate need for Patriot missiles.

"They're not able to get what they want from the United States, in part, because we don't have enough to give them," he said.

He said while the US still enjoyed vast military superiority over Iran, the regime's ability to launch drones and missiles remained "robust".

"As the US has found out the hard way — in Afghanistan, in Iraq, in Libya, in Syria — superior military capability does not always translate into a successful strategic outcome," he said.

World.title: They drink our water and take our power, but do data centres create jobs?
World.content:
Data centres — the new, essential, digital infrastructure of our time — are a hot topic of debate in town halls around Australia.

Despite controversy over the use of AI and the substantial resources required to power data centres, one argument pushed in their favour is that they will create jobs.

But how many jobs do data centres actually create?

What are data centres?

These huge warehouse-like structures house servers and storage systems to process, store and manage digital data.

They are essential to supporting the AI systems becoming increasingly pervasive in our lives, from the ubiquitous Google search AI results to ChatGPT or Microsoft Copilot.

To do so, they require a lot of land, as well as large amounts of water and electricity.

According to the Global Data Centres Report 2025, released by Knight Frank, Australia is one of the world's biggest investors in data centres.

There are 251 data centres already operating across Australia, according to DataCenters.com, with more in the development pipeline.

How much water and power do they use?

It's estimated a 1 megawatt data centre consumes 25.5 million litres of water, more than 10 Olympic swimming pools' worth, a year for cooling.

The new facility AirTrunk data centre in Western Sydney will deliver at least 320 megawatts of computing power. (Reuters: Hollie Adams)

Sydney Water projected data centres could use around a quarter of the city's yearly drinking water by the end of the 2020s, roughly 87.5 billion litres.

The Climate Council says data centres used 2 per cent of Australia's total electricity last year, with that figure set to jump to 6 per cent by the end of the decade.

How South Korea plans to cash in its AI chips South Korea is doubling down on its bid to lead in AI, unveiling plans last month to spend hundreds of billions on developing its chip manufacturing.

Prime Minister Anthony Albanese has outlined new expectations for the AI industry, including an expectation that data centres minimise energy demand and emissions, as well as "secure new and additional clean energy generation or storage to offset demand".

It also expects operators to provide transparent reporting regarding water usage and efficiency, as well as mandating data centres build in drought and climate change resilience to their operations.

How many jobs do they create?

In the short term, data centres can create thousands of jobs.

A report from the Brookings Institution think tank found large workforces were needed to build data centres, with one study estimating construction could support between 1,000 and 10,000 workers, depending on the size of the centre.

But once a data centre has been built, the number of jobs on offer falls significantly.

A UK government report found "data centres are highly automated facilities, and the number of jobs directly created is relatively modest, ranging from a few tens to a few hundreds".

Data centres support large construction workforces. (Reuters: Hollie Adam)

Jobs figures cited in the report from two UK data centre operators estimated only 20-88 full-time employees were needed on site.

A similar report prepared for the Virginia state government in the US found a 23,226sqm data centre, roughly the size of three NRL fields, "may have approximately 50 full-time workers, about half of which are contract workers".

"Construction of an individual data centre building usually takes about 12 to 18 months, and data centre representatives indicated that, at the height of construction, approximately 1,500 workers are on site from various construction-related industries," it said.

So data centres do create jobs, but they are not necessarily going to be supporting a huge, ongoing workforce and, according to the Brookings Institution, data centre advocates "overstate" potential employment benefits.

University of Melbourne senior lecturer in construction technology M. Reza Hosseini warns a data centre construction boom could result in a shortage of workers to build much-needed new houses.

"Data centre construction demands highly specialised trades like high-voltage electricians, industrial cooling technicians and advanced mechanical engineers — jobs that only partly overlap with residential building," Dr Hosseini said.

"But in a market already stretched thin, even partial overlap matters.

" When a hyper-scale project offers premium wages to secure electricians for 18 months, those workers are unavailable for housing. "

The jobs

At the time of writing, there were more than 1,100 job listings for data centre technicians across Australia, according to the listings on SEEK.com.

Many offer lucrative salaries.

One listing for a technician in Melbourne offered a $149,000 salary, plus an annual bonus of $14,900.

China breaking up AI relationships A boyfriend betrayed 17-year-old Xiaoxue, so she made an AI partner. But now the government is trying to end her relationship.

Another listing for an HVAC service technician offered up to $55 per hour for the installation and servicing of cooling towers at data centres in Sydney and across NSW.

A senior facilities technician listing for Melbourne offered $145,000 to help operate "a hyper-scale data centre facility due to go live later this year".

The listing for a day shift electrical technician in Sydney had compensation at $137,000.

World.title: Australia's 'monoculture' might be at the Labor conference
World.content:
If Australia indeed harbours a "monoculture" it might be the ideological version on display at this week's Labor Party National Conference.

For supporters it was orderly, unified and determined. A striking example of political resolve.

For critics? A wearisome parade of Bunyip Juche.

The party's supreme policy-making machine has been busy honing a platform that's as tight and shiny as a button.

Spiky bits like the base's angst over AUKUS, Palestine and greater taxation of resources mostly buffed away and potential troublemakers seemingly co-opted into acquiescence by the logic of power.

The mining industry has taken the whole thing as a big win. As have those who fret about Labor's commitment to the alliance.

On both scores, the party membership's official message has been to prioritise stability and incrementalism.

Loading...

How the sausage is made

Potential threats like the push for a gas tax or an end to the diesel fuel tax credit for mining companies failed to see the light of day or became watered down to a state where they can't offend their targets.

In exchange, the left pushed for and won greater support for voluntary assisted suicide — the first issue to have been contested on the floor after nearly 100 amendments passed with barely a murmur.

There were a series of wins for unions, including the restoration of a Fair Work court to deliver simpler and faster workplace resolutions, support for sovereign power to industry, AI protections and a home-building agenda.

Like it or not, this is how the sausage is made.

For those who believe in the virtue of converting and wrangling political trade-offs into a unified, coherent set of messages, Labor's example is transcendent.

Collectivist movements seeking power require collectivist compromise. Alternatives would include becoming a letter-writing independent or sidelines bomb-tosser.

Labor's public triennial conferences are not only one of the party's defining characteristics — in contrast to the Liberal Party's ad-hoc and leader-driven policymaking structures or the opaque versions used by the Greens.

They might also be the reason why Labor is this era's dominant party of government. Its 50th conference is an expression of institutional stability in a world of turmoil.

Which is how the current crop of leaders view it.

Wayne Swan has stepped down as president of the party this week and his primary warning has been for Labor to renew and brace for a new kind of political contest against Pauline Hanson's "charlatan" populism. (AAP: Lukas Coch)

'We will not go down the American road'

"No, I most certainly don't pine for losing elections or having conferences turn into ugly spectacles," says Wayne Swan in Friday's ABC Insiders podcast with David Speers.

"I don't pine for that at all because the Labor Party, if it is anything, has to be a party of government… we have to be absolutely at our best to represent the Australian people and give them what they expect.

"I know the media would like to see a lot of conflict but there isn't actually a lot."

Separately, in a speech last night to the conference dinner, Swan defended Labor's history in the following way.

"Scrub our years of power — our years of governing with social purpose — from the last 50 and you do not get a fairer, world leading economy.

"You get the United States. Forty years of wage suppression, a hollowed-out middle, and a politics that runs on scapegoating your neighbour.

"We will not go down the American road."

Swan has stepped down as president of the party this week and his primary warning has been for Labor to renew and brace for a new kind of political contest against Pauline Hanson's "charlatan" populism, which he warns is being funded by a wall of money that once backed the Coalition.

"The money has not gone anywhere," he said.

"It has only changed horses.

"Together with our mighty trade union movement we fought Fraser. We fought Howard. We fought Abbott. And now we watch the conservative mantle pass to One Nation, and a new battle awaits us."

This week has established yet again that this government's strategy for retaining political power is well-honed.

But there's also been a reminder, courtesy of a group of what one might call Labor's grumpy old guard.

In a series of interventions over the past few days, a counter-narrative has been spun that undermines the version of government backed by conference delegates.

Former Queensland Premier Peter Beattie has said One Nation's rise in the polls is a sign that the major political parties — including Labor — are not delivering for households. (AAP: Bianca De Marchi, file photo)

Old guard serves a spray

It began with Bill Kelty, former ACTU leader and co-architect of many of the Hawke and Keating era economic reforms, who let spray in a senate committee submission.

"Our taxes are increasing, government expenditure is rising faster than prices. It does say something is wrong with this place," he said.

Kelty also lamented how governments are routinely wasting money.

ABC Politics in your inbox Sign up to the ABC Politics newsletter with Courtney Gould

"It is just part of a bucket where we pay for quarantine centres that are never used, Commonwealth Games that are not held in the country, infrastructure costs that are the highest in the world or at least approach those levels, where [the cost of] some tunnels are now the highest in the history of humanity.

"Where we simply cannot build enough houses because we did not train enough workers."

Separately, former Queensland Premier Peter Beattie told this column during the week that One Nation's rise in the polls is a sign that the major political parties — including Labor — are not delivering for households.

"I never thought I'd ever see One Nation at the level of support that they have now, but that's because the major political parties are not performing and dealing with the issues that ordinary Australians are concerned about," he said.

"When they start doing that, then One Nation's support will dissipate, and they will go through the normal self-destruct processes."

Whether the current generation of Labor leaders care or not, the old guard's grumpiness reflects a good slab of the community's dark mood.

This week's gathering is a precursor to Labor's coming federal election campaign for 2028, when it's program will be about offsetting those concerns with handouts to struggling voter groups.

Jacob Greber is political editor of ABC's 7.30 program.

World.title: Right-wing populist politics is 'extremely anti-women', warns Anna Funder
World.content:
As a student living in West Berlin in the late 80s, Anna Funder would sit with her friends, a clique of East German creatives exiled from their country for criticising the regime, at a café near the Berlin Wall.

For Funder, the walled city deep inside the Eastern Bloc represented the Cold War politics and the oppressive nuclear threat that defined the postwar period.

But West Berlin at the time was an exciting place to be, full of artists, writers and conscientious objectors escaping compulsory military service.

Funder, who was 20, was fascinated by the fact that 100 metres away, on the other side of the wall, were her friends' former lives — a whole network of friends, family and acquaintances — that were now unreachable.

Funder returned to Australia where she worked as an international lawyer before publishing her first book, Stasiland, telling the stories of people who resisted the East German secret police known as the Stasi, in 2003.

Stasiland made several shortlists and won the 2004 Samuel Johnson Prize, now known as the Baillie Gifford Prize for Non-Fiction.

Anna Funder was born in Melbourne and, as a child, lived with her family in San Francisco and Paris. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

Two decades on, Funder is the author of All That I Am (2011), which won the 2012 Miles Franklin Literary Award, and Wifedom (2023), a hybrid work of biography, memoir and fiction exploring the life of George Orwell's wife, Eileen Blair, and her overlooked influence on his writing.

Funder, who was recently appointed as a professor of practice in creative writing at Sydney University, is about to embark on a national speaking tour to discuss the provenance of her three acclaimed literary works.

She sat down with ABC Arts to chat about AI, the state of democracy and her favourite Australian books.

You trained as a lawyer, so how did you end up becoming a writer?

I always wanted to be a writer [but] I'm very happy that I did law. I think it equipped me well for certain situations — facing down Stasi men who wanted to lecture me about human rights in their system.

What drew you to write your first book about the East German Stasi?

The [Berlin] wall fell in '89, so not long after I was there; I left in '88. No-one had any idea it would fall. Really, no-one.

I went back on other little fellowships while I was working as a junior lawyer. I was fascinated by the fact that the wall was down now, so it was possible to go into this country which had been walled in, to go and speak to people who had lived there. It was like an investigation of my friends' past: what was this regime that kicked out its best and brightest, its artists? That was fascinating to me.

Anna Funder studied under Hilary Charlesworth, who became the first Australian female judge to serve on the International Court of Justice. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

And then I came across the story of Miriam, which bookends Stasiland. I was told about someone whose husband had died in Stasi custody but, actually, Miriam's story went way back to when she was 16 years old, in 1968. She had protested about the destruction of a beautiful church in Leipzig and was arrested.

It's a long and tricky and crazy story about Stasi methods, Stasi interrogation, Stasi paranoia, persecuting children and eventually of her trying to escape the country over the wall in Berlin, right near where I used to sit. It's a really extraordinary and wonderful story. It's one of the privileges of my life to have met her.

I knew as soon as I had that story that that would be one of the best stories I would find, and it was. I felt like I was getting up close to human courage and conscience in its purest and most extreme form in her.

How liberating, or not, was it to then fictionalise a true story as you did in All That I Am, after you had told the story of the Stasi in non-fiction?

I had wanted to write a novel but the stories in Stasiland were not right to tell in fiction, it became clear to me, because the regime was too extreme to be believable.

It was not believable that they collected people's dirty underwear, put it in jars to train dogs, to track dissidents.

And it was barely believable that courage like Miriam's existed, the courage to refuse to inform or betray, no matter what the state would do to you.

And the other thing was that the Stasi men were still walking around Berlin, largely unpunished — still the case. It seemed morally wrong to write a fiction out of stories that needed to be told in truth and needed to be put on the historical record.

All That I Am is based on a true story, but it was a story of very, very early resistance to Hitler that had never been told. When I was telling it — I started writing it in 2006, it was published in 2011 — all the people in it were dead and I felt less beholden to real people. I wanted to write a book that made them live again. It was a great liberation.

How did you settle on the three-pronged structure of Wifedom?

The form of the book comes out of what truth is it that I'm trying to tell. I don't set out with a form in mind.

Wifedom was terrifying to write because I'd never read anything that was formally like this. I had no models, but I was writing the story of Orwell and the story of how his biographers had eliminated his feminist suffragette, Fabian mother and aunt from his story, which is obviously where his underdog perspective comes from, which we all find so charming, and eliminated, most importantly, his brilliant wife. So that was an essayistic thing.

Anna Funder doesn't want to cancel George Orwell The Miles Franklin-winning author just wants to set the record straight.

But at some point, the fiction writer in me just couldn't bear it, and I had to bring Eileen back to life. I had her letters to her best friend from Oxford days, which are hilarious and very revealing of her and her marriage. I got permission to use them, so I could write scenes in which she's writing her real letters, but also other scenes in Spain and when she's dying.

I wanted Eileen to live again. I didn't want her to be someone who was just written about by me. I wanted her to be somebody who, often in her own words, will live on in people's minds.

Formally, it's risky to mix fiction and nonfiction and memoir and a feminist analysis of six major biographies of a major 20th-century writer. It's risky to put things very clearly on the public record that have been very deliberately hidden: his repressed homosexuality, his sadism, his paranoia, his infidelities, his complexity out of which the work comes.

Was there any blowback from the Orwell fans?

Yes. The Orwell fans have a fan club, which is a charity called The Orwell Society. It's not a learned society, as its name might imply.

George Orwell and Eileen adopted a boy, a baby, in 1944. His name is Richard Blair, and he and his friend Quentin Kopp are behind this fan club.

And while Richard Blair says that he thinks, for instance, that his mother had a much greater role in writing Animal Farm than she's usually given credit for, they know that everything in Wifedom is true, but they're not used to Orwell being looked at from Eileen's point of view, or my imagined Eileen's point of view, and a woman's point of view, and I think that that's difficult for them to integrate.

Anna Funder says a novel would not show the sly ways in which history has hidden Eileen Blair. (ABC News: Jack Fisher)

I think that they would rather think about Orwell as he wanted to think of himself: as a decent, upstanding, heterosexual man, whereas somebody who was so vanilla could never have had the vision, say, for Nineteen Eighty-Four, which is paranoid and sadistic and wonderful for us.

Having studied totalitarianism, what do you make of Western democracy at this moment?

I think it's under threat from within and without.

The number of democracies in the world is diminishing. The democracy in the US is white-anted or moth-eaten or whichever insect metaphor you like. I lived there with my husband and children for three-and-a-half years during the Obama period, which now looks like halcyon days, but it felt to us like we were inside a dying beast.

Trump's USA — is it fascism yet? Anna Funder joins NYT opinion writer M. Gessen and the University of Toronto's Jason Stanley on ABC Radio National's Big Ideas to discuss the political ideology of Donald Trump.

It is touted as a democracy, but democracies vary. And in a democracy where you have no right to healthcare that isn't connected to your employer, people are very vulnerable and the level of freedom and dignity that they have is much diminished. If you get cancer, you will go bankrupt and have to sell your house because very likely, even if you are employed, your insurance will not cover treatment.

Also, 60 per cent vote. It is a less robust democracy in terms of its structures than Australia, where we have compulsory voting, preferential voting. These things are rare. We have an electoral commission that deals with gerrymandering. We have limits on political donations, so companies cannot, as they can in the States, effectively buy a politician to represent them.

And we are not such a religious country, so we don't have faith in prayer. We want practical, real solutions.

Worldwide, the rise of largely right-wing populism is something to be taken very seriously.

It's a threat to democracy because it's essentially an anti-democratic, quasi-fascist movement that is extremely anti-women — we have Pauline [Hanson] coming out against childcare, against abortion, against parental leave.

It's tricky times for democracy. We need to really protect it and cherish it.

What is your view on AI and the arts?

In order to make AI have content, it's not enough to scrape the internet and everyone's emails. If you want high-quality content, it comes from books, so what the tech companies have done is steal all books in violation of copyright.

These businesses are worth vast amounts of money. Of course, your business will be worth more money if you do not pay for the raw materials you are using and then offering up for a fee eventually. And the raw materials are the thinking and research and writing and creative thinking in all of our books.

June's best books This month's best books include an Irish saga by Maggie O'Farrell, a gritty memoir by Ralph Jackman and a comic Italian romp by Andrew Sean Greer.

A massive crime has occurred, and the tech companies have been lobbying the government to retrospectively make that copyright crime and theft legal, which the government is holding firm on. We should not be giving all of our best thinking, music, art and films away for free to be broken up for parts and offered up as answers to AI questions.

People will not continue to make work if we're not paid for it. There's no point in me writing a book if it's immediately stolen and distributed globally for free.

It's not difficult to establish a consent and licensing scheme for money, and that's what needs to happen now. We've done it for every other technology that's existed. We do it for universities, we do it for photocopying, we do it for electronic lending, we do it for libraries. If you can be made to pay $5.99 on your television at home for a movie that Netflix is offering you, the tech companies can easily be made to pay for our books.

What do you make of the prime minister's recent comments on the issue of AI and copyright?

Big Tech has been walking the corridors of Parliament House for months, lobbying politicians hard to gut copyright instead of talking to us, the creators whose works they need, have stolen, and wanted for free in future.

It was a magnificent speech by the prime minister, putting the regulations and guardrails to come on AI into the context of other Australian innovations and protections such as Medicare, universal voting, universal superannuation and the under-16s social media ban.

Big Tech won't want to behave legally in Australia because it would be the first jurisdiction to make them do so — but Australia is good at firsts.

We now need the government to require them to negotiate consent and licenses with us, or not be given permission to set up here with our stolen goods.

What do you think AI's impact will be on human creativity? Because I wonder what is the future of the novel when we can't necessarily trust that a human has written what we're reading?

Art is about human connection. A novel is a way in which you can see inside other people's minds: the writer's, for one thing, and the characters that they're presenting to you. And that's extremely fundamental to our self-knowledge, to pleasure, to connection, to community, to solace, to consolation.

I have no interest in reading a book written by AI. A novel written by AI is a category error.

Watching a short grab of a cat playing basketball is one thing, but a novel is totally another.

I think that we are going to value the products of genuine human creativity more in an age of dross and slop and stolen material.

I think AI will find its place. I think it's going to be an incredibly useful tool for number-crunching statistically, in medicine, in all kinds of things. In the arts, no. And they need to pay. They need to get consent for our work and pay us.

ABC Radio National’s Top 100 Australian Books Countdown We take over Radio National on Saturday, 17 and Sunday, 18 October to count down the Top 100 Australian books as voted by you.

This year, Radio National is asking people to vote for their top 100 Australian books. What are some of your favourites?

I've just been looking at an essay I wrote about Jessica Anderson's Tirra Lirra by the River, a beautiful novel, and also about Christina Stead's The Man Who Loved Children. I think it's her best book; it's a liberation coming-of-age story. They are absolutely extraordinary Australian novels, and they were very formative for me.

More recently, I loved Fiona McFarlane's Highway 13, which I thought was incredible. I would also recommend all the books, particularly The Watchtower, of Elizabeth Harrower, a writer who was forgotten for many years.

Our literature is so wonderful, thriving, and it's the only way that we know what we're thinking and what we're feeling and who we are.

An Evening with Anna Funder is at Perth on July 31; Adelaide on August 2; Sydney on August 4; Brisbane on August 6 and Melbourne on August 10.

Quotes have been edited for clarity and brevity.

World.title: Japan's popular princess sparks calls to ditch male-only succession law
World.content:
Japan is running out of royals, and it's putting the world's oldest continuous hereditary monarchy at risk.

There are only three people in line to inherit Japan's Chrysanthemum Throne, and one of them is 90 years old. All three of them are men.

In a bid to secure the line, the Japanese government recently passed changes to allow males from former branches of the imperial family to be adopted into the current royal family.

Born as commoners, the adoptees would not be eligible to inherit the throne themselves, but their sons would be.

The proposed solution has proved contentious, with many people in the country asking why the law was not instead changed to allow women to succeed to the throne.

Emperor Naruhito has only one child, a daughter, prompting the succession law changes. (Reuters: Nicolas Economou)

Japan's Emperor Naruhito does not have a son, but he does have a daughter: the enormously popular Princess Aiko.

Chuo University professor Okawa Makoto, who specialises in imperial lineage and succession, said allowing a female emperor would be "the simplest solution".

He said you would need to go back more than 600 years to find a common ancestor with the adoptees.

"To put it bluntly, they are practically complete strangers," he said.

"This proposal involves welcoming such outsiders into the Imperial Family."

'Out of step with the times'

The family tree of Japan's imperial family includes Crown Prince Fumihito and his son, Prince Hitachi. (ABC News: Lindsay Dunbar)

Emperor Naruhito's first eligible heir is his 60-year-old-brother, Crown Prince Fumihito, followed by Fumihito's son, 19-year-old Prince Hisahito.

After that, the next — and final — man in line is the emperor's 90-year-old uncle, Prince Hitachi.

It means if the 19-year-old prince did not have a son, the line would end within the next generation.

Princess Aiko, 24, enjoys a high level of support among the public and regularly attracts large crowds at events.

Tokyo resident, 59-year-old Miwa, said Princess Aiko was a "truly wonderful person".

"I think everyone would like to see her become emperor," she said, while out walking her dog, Merci, in the city's Yoyogi Park.

Miwa, 59, is in favour of having a female emperor. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

A poll conducted in May by Mainichi Shimbun, a major Japanese newspaper, found 72 per cent of people supported having a female emperor.

Everyone the ABC spoke to in and around the park was in favour.

One 29-year-old woman said she "didn't see it as a big deal" and "couldn't pinpoint the real reason why some people are so adamant that it has to be a man".

Her 40-year-old male friend said it was "completely out of step with the times".

Tobai Juju, 17, said only allowing men to succeed was "outdated".

"It's discriminatory," she said.

Her 16-year-old friend Oishi agreed and said she didn't think being emperor "had anything to do with gender".

Oishi and Tobai Juju both support the idea of allowing female empresses in Japan. (ABC News: Natalie Whiting)

A 25-year-old woman said she'd "love to see a female emperor" but supposed the "restrictions exist because tradition is being upheld".

"But times have changed," she said.

'Authority and legitimacy' at stake

Japan's first female Prime Minister, Takaichi Sanae, ushered through the recent changes to the law that will keep men on the throne.

Japan may have its first female PM, but some say it is not a win for women In the world of male-dominated politics, Sanae Takaichi has broken through an incredibly tough glass ceiling.

In the lead-up to the parliamentary sitting, she said the emperor's "authority and legitimacy" was linked to the fact the position had been handed down "the male line over 126 generations".

Those who support maintaining the male-only succession are concerned the authority of the role could be undermined by a female emperor.

A key role of the emperor is to promote national unity, and some have said introducing a woman could be destabilising.

Princess Aiko has gained admirers since debuting as an adult royal in 2021. (Reuters: Shuji Kajiyama)

Part of their concern is that a woman could take the throne and hand it down to one of her children under a female line, breaking the chain of patrilineal succession.

"Patrilineal succession to the throne is a tradition our predecessors have defended for over 2,600 years," government MP Kobayashi Takayuki said during a parliamentary committee deliberation on the issue.

But Professor Okawa, who is critical of the recent changes to law, said there was "virtually no-one" in the empirical history field who believed there had been consistent patrilineal succession, and said accession was far more complex in earlier days.

Japan has had eight female emperors in its history. They took the throne to provide stability when there was disagreement on who should succeed, or when a male heir was too young to lead.

Empress Suiko, who ruled Japan between 592 and 628, was the first of eight documented female empresses. (Public domain: Tosa Mitsuyoshi)

It was not until 1889, when the imperial house law was introduced, that succession was formally restricted to males.

Japan has faced international scrutiny over this decision.

In 2024, a United Nations Committee recommended it amend the law to allow women to become emperor, prompting a strong protest from the Japanese government.

When the UN Secretary-General's deputy spokesperson, Farhan Haq, was recently asked to comment on the issue, he said the Secretary-General "encourages all countries to adopt inclusive policies that will empower women in all walks of life and in all forms of employment".

Who could be adopted into Japan's royal family?

The changes to the law that allow the imperial family to adopt long-lost male relatives will come into effect in about three months.

The potential adoptees would be from 11 former imperial houses which lost their royal status during World War II.

Historically, these other houses were used as a back-up to ensure succession, in case the main imperial family ran out of members.

The candidates must be male-line descendants, aged 15 years or older, and with no wife or children.

Professor Okawa said no specific candidates had been announced.

"There is still a significant chance that even if they identify potential candidates and approach them, they will be turned down," Professor Okawa said.

Support for Princess Aiko as a future monarch increased after her first solo official overseas trip to Laos in November. (AP: Kyodo News)

He has cast doubt over whether a "boy of around 15 years of age" being told "out of the blue to become an adopted son in a household he knows nothing about" would agree.

"From the perspective of children's rights, and indeed by any standard of common sense, this is a proposal that is rather chilling," he said.

Princess Mako paid a steep price for her love story Japan's Princess Mako gave up her imperial title and money to be with commoner Kei Komuro. But there is a cloud of uncertainty over what this means for the imperial line's lasting legacy.

The changes to the law will also allow female members of the imperial family to keep their royal status and continue working as representatives if they marry a commoner.

The Imperial family has lost royals to marriage in the past. Most recently, in 2021, then-Princess Mako, niece to the current Emperor, gave up her title to marry her long-term boyfriend. Her decision to finally leave and marry her university sweetheart followed an almost eight-year engagement, scandal and plenty of public scrutiny.

But Professor Okawa said the problem of dwindling numbers of heirs would continue, despite the recent changes.

He said if "we continue to exclude women simply on the grounds of their gender", the gap with public opinion and societal expectations would continue to grow.

"Ultimately, that raises the question of whether the symbolic imperial system itself is meaningless. There is a real risk that that could happen," he said.

World.title: It took 48 years but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait
World.content:
MUSICALS

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical ★★★★★

Victorian Opera, Union Theatre, until July 25

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical sets itself a challenge from the outset. First of all, which version of the much disputed Kelly story do you tell? Do you portray the famous outlaw as a folk hero or a villain? Then, once that is sorted, what tone should the whole thing have? After all, there are very real deaths and tragedies scattered throughout this story – and we all know how badly things turn out for the Kelly gang.

Luke London, Liam Head, Ethan Jones, Darcy Wain as the Kelly Gang. Casey Horsfield

This new production by Victorian Opera navigates all of this deftly. The story firmly has its flag planted in the folk hero camp, but does not gloss over the harsher realities of the story. The crimes are grounded in their context and the scenes slip from high-energy numbers to heart-wrenching grief with deceptive ease. It’s fun without ever being glib and serious without seeming insincere.

There are many times you’ll watch a musical, have a great time, then not be able to hum a single bar the moment you get home. That’s not the case here. In Ned Kelly the music is exceptional: memorable, eclectic and highly accomplished. Conductor Simon Holt – who also provided additional music and orchestration, necessary because there was no complete score of the original – conducts the Victorian Opera Chamber Orchestra with verve.

World.title: Brisbane’s best behaved schools according to parents, students and teachers
World.content:
NationalQueenslandSchools Brisbane’s best behaved schools according to parents, students and teachers Catherine Strohfeldt July 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cindy Leckey has six children, and all but one have been educated at the same primary school on Brisbane’s northside. Like every other parent at Zillmere State School – according to official surveys – she believes behaviour is well managed there. Leckey knows firsthand what happens when a child is suspended, but it hasn’t made her upset with teachers or admin staff. Cindy Leckey has been a Zillmere State School parent since 2006. Catherine Strohfeldt “We’ve had a few hard conversations, but it’s been dealt with how it has to be dealt with,” she said.
