“[School staff] do have a lot of different things in place, but then sometimes even all of them don’t work.” Related Article Schools Inner Brisbane state school slashes suspension rates as others spike Nestled in northern Brisbane suburbia, Zillmere recorded the highest level of agreement from parents that it appropriately handed school behaviour, according to surveys carried out by the Education Department in 2025 and released recently in its annual report. The 106-student primary school also recorded the highest uptick in suspensions from 2024 to 2025 of any Brisbane state school, with the rate increasing by 19.1 percentage points. The Australian Catholic University’s Dr Matthew White, who specialises in school inclusion and attendance, said how a school managed behaviour, including disciplinary absences such as suspensions or exclusions, was also a “double-sided sword”.



“One of the balancing acts for schools is parent expectations, and parents have this expectation that any issues in schools will be dealt with appropriately,” he said. White said a spike in suspensions could be viewed favourably by the bulk of the parent body as a “zero-tolerance” response. However, that approach could alienate the family of the child if the school overused suspensions as a punitive measure, White said. In Leckey’s case, she was satisfied with how Zillmere State School managed behaviour because suspensions were firmly a last resort.



The school also offered students multiple in-school options to regulate their behaviour, she said, including speaking with a chaplain or therapy dog once each week and nominating themselves for a time-out with a wristband system. Related Article Education One in 10 Queensland students need support for emotional, mental struggles More than 93 per cent of Zillmere teachers who responded said the school managed behaviour well, as did 84.6 per cent of student respondents. No Brisbane state school received a 100 per cent satisfaction rate from students. White said this could come down to students reacting differently to disciplinary action, having different expectations, or seeing more of what happens in the classroom or schoolyard.



Across Brisbane, five schools had 100 per cent of staff agree that behaviour was well-managed at their school, including Kedron, Taigum, Wondall Heights, Northgate, and Darra state schools. Kedron State School principal Susie Randel-Kneipp said her students often described her school as “the school with no rules”. Kedron State School had the fourth-highest level of student satisfaction with behaviour management, at 92 per cent. Catherine Strohfeldt “We took away the notion of having a shopping list of micro-behaviours that they shouldn’t engage in, or were framed in a negative light, years and years ago,” she said. Randel-Kniepp said the school was effectively helping kids guide their own good behaviour from as early as prep.



“The faster we get a young person to recognise they are respected, that they have agency and self-efficacy, and, a voice that’s important, the quicker they are to feel a sense of responsibility as to how they conduct themselves,” she said. Related Article Schools How this small school is producing some of Brisbane’s happiest kids The school had the fourth-highest level of student satisfaction with behaviour management, at 92 per cent. The highest proportion of students who thought their school managed behaviour well was recorded at Buranda State School, with 93.8 per cent of respondents. Families, students and teachers were most closely aligned at Greenslopes State School. Among students who responded, 86.4 per cent were satisfied.



Responses varied the greatest at Upper Brookfield State School. Although between 85 and 91 per cent of parents and teachers who responded were satisfied with behaviour management, more than two-thirds of students disagreed the school managed it well. World.title: ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island
World.content:
EnvironmentConservationBiodiversity ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island Caitlin Fitzsimmons July 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kangaroo Island off the coast of South Australia has no feral foxes, rabbits, deer, pigs or goats. Now the dream of eradicating cats from Australia’s third-biggest island is a step closer to reality. The Albanese government is adding $2.7 million to the effort, the final piece of funding to complete an ambitious multiyear feral cat control project led by the Kangaroo Island Landscape Board. Loading The funding injection combines with $370,000 in new philanthropic donations via the Invasive Species Council, and $800,000 from the South Australian government announced in March. Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough said “the finish line is in sight” for one of Australia’s most important island conservation programs to date.



“This is a nationally significant investment in what will become the largest feral cat eradication ever undertaken on an inhabited island anywhere in the world,” Gough said. “Backing this eradication program is backing the survival of species found nowhere else on earth.” One of the AI cameras on the Dudley Peninsula detecting a feral cat with a native animal. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board Since 2020, the landscape board, an arm of the South Australian government, has killed 1900 feral cats by trapping and hunting using a large network of AI-connected cameras. An estimated 150 remain on the Dudley Peninsula, separated from the rest of the island by an electric fence. Last year, a dwindling budget forced the landscape board to focus on maintaining gains rather than making progress. The new funding will pay for a fresh push to eliminate feral cats on the peninsula by 2030. The catproof electric fence that separates Dudley Peninsula from the west on Kangaroo Island. Janie Barrett



Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt said feral cats had already contributed to the extinction of more than 20 mammal species. Kangaroo Island was home to more than 30 threatened species. “The KI community has achieved great results in recent years in reducing feral cat numbers, but we’re conscious that, without further effort, numbers could rebound,” Watt said. Chantelle Geissler with a cat that was caught in one of the many traps as part of the Feral Cat Eradication Program on Kangaroo Island. Janie Barrett Monitoring activity suggests the landscape board is on track to reduce the remaining feral cat population by more than 95 per cent this winter, before moving into mop-up operations and then 24 months of monitoring to prove the absence of cats. There are no more easy wins and the final 150 cats will be the hardest and most expensive to remove. The ultimate goal of the landscape board is to eradicate feral cats from the entire island, while the local government has a policy to phase out ownership of pet cats.



As the apex predator on the island, feral cats devastate native wildlife including Kangaroo Island dunnarts, southern brown bandicoots, Kangaroo Island echidnas, little penguins, hooded plovers and western whipbirds. The cats drain farmers’ resources – money and time – as they spread diseases to sheep, such as toxoplasmosis. The little penguin colony in Penneshaw has increased since the start of the feral cat eradication program. Janie Barrett A feral cat stalking a little penguin on Kangaroo Island, caught on camera. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly, a sheep farmer, said the community solidly backed feral cat eradication and the results so far were encouraging. Pengilly acknowledged that council’s “last cat policy” to end cat ownership on the island by allowing people to retain their existing pets, but not replace them was “by its nature, more problematic”. It would require state legislation to take effect, he added.



“We’re not going in to get rid of Granny’s cat, we know people like their cats, and the end of family cats particularly in towns is a long way off,” Pengilly said. “It’s something that has to be on the radar in the long term to make the place cat free.” Farmer Jayne Bates says community support for feral cat eradication on Kangaroo Island is high. Janie Barrett Kangaroo Island is Australia’s next biggest after Tasmania and the Northern Territory’s Melville Island. It has never had feral rabbits or foxes, and it was declared free of feral goats and deer several years ago, and pigs in June this year. The project has relied on community support because most of the Dudley Peninsula is on private land. Jayne Bates, a sheep farmer and former mayor, believed the feral cat eradication had 100 per cent support, and people were warming to the idea of a pet cat ban. “We’ve been hoping for three decades to get rid of these cats because of the environmental impact and the financial impact on farmers, and finally, we’re within sight – we can almost feel it,” Bates said.



Invasive Species Council policy director Dr Carol Booth said removing feral cats, foxes and rodents from islands was urgent because of the looming threat of H5N1 bird flu. “We can’t stop H5N1 reaching Australia’s wildlife, but we can give threatened species a much better chance of surviving by removing invasive predators and restoring healthier ecosystems,” Booth said. A glossy black cockatoo on Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board A pardalote on Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board



Feral animal and weed control on islands has an outsize benefit for conservation because islands have a high concentration of unique biodiversity. In less than 0.5 per cent of Australia’s landmass, islands contain more than 11.5 per cent of species listed as nationally threatened under federal environmental laws. Globally, most species extinctions have occurred on islands. Related Article Biodiversity It’s gruesome work, but on Kangaroo Island, it’s one of the best things an animal lover can do More than 240 introduced vertebrate populations have been eradicated on more than 170 Australian islands, according to the now-closed Threatened Species Recovery Hub. The threat of bird flu has prompted the government to increase efforts, with new programs under way to eradicate rodents on Adele, Beacon and Gun Islands in Western Australia, cats on Lungtalanana (Clarke) and Three Hummock Islands in Tasmania, goats and cats on French Island in Victoria, and black rats on Warul Kawa (Deliverance Island) in the Torres Strait. The Invasive Species Council is pushing for a national islands eradication fund with $200 million from the federal government over 10 years, plus matching funds from state and territory governments and philanthropists. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Budjerah grew up in the national spotlight. Now he’s ready to reintroduce himself
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At a time when the manosphere has taken over corners of social media, with figures like Andrew Tate and Myron Gaines pushing a conservative and aggressive take on what it means to be a man, singer Budjerah wants to recapture what it means to be a gentleman. The 24-year-old, a Coodjinburra man from the Bundjalung nation, says the way masculinity was represented in his life was consistently positive. “I was very blessed to have so many incredible role models in my family. My dad, my cousins, my brothers, they influenced me in a good way,” he says. “You hear a lot of bad stereotypes about Aboriginal men in particular that aren’t always true. That’s the definition of prejudice.” The idea is at the centre of his debut album, Gentleman. ”I wanted this album to represent positive ways that men can be and the positive effects we can have on other people,” he says. “I think there are positive qualities in a gentleman that everyone can have, like opening doors for someone. Whether you’re a gentleman or not, or you believe in chivalry or not, it’s always best to lead with kindness and respect.” Gentleman is funky, upbeat and assured. The titular opening track oozes swagger, while the swirling Pretty is emblematic of the confidence that Budjerah’s found as an artist. “I like the idea of the gentleman as an aspirational character I could play – this idea of being cool, calm, collected, put together, suave. Really putting in the effort, getting dressed up. I thought that was something cool I could aspire to be.” Budjerah poses with the ARIA award for the Michael Gudinski Breakthrough Artist, which he won in 2021. Brendon Thorne/Getty Images The album arrives after years of percolation, and finds Budjerah carrying the weight of expectation on his shoulders. The singer won the ARIA award for Michael Gudinski Breakthrough Artist in 2021, and has spent the better part of the last decade adding to that success, amassing tens of millions of streams and collaborating with the likes of Ed Sheeran and Kylie Minogue, all off the back of a 2021 self-titled EP and a 2022 EP called Conversations. It’s a career trajectory that is seldom seen in Australia where, all too often, artists aren’t given the time to grow into themselves.



The release of Gentleman, then, is a coming-of-age for an artist who has grown up in the national spotlight, and he’s understandably itching for the album to be out. “The day before a release is always the worst day of my life,” he says. “I just can’t wait for it to be out in the world and I don’t have to think about it any more, and the people can just have their opinions on it. I’m just really excited for that ‘let go’ moment.” That feeling would be understandable for any artist, but especially for Budjerah. Work began on Gentleman when he was 20. He’s now 24, married, and has lived a lot more life. “Since I released my first single, it’s just been about learning and getting myself together. I feel like it was artist development in a way, getting mentored by all these incredible artists and producers and musicians,” he says. With Grammy-winning producer Om’Mas Keith at the helm, Gentleman is an album that is lush and expansive, painting a full picture of Budjerah’s musical journey. “It’s been a whirlwind, a lot of trial and error, trying different things and experimenting. We could do whatever we wanted,” he says. “I felt like I definitely was challenged a lot in the making of this, and my skill was pushed to the limit. I had to really push my singing harder than I’ve sung before, and learning how to dance and sing at the same time was a challenge.” ‘Whether you’re a gentleman or not, or you believe in chivalry or not, it’s always best to lead with kindness and respect.’ His family’s influence is present throughout Gentleman. Budjerah’s parents are both licensed pastors, and he cut his teeth performing at his local church in Fingal Head, long before the world discovered his talents. His band, meanwhile, is made up of his cousins, and his little brother plays keys on Remember Your Name.



His family always hears his music before anyone else. “I always show my demos to my dad and my mum as soon as I leave a studio. It’s straight to them immediately. It’s always good to have honest feedback,” he says with a smile. Budjerah wears his musical influences on his sleeve, looking to Michael Jackson, Usher and Beyoncé for inspiration. The latter even launched a moment of serendipity while he was in Los Angeles and contemplating a trip to Las Vegas to sample the city’s high-profile residencies. “I was gonna see Lady Gaga because she was doing a big band jazz concert, but then I saw Beyoncé was doing the Renaissance tour that weekend and I booked the tickets,” he recalls. “She sang a song called Flaws and All, which is a gratitude song to her fans. I was like, I need a song like Flaws and All. I wanted something to express my gratitude to my family and to my fans.” The day after the concert, his producer Keith (who he affectionately describes as “uncle”) told him they were off to work with the legendary songwriter Diane Warren. Warren, a Grammy-winner and 17-time Oscar nominee, penned I Was Here from Beyoncé‘s Four, Budjerah’s favourite album. During the session, she played the pair Even At My Worst, which became Gentleman’s closing track. Related Article Live music This Oscar winner can’t be here to debut her new work. She has a very good excuse He beams from ear to ear recounting their time together. “She has written so many songs that I love, so getting to meet her and go to her studio, someone I’ve learned from as a songwriter myself, and to be able to hear her songs and to hear her as I’m singing the song, and she’s telling me how to sing it, how to shape the vowels, the specific notes. And if I was a little bit off, she’d correct it and tell me to do it again.” Gentleman is a reintroduction of sorts to the world of Budjerah, a summary of the personal growth he’s experienced over the last half-decade. “A lot of people met me when I was like 16 or 17. Now I’m 24 and the content of the lyrics is a little bit more mature, singing about romance and heartbreak and stuff like that in a different kind of way than what I did six or seven years ago,” he says.

World.title: I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessHealth Opinion I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist July 25, 2026 — 5:30am

July 25, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apparently, it’s a bad habit to cross your legs. It twists your pelvis, elevates your blood pressure and results in lower back pain. The other day someone explained the perils of crossing your legs, detailing the structure of the hominid skeleton. At one point they pulled out their masterstroke argument: “Gorillas don’t cross their knees.” Later on, I wondered: is that right? I fell into a pensive mood. I would have crossed my knees, supercharging my thinking, except I now knew how dangerous that would be. I fantasised about seeing a gorilla with their knees crossed, just sitting there, flipping through a copy of the newspaper, which is what I often do when I have my legs crossed. Embrace your bad habits. It may be all we have left. Getty Images I’d also enjoy seeing a monkey bite their nails or a dolphin scratch their crotch. Human beings have so many bad habits, I’d like to think we’re not the only ones to have parts of ourselves in need of reform. Dogs, after all, have plenty of bad habits. Some of their habits are even worse than those of humans. You won’t find me chewing on other people’s shoes or barking at children just because they’ve decided to walk past our front door. I don’t rush my food. I rarely shed fur. I have never knowingly bitten a postman.



Cats are even worse. I may cross my legs but, compared to a cat, I’m relatively well-behaved. I don’t cough up fur balls. I don’t scratch the furniture. I have only once vomited on a bed, something that for a cat is so commonplace an activity as to be hardly worth recording. Then again, cats rarely drink three beers too many, yell at politicians on the TV, or eat a whole packet of peanuts just before bedtime, so maybe we are even. By the time you get to my age, what’s called your ‘personality’ is just an accretion of bad habits. Emus are total bastards. I know they are on the country’s coat of arms – a privilege they owe to the fact that, alongside the kangaroo, they are unable to go backwards. This, it seems to me, is making a positive out of a negative. It also ignores the fact that if you get too close to them, they’ll bite you. The coat of arms should, at the very least, come with some sort of warning. Put it in Latin if you like: “Hic avis mordet.” By the time you get to my age, what’s called your “personality” is just an accretion of bad habits. Crossing your legs is the least of them. A personality that, in your twenties, was described as “exuberant and carefree” is now “talks too much and refuses to use deodorant”.



Likewise, “thoughtful” somehow becomes “dreary”. “Caring”, even worse, becomes “interfering”. If we all triumphed over our bad habits, I sometimes wonder what would be left? “Oh, that’s Richard. He just sits there.” It could be worse. We could be mice. Our household experienced a mouse infestation a month after the neighbour decided to get chickens. The mice lacked all etiquette. First, they chewed through all the food in the pantry, then they cavorted on the kitchen benchtops. Some nights, once we were asleep, they had an orgy on the couch. It was like living in a student share house in 1983. Every morning, I’d have to apply a heavy application of Domestos. It was even worse when I was dealing with the mice. Related Article Opinion

AI Are we supposed to be impressed by AI? It’s still so dumb Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Humans, it’s true, are the champions when it comes to bad habits. Some bad habits are small, but some are big. Climate change is nothing more than the bad habit of selfishness, expressed on a global scale. World poverty? It’s just an ill-mannered refusal to share. Did no one have parents to teach them how to behave? All the same, is the animal kingdom an appropriate yardstick against which to measure ourselves? Is it fair to use the gorilla as a template for human behaviour? Sure, gorillas don’t cross their knees, hurrah for them, but they also tend to walk on their knuckles and to roar. If I did that in Colesworth, they’d call in the authorities. And if gorillas travelled on trains, lolling on their large backsides, they’d be accused of manspreading. “Can’t you at least cross your legs?” would be the chorus heard up and down the carriage.



Meanwhile, I sit and fret. I’ve spent so many decades crossing my legs, I now find it impossible to stop. Ditto: biting my nails, jiggling my right leg, and reading the best bits of the newspaper aloud to Jocasta, a minute-and-a-half before she was about to read the paper for herself. Could I at least cross my ankles? Apparently not. That’s dangerous too. And so I sit, my pelvis perfectly aligned. My blood pressure is fine, and I have no pain in my lower back. All the same, I have an urge to beat my chest, roar aggressively and then assemble a harem of six females. Which, presumably, is the explanation for all that gorilla bad behaviour. Someone told them they weren’t allowed to cross their legs. Poor saps. I say: embrace your bad habits. It may be all we have left. World.title: Confused by the gods, monsters and mortals of The Odyssey? This is your cheat sheet
World.content:
Can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, we’ve got you.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

So you’ve seen The Odyssey, or you’re planning on seeing it, but can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus*? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, you don’t need a detailed knowledge of Greek mythology to get through Christopher Nolan’s three-hour epic, but a little bit goes a long way. Consider this your starter guide to this Troy story filled with the gods, monsters and mortals of Homer’s epic 3000-year-old tale. Matt Damon as the easily distracted Odysseus in The Odyssey. Odysseus (Matt Damon) The king of Ithaca and a cunning and wise warrior. His journey home from the Trojan War (more on that later) should have taken about two weeks, but it turned into a 10-year epic that is the basis of Homer’s The Odyssey. Married to Penelope, with a son, Telemachus, and faithful dog Argos. Susceptible to witches, sea nymphs and long detours. Odysseus is a faithful yet forgetful husband in the film, which pretty much lines up with the original story, but skips over the bit where he also fathered a son with the witch Circe during his “lost weekend”, aka year on the island of Aeaea. Anne Hathaway as Penelope, and Tom Holland as her son Telemachus. Penelope (Anne Hathaway) Odysseus’ wife, who spent 20 years fending off suitors while her husband was fighting in the Trojan War and then taking a “shortcut” to get home. To deter the suitors, who have essentially moved into the palace, she announces she will only marry once she has finished weaving the burial shroud for her father-in-law, which she unravels every night. Smart! Penelope is also the cousin of Helen, whose affair with Paris kicked off the Trojan War (he was kinda tricked by Zeus and Aphrodite into falling for Helen, but that story is in The Iliad).



Related Article Cinema Every Christopher Nolan movie ranked: How does The Odyssey compare to Oppenheimer? Telemachus (Tom Holland) The son of Odysseus and Penelope. In his 20s, he is a young man keen to do the right thing by his mum, but also has no real idea of who his dad is. He is the ultimate nepo baby but generally a good guy, who – post-Odyssey – goes with his mum to hang out with Circe and his half-brother Telegonus. Antinous (Robert Pattinson) A real jerk who takes advantage of Penelope’s hospitality while trying to woo her. A walking red flag. Argos Odysseus’ faithful hunting dog who waits 20 years for his master’s return. The original good boy.



Loading The Trojan War Essentially, two countries, Greece and Troy, went to war because Helen (played by Lupita Nyong’o), widely considered the most beautiful woman to have ever lived, left her husband, King Menelaus of Sparta (Jon Bernthal), for pretty boy Paris of Troy. Menelaus’ brother Agamemnon (Benny Safdie) then decided war was the next best step. Odysseus became involved because, as one of Helen’s former suitors, he made a pact to always defend her chosen husband. The war lasted roughly 10 years, coming to a bloody conclusion when the Greeks hid in a giant statue of a horse that the Trojans then unwittingly dragged inside the city gates, giving rise to the saying, “Never look a gift horse in the mouth”. Helen, who by this point was married to Paris’ brother Deiphobus after Paris was killed in battle, was dragged back home to Menelaus where they lived unhappily ever after. Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy. Universal Pictures Athena (Zendaya) Daughter of Zeus (ruler of Mount Olympus, aka No.1 God) and the goddess of wisdom and warfare. She sprung fully grown directly from Zeus’ head, after he – totally normally – swallowed her mother Metis, while she was pregnant. In The Odyssey, Athena acts as Odysseus’ protector and mentor. She is a bit of a downer in the film, whereas in the Greek myths, Athena is a total badass who also guided the demigods Perseus and Heracles, defeated a fire-breathing giant and wore armour emblazoned with the head of Medusa. Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as his protector, the Greek goddess Athena.



Circe (Samantha Morton) An independent woman living her best life on the island of Aeaea who just so happens to be a powerful witch. Daughter of the sun god Helios, she bewitches Odysseus’ men, but he manages to talk his way out of it. In the film, Odysseus and his men leave after lunch, but in Homer’s epic, Circe and Odysseus spend one year together after Hermes, the messenger god, convinces Odysseus that sleeping with Circe is the best way to solve his problems. It is not! In another post-Odyssey twist – and real Housewives of Aeaea situation – Circe and Penelope end up living together on Circe’s island, and Circe and Telemachus eventually marry. Write that sequel, Christopher Nolan! Tom Holland as nepo-baby Telemachus, who ends up marrying Circe. Universal Pictures via AP Calypso (Charlize Theron) A sea nymph and minor goddess and possibly the daughter of the Titan Atlas (the Titans ruled before they were overthrown by Zeus etc). She enchants Odysseus and keeps him as her (sex) slave for seven years on the island of Ogygia, while he cries on the beach and sleeps in a cave. Again, this is not in the movie! In the film, she eventually helps Odysseus on his way, but in Homer’s telling, Zeus and Hermes have a stern word before she lets him go. Polyphemus A giant man-eating cyclops who lives in a cave in Sicily tending to his sheep and making artisanal cheese (this is not in the original text). The son of the sea god Poseidon (who is the brother of Zeus and Hades, the god of the underworld), Polyphemus is blinded by Odysseus, who was trying to steal his sheep (again, Odysseus is the, ahem, hero in all of this). As revenge, Polyphemus prays to his father, who then curses Odysseus’ trip home. It works.



Related Article Podcasts The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good The Laestrygonians More giants who also enjoy eating humans. They, apparently, came from one of Poseidon’s sons, making them the nephews of Polyphemus (kind of). They destroy 11 of 12 of Odysseus’ boats. Not happy. The Underworld and Tiresias On the advice of Circe, Odysseus and his men head to the Underworld, which is ruled by Hades, to honour the dead (including the Greek soldier Sinon, played by Eliot Page, a character Nolan borrowed from Virgil’s Aeneid) and seek guidance from the blind prophet Tiresias. In Greek mythology, he’s considered a bit of a gender bender, having also spent seven years as a woman before switching back. In the film, Tiresias is the one giving Odysseus good but dangerous advice about getting home, whereas in the original text, it’s Circe who points Odysseus correctly in the right direction. #justiceforcirce. Robert Pattinson as the ultimate jerk, Antinous, in The Odyssey. Universal Pictures via AP

World.title: Australia had a chance to do something big. Then came weak leadership and fatal errors
World.content:
Under the terms initially laid out by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese , states and territories were meant to agree to reforms by March, and legislate the changes no later than July 1. Both deadlines have come and gone, and a mooted September start date in NSW is looking unlikely.

Of Australia’s eight states and major territories, just two are proceeding with a post-Bondi buyback: NSW and the ACT.

Mikac had hoped to witness a similar national moment following December’s Bondi terror attack , in which 15 people were killed and many more physically and mentally scarred. But a potential repeat of Howard’s 1996 triumph has collapsed under the weight of shifting politics, absent leadership, and disagreement over who foots the bill.

Spurred on by the note, which is now held at the National Museum of Australia, Howard announced his legacy-defining national gun buyback scheme . Some 644,000 newly prohibited semi-automatic and pump-action firearms – one-third of all privately owned guns in Australia – were eventually handed over and destroyed.

“As the person who lost his wife and two beautiful daughters at Port Arthur, I am writing to you to give you the strength to ensure no person in Australia ever has to suffer such a loss,” he pleaded with the then-prime minister.

A little over a week after his wife Nanette and six-year-old daughters Alannah and Madeline were gunned down in Australia’s deadliest mass shooting , Walter Mikac sat down to write a letter to John Howard.

In the Jewish community, patience is wearing thin. Farmers and recreational shooters who will be caught up in the fallout are also in a state of limbo.

To make matters worse, the small number of jurisdictions that do want to take part in Albanese’s scheme still haven’t been able to finish the design of the scheme and strike a funding deal with Canberra.

Howard told this masthead this week: “Although the circumstances do vary, I am very disappointed that Anthony Albanese hasn’t got everybody on side.”

It took Howard just five months to announce, negotiate and begin his national gun buyback scheme following the Port Arthur massacre. By contrast, more than seven months have passed since the Bondi Beach antisemitic attack with no agreement.

Queensland is also out, as is South Australia. Tasmania won’t have a cap and Western Australia has just had 83,000 guns returned under a voluntary return program and feels no need to tie itself to Albanese’s proposal.

Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan rejected a key recommendation by her own independent expert, Ken Lay, to place a cap on how many guns a person can have, fearful of regional voters angrily handing back firearms at the same time as her beleaguered Labor government heads to the polls in November. Victoria Police also wanted a cap and was ignored.

The first was who would pay. Unlike Howard’s buyback, which was federally funded via a temporary increase to the Medicare levy from 1.5 to 1.7 per cent, Albanese’s model called for a 50:50 cost sharing with the states.

But there were three problems with the prime minister’s commitment that meant the idea was fatally flawed from the start.

Billed as “the largest since the Howard government in 1996”, Albanese said the buyback was critical and argued there were now 4 million firearms in Australia – more than at the time of the Port Arthur massacre.

The rot set in the day Albanese announced his plan for a national buyback nearly a week after father and son duo Naveed and Sajid Akram allegedly opened fire on Jewish families at Bondi Beach.

The failure to land a new national gun buyback scheme – one of the key policy responses to flow from the Bondi atrocity – offers an insight into the state of politics in 2026 and the profound power of self-interest.

Albanese eventually relented and agreed to a royal commission – but the father of gun reform speaking in such negative terms offered conservatives cover to shirk bipartisan support.

“I do not want this debate post this horrible event to be used, the focus on guns be used, as a pretext to avoid the broader debate about the spread of hatred of Jewish people and antisemitism,” Howard said in December.

Ironically, Howard – who supports the principle of a fresh buyback – damaged its chances of success in the days after Bondi. Savaging what he said was a failure of Albanese to combat antisemitism, Howard dubbed the prime minister’s proposed buyback a “ diversion ”.

Guns about to be destroyed as part of the 1996 buyback.

Albanese’s second failure was his initial refusal to announce other strong measures. His stubborn resistance to calling a royal commission into the deadly attack meant the measures outlined in his early response – however well-intentioned or needed – suffered by association.

Either way, an argument over costs gave leaders an easy way to sidestep the scheme. Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro was the first leader to baulk at forking out. “We welcome the federal government to have a gun buyback scheme, but Territorians won’t be the ones footing the bill,” she said. “I’ve been very upfront and honest about that from day one.”

Would the deal have got up had Albanese stumped up 100 per cent of the funding? “I’m not so sure,” Australian Gun Safety Alliance convenor Stephen Bendle said this week. “What we’ve seen is that there has been political hesitation more than financial.”

Estimates based on current Victorian firearms ownership data have revealed that less than 20 per cent of the state’s firearms users would be impacted by the cap rejected by Allan.

Critics don’t buy it. The leader of the Victorian Greens, Ellen Sandell, said Allan’s refusal to support a cap was a “total capitulation to One Nation, the gun lobby, or probably both”.

Federal Labor MP Dan Repacholi, who represents the NSW seat of Hunter, supports a buyback scheme but has criticised the four-weapon cap for recreational shooters proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns . Allan, the Victorian premier, holds the regional seat of Bendigo East but denies her political survival was a factor in not following the lead of her NSW Labor counterpart.

Costs are one factor. However, the rise of One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson has seriously spooked state leaders and oppositions. One Nation, which is vehemently opposed to a buyback and has pledged to repeal it, poses a real threat in Labor and Coalition-held electorates with high rates of gun ownership.

But there is much blame to go around. The majority of states have refused to take part even though Virginia Bell explicitly recommended a national buyback in her interim report from the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

The third setback was Albanese’s apparent unwillingness to use his prime ministerial authority to campaign for the changes. Whereas Howard travelled around the country making the case for a buyback, Albanese has been nowhere to be seen. He has spoken of the scheme publicly just a handful of times since February, according to an analysis of Hansard and his own transcripts.

Despite that proportionately small number, 287,000 firearms could have been disposed of had she agreed to the limit and participated in the national buyback.

“Any leader worth their weight would do what’s necessary to keep the community safe after such a horrific massacre as Bondi,” Sandell said in an interview this week. “People expect leaders to stand up and do what is right, even if that might be difficult and requires you to show some guts.

“And that’s why this is so disappointing with what Jacinta Allan has done here – she just does not have the guts to do what must be done.”

One senior Labor figure defended Albanese’s handling of the matter and said weak state leaders like Allan were really to blame for the scheme’s collapse. “They all need to explain why they are ignoring the recommendation of a royal commission that everyone was demanding,” the source, who declined to be named, said.

Prime Minister John Howard addresses a gun rally with a protective vest under his jacket. Andrew Meares

The department of Home Affairs, the domestic spy agency ASIO and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission have also endorsed a buyback, arguing it would help manage individuals with violent extremist ideologies, and frustrate serious and organised crime from obtaining lawful access.

Stolen or missing registered firearms account for nearly 10 per cent of illicit longarms and around 31 per cent of illicit handguns in Australia. Authorities estimate there are at least 250,000 illegal longarms and handguns in Australia, and potentially as many as 500,000.

Bendle also said limiting access would have other benefits, noting the “No.1 cause of firearm deaths is still by suicide”.

Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia chief executive officer James Walsh argued a cap in NSW and other states would not target the right gun owners. “These policies are not going to take a single firearm off a terrorist or a criminal – you’re just taking guns out of a safe,” he said.

“Taking those guns doesn’t increase public safety. Go out and go hard in south-western Sydney and take all the illegal pistols, illegal firearms, and the semi-automatic firearms that are being used. That will actually have tangible public-safety benefits.”

The argument that law-abiding owners saddle the biggest burden in any buyback was given short shrift by Howard in 1996. In his response to Mikac’s emotional letter of early 1996, the then-prime minister replied, saying: “I regret that many people who have never done anything wrong in their lives will be inconvenienced by the new laws, but this is ultimately a small price to pay for a community that feels, and is, more secure.”

Of course, Howard could rely on the crucial support of his deputy, Nationals leader Tim Fischer, who was instrumental in persuading rural Australia of the need for change.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan during a press conference criticising the buyback. Dominic Lorrimer

Walsh said claims his industry and its lobbying arm had too much influence over the failed buyback were wrong. He claimed his organisation had to do little if any campaigning before most states pledged to not take part, and said the Minns government had “refused to speak to us”.

“We have his backbenchers calling, going, ‘there’s nothing that we can do. We know it’s going to cost us our jobs. We know we’re going to lose votes over this, but it’s a captain’s call. He won’t change his mind’.”

An analysis commissioned by his association recently found the cost of buying back weapons in NSW would be about $415 million before other costs such as compensation and administration were added. The government has not publicly disputed the findings of that study.

The delay in securing an agreement between Macquarie Street and Canberra has caused legitimate angst among recreational shooters and primary producers in NSW, who still have no idea whether the government will pay market value for a firearm, rather than a lower set price.

Walsh was scathing of Albanese’s handling of the issue, and his absence from the debate over recent months. “The prime minister seems to say a lot and then change his mind, doesn’t he?

“He came out in an emotion-fuelled speech saying he was going to do this and going to do that. But he hadn’t come to the industry. He hadn’t gone to the states. He didn’t know how many firearms are out there.

“There were questions he should have asked before he came out with this.”

The Herald and The Age asked the prime minister a series of questions, including why he had not been more forceful in his public advocacy for the scheme and whether promising to fully fund the program might have delivered more participation by the states.

In a statement, he said: “We’re continuing to work on the buyback scheme. We’re confident it will lead to a significant reduction in the number of firearms in our community, and that’s a good thing.

“I want fewer guns on our streets.

“The states and territories will make their own decisions about how they choose to participate – but all governments have a responsibility to do all they can to keep Australians safe.”

Chris Minns, whose premiership was redefined by the horror of Bondi, remains 100 per cent behind the gun buyback and has been overheard telling colleagues he thinks it’s an issue worth losing an election over.

Laws that passed parliament in December restrict firearms licences to Australian citizens, reduce the standard term for firearm licences from five years to two years, cap the number of firearms an individual may possess at four, with a higher limit of 10 for primary producers, and restrict access to pump-action, button or lever-release, or straight-pull firearms – such as those used in the Bondi attack – to primary producers.

However, progress on making those laws reality has been painfully slow. Some of the yet-to-be-resolved issues include whether the state can afford to offer market value for guns, which will increase the cost of the scheme, how much should be paid for ammunition and other soon-to-be redundant firearm paraphernalia, potential compensation for gun clubs and stores, and what other exemptions may need to be written into the regulation. There is also a huge amount of work being done on the mechanics of how guns would be collected and destroyed, which NSW Police have had to play a central role in navigating.

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Police Minister Yasmin Catley. Sam Mooy

One senior member of the Minns government, who declined to be named due to cabinet confidentiality, said the work had been frustrating, “but I am sure there will be a deal and this will go ahead”.

Minns and Albanese have been under little political pressure to hurry up because oppositions state and federally do not see a political dividend in supporting the buyback.

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane told a NSW Farmers’ conference in Sydney this week that while the NSW Liberals supported Minns’ gun laws in December, they wanted changes.

Bondi is personal for Sloane – she was one of the first on the scene to render assistance to the dead and wounded – but like her Victorian counterparts she is being squeezed by One Nation ahead of the March election.

“There were two terrorists that caused that attack,” Sloane told the crowd. “It was not farmers. I know you feel like you’re being punished. I know that those 10-gun caps in your communities feel unworkable. So I want to say that we are working with the government, with stakeholders, to make amends.”

Privately, the state government is angry at other states for capitulating to the threat of a backlash and does not blame Albanese.

Minns told this masthead on Friday: “There is goodwill from both the NSW and federal governments on this, and we’ll get it done. We remain absolutely committed to the buyback scheme.”

Minns has previously argued NSW will end up with the “strongest gun laws in Australia”. That may be true, but it would be easy for someone to cross a border and more easily obtain weapons in states with a higher supply.

Perhaps aware of the potential for states to go their own ways, the royal commission’s interim report warned against patchy laws. “There is a public interest in national consistency in firearms regulation in Australia, where extensive and largely unmonitored state and territory borders make it possible for people and firearms to move between jurisdictions with relative ease,” the report noted.

Bendle from the Gun Safety Alliance agreed things had not landed where he had hoped. “There was some hope among public health experts that there might be some light come out of the shadow of a Bondi,” he said.

He said while some states won’t sign up to a full national gun buyback, many may still alter their gun laws, and that would be a good thing. “But it won’t be the same as 1996.”

World.title: How to (safely) access the cash locked up in your property
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingBudgeting Opinion How to (safely) access the cash locked up in your property Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor July 25, 2026 — 5:01am

July 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are times in your life – and possibly through different stages of your life – when your money requirements are larger than your income. I don’t mean a straight imbalance between your salary and your expenses. I’m talking about big ticket things like the need to renovate, replace a car (without an expensive personal loan), maybe pay for kids’ education last minute. Or it’s a retirement funding shortfall that’s making life, well, miserable. The big potential disadvantage from any reverse mortgage is compounding interest rates could take a big bite from the estate when the borrower dies and the outstanding loan is repaid. Simon Letch Perhaps, increasingly commonly, you want to financially help adult children when they need it most. Thanks to the huge rise in property prices benefiting the older generation, the so-called living inheritance to get the next generation into housing is growing in popularity. No matter why, there are options at every age to get out the equity you might think is locked in your property.



Until your mid-50s Mortgage refinance: Often – and particularly after three rate rises this year – a mortgage refinance is about cutting your monthly repayments. But sometimes it is about getting a larger loan. And it’s even possible that, with the combination of both, you could extract equity without increasing your minimum repayment. This option is available earliest – just as soon as you have built enough equity to withdraw and maintain the maximum loan-to-value ratio. For asset rich but cash poor Aussies, at every age there are options. But it’s also an opportunity that evaporates as your retirement approaches, as lenders don’t love retired borrowers. So, if it’s something that features in your financial strategy, don’t leave it too late – keep a close eye on that retirement date.



And be aware, too, that if you extend your loan term, though it’s another way of keeping repayments low, you could end up paying way more interest overall. Editor's pick Opinion

Income tax The five tax return mistakes that could get you audited Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor From your mid-50s Downsize: Don’t miss that the cheapest way of using your home for a cash injection is to sell it and buy something of a lesser value (bearing in mind that many people who trade a house for an apartment end up down-sizing but up-pricing). From age 55, the government has also increased the incentive by allowing you to deposit $300,000 of the proceeds into super, where they can grow with only 15 per cent tax on earnings (for balances under $3 million), becoming tax-free once you retire or turn 65.



The further beauty is that each person in a couple can do this. The only restriction is that you need to have owned the property for 10 years. But there are two ways to get out equity without selling, also usually from age 55... The reverse mortgage and home reversion scheme: A reverse mortgage is still a type of home loan but works the opposite way in that the debt ratchets up rather than whittles down. Available as a lump sum or income stream, you make no repayments. Instead, the ultimate debt is repaid by other funds if you choose, or from the sale of your house earlier or on your death (check that all options are available). The interest due will roll up until that time, and because you will pay interest on interest, can become large. Of course, the value of the property might also increase over that time. Most importantly, a no-negative-equity guarantee means the debt can never grow to more than the value of the property, and you can never be evicted for this reason (see if there are any other reasons though).



The home reversion scheme is an alternative with different advantages and disadvantages. Here, there is no interest payable, rather this is a shared ownership arrangement from the outset. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should I sell my home to help my three children buy a house? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You sign over a portion of your home that is then recouped by the financial institution, again from your other funds if you choose or from your property’s sale before or on your death (check). It’s essential to get advice before making either a reverse mortgage or home reversion move. Some considerations are that with a home reversion scheme, you have an immediate liability … say, 40 per cent of your home is gone the day you settle. Of course, your – in this case – 60 per cent could still increase in value. You can delay this liability with the reverse mortgage approach – the debt only grows over time. The less time it has to grow, the better, and you might also have the option not to draw down on your funds until you need them.



The longer you wait before taking out either product, the more money you can extract. Finally, both moves can potentially deplete your kids’ inheritance – just so you know. And there may be less money left to fund aged care down the track. Speaking of, there is a cheaper option available later in life… From age 67 Home equity access scheme: At age 67, a government opportunity kicks in for people eligible for the age pension. The home equity access scheme via Services Australia is like a reverse mortgage in that you take out a loan against your equity that rolls up. However, the interest rate is far cheaper – it’s currently 3.95 per cent versus, say, 8 per cent for a commercial reverse mortgage. Being an official scheme, however, you can also get out far less and only as a small lump sum and then regular income. Your pension and loan payment can’t be more each fortnight than 1.5 times the full age pension.



Know, though, that for asset rich but cash poor Aussies, at every age there are options. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: It took 48 years but this show has finally made it to Melbourne. It was worth the wait
World.content:
MUSICALS

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical ★★★★★

Victorian Opera, Union Theatre, until July 25

Reg Livermore’s Ned Kelly: The Musical sets itself a challenge from the outset. First of all, which version of the much disputed Kelly story do you tell? Do you portray the famous outlaw as a folk hero or a villain? Then, once that is sorted, what tone should the whole thing have? After all, there are very real deaths and tragedies scattered throughout this story – and we all know how badly things turn out for the Kelly gang.

Luke London, Liam Head, Ethan Jones, Darcy Wain as the Kelly Gang. Casey Horsfield

This new production by Victorian Opera navigates all of this deftly. The story firmly has its flag planted in the folk hero camp, but does not gloss over the harsher realities of the story. The crimes are grounded in their context and the scenes slip from high-energy numbers to heart-wrenching grief with deceptive ease. It’s fun without ever being glib and serious without seeming insincere.

There are many times you’ll watch a musical, have a great time, then not be able to hum a single bar the moment you get home. That’s not the case here. In Ned Kelly the music is exceptional: memorable, eclectic and highly accomplished. Conductor Simon Holt – who also provided additional music and orchestration, necessary because there was no complete score of the original – conducts the Victorian Opera Chamber Orchestra with verve.

World.title: Brisbane’s best behaved schools according to parents, students and teachers
World.content:
NationalQueenslandSchools Brisbane’s best behaved schools according to parents, students and teachers Catherine Strohfeldt July 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Cindy Leckey has six children, and all but one have been educated at the same primary school on Brisbane’s northside. Like every other parent at Zillmere State School – according to official surveys – she believes behaviour is well managed there. Leckey knows firsthand what happens when a child is suspended, but it hasn’t made her upset with teachers or admin staff. Cindy Leckey has been a Zillmere State School parent since 2006. Catherine Strohfeldt “We’ve had a few hard conversations, but it’s been dealt with how it has to be dealt with,” she said.



“[School staff] do have a lot of different things in place, but then sometimes even all of them don’t work.” Related Article Schools Inner Brisbane state school slashes suspension rates as others spike Nestled in northern Brisbane suburbia, Zillmere recorded the highest level of agreement from parents that it appropriately handed school behaviour, according to surveys carried out by the Education Department in 2025 and released recently in its annual report. The 106-student primary school also recorded the highest uptick in suspensions from 2024 to 2025 of any Brisbane state school, with the rate increasing by 19.1 percentage points. The Australian Catholic University’s Dr Matthew White, who specialises in school inclusion and attendance, said how a school managed behaviour, including disciplinary absences such as suspensions or exclusions, was also a “double-sided sword”.



“One of the balancing acts for schools is parent expectations, and parents have this expectation that any issues in schools will be dealt with appropriately,” he said. White said a spike in suspensions could be viewed favourably by the bulk of the parent body as a “zero-tolerance” response. However, that approach could alienate the family of the child if the school overused suspensions as a punitive measure, White said. In Leckey’s case, she was satisfied with how Zillmere State School managed behaviour because suspensions were firmly a last resort.



The school also offered students multiple in-school options to regulate their behaviour, she said, including speaking with a chaplain or therapy dog once each week and nominating themselves for a time-out with a wristband system. Related Article Education One in 10 Queensland students need support for emotional, mental struggles More than 93 per cent of Zillmere teachers who responded said the school managed behaviour well, as did 84.6 per cent of student respondents. No Brisbane state school received a 100 per cent satisfaction rate from students. White said this could come down to students reacting differently to disciplinary action, having different expectations, or seeing more of what happens in the classroom or schoolyard.



Across Brisbane, five schools had 100 per cent of staff agree that behaviour was well-managed at their school, including Kedron, Taigum, Wondall Heights, Northgate, and Darra state schools. Kedron State School principal Susie Randel-Kneipp said her students often described her school as “the school with no rules”. Kedron State School had the fourth-highest level of student satisfaction with behaviour management, at 92 per cent. Catherine Strohfeldt “We took away the notion of having a shopping list of micro-behaviours that they shouldn’t engage in, or were framed in a negative light, years and years ago,” she said. Randel-Kniepp said the school was effectively helping kids guide their own good behaviour from as early as prep.



“The faster we get a young person to recognise they are respected, that they have agency and self-efficacy, and, a voice that’s important, the quicker they are to feel a sense of responsibility as to how they conduct themselves,” she said. Related Article Schools How this small school is producing some of Brisbane’s happiest kids The school had the fourth-highest level of student satisfaction with behaviour management, at 92 per cent. The highest proportion of students who thought their school managed behaviour well was recorded at Buranda State School, with 93.8 per cent of respondents. Families, students and teachers were most closely aligned at Greenslopes State School. Among students who responded, 86.4 per cent were satisfied.



Responses varied the greatest at Upper Brookfield State School. Although between 85 and 91 per cent of parents and teachers who responded were satisfied with behaviour management, more than two-thirds of students disagreed the school managed it well. World.title: ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island
World.content:
EnvironmentConservationBiodiversity ‘Finish line in sight’ for world-leading cat eradication on Kangaroo Island Caitlin Fitzsimmons July 25, 2026 — 6:00am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Kangaroo Island off the coast of South Australia has no feral foxes, rabbits, deer, pigs or goats. Now the dream of eradicating cats from Australia’s third-biggest island is a step closer to reality. The Albanese government is adding $2.7 million to the effort, the final piece of funding to complete an ambitious multiyear feral cat control project led by the Kangaroo Island Landscape Board. Loading The funding injection combines with $370,000 in new philanthropic donations via the Invasive Species Council, and $800,000 from the South Australian government announced in March. Invasive Species Council chief executive Jack Gough said “the finish line is in sight” for one of Australia’s most important island conservation programs to date.



“This is a nationally significant investment in what will become the largest feral cat eradication ever undertaken on an inhabited island anywhere in the world,” Gough said. “Backing this eradication program is backing the survival of species found nowhere else on earth.” One of the AI cameras on the Dudley Peninsula detecting a feral cat with a native animal. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board Since 2020, the landscape board, an arm of the South Australian government, has killed 1900 feral cats by trapping and hunting using a large network of AI-connected cameras. An estimated 150 remain on the Dudley Peninsula, separated from the rest of the island by an electric fence. Last year, a dwindling budget forced the landscape board to focus on maintaining gains rather than making progress. The new funding will pay for a fresh push to eliminate feral cats on the peninsula by 2030. The catproof electric fence that separates Dudley Peninsula from the west on Kangaroo Island. Janie Barrett



Federal Environment Minister Murray Watt said feral cats had already contributed to the extinction of more than 20 mammal species. Kangaroo Island was home to more than 30 threatened species. “The KI community has achieved great results in recent years in reducing feral cat numbers, but we’re conscious that, without further effort, numbers could rebound,” Watt said. Chantelle Geissler with a cat that was caught in one of the many traps as part of the Feral Cat Eradication Program on Kangaroo Island. Janie Barrett Monitoring activity suggests the landscape board is on track to reduce the remaining feral cat population by more than 95 per cent this winter, before moving into mop-up operations and then 24 months of monitoring to prove the absence of cats. There are no more easy wins and the final 150 cats will be the hardest and most expensive to remove. The ultimate goal of the landscape board is to eradicate feral cats from the entire island, while the local government has a policy to phase out ownership of pet cats.



As the apex predator on the island, feral cats devastate native wildlife including Kangaroo Island dunnarts, southern brown bandicoots, Kangaroo Island echidnas, little penguins, hooded plovers and western whipbirds. The cats drain farmers’ resources – money and time – as they spread diseases to sheep, such as toxoplasmosis. The little penguin colony in Penneshaw has increased since the start of the feral cat eradication program. Janie Barrett A feral cat stalking a little penguin on Kangaroo Island, caught on camera. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board Kangaroo Island Mayor Michael Pengilly, a sheep farmer, said the community solidly backed feral cat eradication and the results so far were encouraging. Pengilly acknowledged that council’s “last cat policy” to end cat ownership on the island by allowing people to retain their existing pets, but not replace them was “by its nature, more problematic”. It would require state legislation to take effect, he added.



“We’re not going in to get rid of Granny’s cat, we know people like their cats, and the end of family cats particularly in towns is a long way off,” Pengilly said. “It’s something that has to be on the radar in the long term to make the place cat free.” Farmer Jayne Bates says community support for feral cat eradication on Kangaroo Island is high. Janie Barrett Kangaroo Island is Australia’s next biggest after Tasmania and the Northern Territory’s Melville Island. It has never had feral rabbits or foxes, and it was declared free of feral goats and deer several years ago, and pigs in June this year. The project has relied on community support because most of the Dudley Peninsula is on private land. Jayne Bates, a sheep farmer and former mayor, believed the feral cat eradication had 100 per cent support, and people were warming to the idea of a pet cat ban. “We’ve been hoping for three decades to get rid of these cats because of the environmental impact and the financial impact on farmers, and finally, we’re within sight – we can almost feel it,” Bates said.



Invasive Species Council policy director Dr Carol Booth said removing feral cats, foxes and rodents from islands was urgent because of the looming threat of H5N1 bird flu. “We can’t stop H5N1 reaching Australia’s wildlife, but we can give threatened species a much better chance of surviving by removing invasive predators and restoring healthier ecosystems,” Booth said. A glossy black cockatoo on Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board A pardalote on Kangaroo Island. Kangaroo Island Landscape Board



Feral animal and weed control on islands has an outsize benefit for conservation because islands have a high concentration of unique biodiversity. In less than 0.5 per cent of Australia’s landmass, islands contain more than 11.5 per cent of species listed as nationally threatened under federal environmental laws. Globally, most species extinctions have occurred on islands. Related Article Biodiversity It’s gruesome work, but on Kangaroo Island, it’s one of the best things an animal lover can do More than 240 introduced vertebrate populations have been eradicated on more than 170 Australian islands, according to the now-closed Threatened Species Recovery Hub. The threat of bird flu has prompted the government to increase efforts, with new programs under way to eradicate rodents on Adele, Beacon and Gun Islands in Western Australia, cats on Lungtalanana (Clarke) and Three Hummock Islands in Tasmania, goats and cats on French Island in Victoria, and black rats on Warul Kawa (Deliverance Island) in the Torres Strait. The Invasive Species Council is pushing for a national islands eradication fund with $200 million from the federal government over 10 years, plus matching funds from state and territory governments and philanthropists. Get to the heart of what’s happening with climate change and the environment.

World.title: Budjerah grew up in the national spotlight. Now he’s ready to reintroduce himself
World.content:
Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

At a time when the manosphere has taken over corners of social media, with figures like Andrew Tate and Myron Gaines pushing a conservative and aggressive take on what it means to be a man, singer Budjerah wants to recapture what it means to be a gentleman. The 24-year-old, a Coodjinburra man from the Bundjalung nation, says the way masculinity was represented in his life was consistently positive. “I was very blessed to have so many incredible role models in my family. My dad, my cousins, my brothers, they influenced me in a good way,” he says. “You hear a lot of bad stereotypes about Aboriginal men in particular that aren’t always true. That’s the definition of prejudice.” The idea is at the centre of his debut album, Gentleman. ”I wanted this album to represent positive ways that men can be and the positive effects we can have on other people,” he says. “I think there are positive qualities in a gentleman that everyone can have, like opening doors for someone. Whether you’re a gentleman or not, or you believe in chivalry or not, it’s always best to lead with kindness and respect.” Gentleman is funky, upbeat and assured. The titular opening track oozes swagger, while the swirling Pretty is emblematic of the confidence that Budjerah’s found as an artist. “I like the idea of the gentleman as an aspirational character I could play – this idea of being cool, calm, collected, put together, suave. Really putting in the effort, getting dressed up. I thought that was something cool I could aspire to be.” Budjerah poses with the ARIA award for the Michael Gudinski Breakthrough Artist, which he won in 2021. Brendon Thorne/Getty Images The album arrives after years of percolation, and finds Budjerah carrying the weight of expectation on his shoulders. The singer won the ARIA award for Michael Gudinski Breakthrough Artist in 2021, and has spent the better part of the last decade adding to that success, amassing tens of millions of streams and collaborating with the likes of Ed Sheeran and Kylie Minogue, all off the back of a 2021 self-titled EP and a 2022 EP called Conversations. It’s a career trajectory that is seldom seen in Australia where, all too often, artists aren’t given the time to grow into themselves.



The release of Gentleman, then, is a coming-of-age for an artist who has grown up in the national spotlight, and he’s understandably itching for the album to be out. “The day before a release is always the worst day of my life,” he says. “I just can’t wait for it to be out in the world and I don’t have to think about it any more, and the people can just have their opinions on it. I’m just really excited for that ‘let go’ moment.” That feeling would be understandable for any artist, but especially for Budjerah. Work began on Gentleman when he was 20. He’s now 24, married, and has lived a lot more life. “Since I released my first single, it’s just been about learning and getting myself together. I feel like it was artist development in a way, getting mentored by all these incredible artists and producers and musicians,” he says. With Grammy-winning producer Om’Mas Keith at the helm, Gentleman is an album that is lush and expansive, painting a full picture of Budjerah’s musical journey. “It’s been a whirlwind, a lot of trial and error, trying different things and experimenting. We could do whatever we wanted,” he says. “I felt like I definitely was challenged a lot in the making of this, and my skill was pushed to the limit. I had to really push my singing harder than I’ve sung before, and learning how to dance and sing at the same time was a challenge.” ‘Whether you’re a gentleman or not, or you believe in chivalry or not, it’s always best to lead with kindness and respect.’ His family’s influence is present throughout Gentleman. Budjerah’s parents are both licensed pastors, and he cut his teeth performing at his local church in Fingal Head, long before the world discovered his talents. His band, meanwhile, is made up of his cousins, and his little brother plays keys on Remember Your Name.



His family always hears his music before anyone else. “I always show my demos to my dad and my mum as soon as I leave a studio. It’s straight to them immediately. It’s always good to have honest feedback,” he says with a smile. Budjerah wears his musical influences on his sleeve, looking to Michael Jackson, Usher and Beyoncé for inspiration. The latter even launched a moment of serendipity while he was in Los Angeles and contemplating a trip to Las Vegas to sample the city’s high-profile residencies. “I was gonna see Lady Gaga because she was doing a big band jazz concert, but then I saw Beyoncé was doing the Renaissance tour that weekend and I booked the tickets,” he recalls. “She sang a song called Flaws and All, which is a gratitude song to her fans. I was like, I need a song like Flaws and All. I wanted something to express my gratitude to my family and to my fans.” The day after the concert, his producer Keith (who he affectionately describes as “uncle”) told him they were off to work with the legendary songwriter Diane Warren. Warren, a Grammy-winner and 17-time Oscar nominee, penned I Was Here from Beyoncé‘s Four, Budjerah’s favourite album. During the session, she played the pair Even At My Worst, which became Gentleman’s closing track. Related Article Live music This Oscar winner can’t be here to debut her new work. She has a very good excuse He beams from ear to ear recounting their time together. “She has written so many songs that I love, so getting to meet her and go to her studio, someone I’ve learned from as a songwriter myself, and to be able to hear her songs and to hear her as I’m singing the song, and she’s telling me how to sing it, how to shape the vowels, the specific notes. And if I was a little bit off, she’d correct it and tell me to do it again.” Gentleman is a reintroduction of sorts to the world of Budjerah, a summary of the personal growth he’s experienced over the last half-decade. “A lot of people met me when I was like 16 or 17. Now I’m 24 and the content of the lyrics is a little bit more mature, singing about romance and heartbreak and stuff like that in a different kind of way than what I did six or seven years ago,” he says.

World.title: I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla
World.content:
LifestyleHealth & wellnessHealth Opinion I’m just a creature of habit. Sometimes that creature is a gorilla Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist July 25, 2026 — 5:30am

July 25, 2026 — 5:30am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Apparently, it’s a bad habit to cross your legs. It twists your pelvis, elevates your blood pressure and results in lower back pain. The other day someone explained the perils of crossing your legs, detailing the structure of the hominid skeleton. At one point they pulled out their masterstroke argument: “Gorillas don’t cross their knees.” Later on, I wondered: is that right? I fell into a pensive mood. I would have crossed my knees, supercharging my thinking, except I now knew how dangerous that would be. I fantasised about seeing a gorilla with their knees crossed, just sitting there, flipping through a copy of the newspaper, which is what I often do when I have my legs crossed. Embrace your bad habits. It may be all we have left. Getty Images I’d also enjoy seeing a monkey bite their nails or a dolphin scratch their crotch. Human beings have so many bad habits, I’d like to think we’re not the only ones to have parts of ourselves in need of reform. Dogs, after all, have plenty of bad habits. Some of their habits are even worse than those of humans. You won’t find me chewing on other people’s shoes or barking at children just because they’ve decided to walk past our front door. I don’t rush my food. I rarely shed fur. I have never knowingly bitten a postman.



Cats are even worse. I may cross my legs but, compared to a cat, I’m relatively well-behaved. I don’t cough up fur balls. I don’t scratch the furniture. I have only once vomited on a bed, something that for a cat is so commonplace an activity as to be hardly worth recording. Then again, cats rarely drink three beers too many, yell at politicians on the TV, or eat a whole packet of peanuts just before bedtime, so maybe we are even. By the time you get to my age, what’s called your ‘personality’ is just an accretion of bad habits. Emus are total bastards. I know they are on the country’s coat of arms – a privilege they owe to the fact that, alongside the kangaroo, they are unable to go backwards. This, it seems to me, is making a positive out of a negative. It also ignores the fact that if you get too close to them, they’ll bite you. The coat of arms should, at the very least, come with some sort of warning. Put it in Latin if you like: “Hic avis mordet.” By the time you get to my age, what’s called your “personality” is just an accretion of bad habits. Crossing your legs is the least of them. A personality that, in your twenties, was described as “exuberant and carefree” is now “talks too much and refuses to use deodorant”.



Likewise, “thoughtful” somehow becomes “dreary”. “Caring”, even worse, becomes “interfering”. If we all triumphed over our bad habits, I sometimes wonder what would be left? “Oh, that’s Richard. He just sits there.” It could be worse. We could be mice. Our household experienced a mouse infestation a month after the neighbour decided to get chickens. The mice lacked all etiquette. First, they chewed through all the food in the pantry, then they cavorted on the kitchen benchtops. Some nights, once we were asleep, they had an orgy on the couch. It was like living in a student share house in 1983. Every morning, I’d have to apply a heavy application of Domestos. It was even worse when I was dealing with the mice. Related Article Opinion

AI Are we supposed to be impressed by AI? It’s still so dumb Richard Glover Broadcaster and columnist Humans, it’s true, are the champions when it comes to bad habits. Some bad habits are small, but some are big. Climate change is nothing more than the bad habit of selfishness, expressed on a global scale. World poverty? It’s just an ill-mannered refusal to share. Did no one have parents to teach them how to behave? All the same, is the animal kingdom an appropriate yardstick against which to measure ourselves? Is it fair to use the gorilla as a template for human behaviour? Sure, gorillas don’t cross their knees, hurrah for them, but they also tend to walk on their knuckles and to roar. If I did that in Colesworth, they’d call in the authorities. And if gorillas travelled on trains, lolling on their large backsides, they’d be accused of manspreading. “Can’t you at least cross your legs?” would be the chorus heard up and down the carriage.



Meanwhile, I sit and fret. I’ve spent so many decades crossing my legs, I now find it impossible to stop. Ditto: biting my nails, jiggling my right leg, and reading the best bits of the newspaper aloud to Jocasta, a minute-and-a-half before she was about to read the paper for herself. Could I at least cross my ankles? Apparently not. That’s dangerous too. And so I sit, my pelvis perfectly aligned. My blood pressure is fine, and I have no pain in my lower back. All the same, I have an urge to beat my chest, roar aggressively and then assemble a harem of six females. Which, presumably, is the explanation for all that gorilla bad behaviour. Someone told them they weren’t allowed to cross their legs. Poor saps. I say: embrace your bad habits. It may be all we have left.
