World.title: Confused by the gods, monsters and mortals of The Odyssey? This is your cheat sheet
World.content:
Can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, we’ve got you.

Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

So you’ve seen The Odyssey, or you’re planning on seeing it, but can’t tell your Zeus from your Zelus*? Or think Scylla is some kind of hip-hop fusion band? Don’t worry, you don’t need a detailed knowledge of Greek mythology to get through Christopher Nolan’s three-hour epic, but a little bit goes a long way. Consider this your starter guide to this Troy story filled with the gods, monsters and mortals of Homer’s epic 3000-year-old tale. Matt Damon as the easily distracted Odysseus in The Odyssey. Odysseus (Matt Damon) The king of Ithaca and a cunning and wise warrior. His journey home from the Trojan War (more on that later) should have taken about two weeks, but it turned into a 10-year epic that is the basis of Homer’s The Odyssey. Married to Penelope, with a son, Telemachus, and faithful dog Argos. Susceptible to witches, sea nymphs and long detours. Odysseus is a faithful yet forgetful husband in the film, which pretty much lines up with the original story, but skips over the bit where he also fathered a son with the witch Circe during his “lost weekend”, aka year on the island of Aeaea. Anne Hathaway as Penelope, and Tom Holland as her son Telemachus. Penelope (Anne Hathaway) Odysseus’ wife, who spent 20 years fending off suitors while her husband was fighting in the Trojan War and then taking a “shortcut” to get home. To deter the suitors, who have essentially moved into the palace, she announces she will only marry once she has finished weaving the burial shroud for her father-in-law, which she unravels every night. Smart! Penelope is also the cousin of Helen, whose affair with Paris kicked off the Trojan War (he was kinda tricked by Zeus and Aphrodite into falling for Helen, but that story is in The Iliad).



Related Article Cinema Every Christopher Nolan movie ranked: How does The Odyssey compare to Oppenheimer? Telemachus (Tom Holland) The son of Odysseus and Penelope. In his 20s, he is a young man keen to do the right thing by his mum, but also has no real idea of who his dad is. He is the ultimate nepo baby but generally a good guy, who – post-Odyssey – goes with his mum to hang out with Circe and his half-brother Telegonus. Antinous (Robert Pattinson) A real jerk who takes advantage of Penelope’s hospitality while trying to woo her. A walking red flag. Argos Odysseus’ faithful hunting dog who waits 20 years for his master’s return. The original good boy.



Loading The Trojan War Essentially, two countries, Greece and Troy, went to war because Helen (played by Lupita Nyong’o), widely considered the most beautiful woman to have ever lived, left her husband, King Menelaus of Sparta (Jon Bernthal), for pretty boy Paris of Troy. Menelaus’ brother Agamemnon (Benny Safdie) then decided war was the next best step. Odysseus became involved because, as one of Helen’s former suitors, he made a pact to always defend her chosen husband. The war lasted roughly 10 years, coming to a bloody conclusion when the Greeks hid in a giant statue of a horse that the Trojans then unwittingly dragged inside the city gates, giving rise to the saying, “Never look a gift horse in the mouth”. Helen, who by this point was married to Paris’ brother Deiphobus after Paris was killed in battle, was dragged back home to Menelaus where they lived unhappily ever after. Lupita Nyong’o as Helen of Troy. Universal Pictures Athena (Zendaya) Daughter of Zeus (ruler of Mount Olympus, aka No.1 God) and the goddess of wisdom and warfare. She sprung fully grown directly from Zeus’ head, after he – totally normally – swallowed her mother Metis, while she was pregnant. In The Odyssey, Athena acts as Odysseus’ protector and mentor. She is a bit of a downer in the film, whereas in the Greek myths, Athena is a total badass who also guided the demigods Perseus and Heracles, defeated a fire-breathing giant and wore armour emblazoned with the head of Medusa. Matt Damon as Odysseus and Zendaya as his protector, the Greek goddess Athena.



Circe (Samantha Morton) An independent woman living her best life on the island of Aeaea who just so happens to be a powerful witch. Daughter of the sun god Helios, she bewitches Odysseus’ men, but he manages to talk his way out of it. In the film, Odysseus and his men leave after lunch, but in Homer’s epic, Circe and Odysseus spend one year together after Hermes, the messenger god, convinces Odysseus that sleeping with Circe is the best way to solve his problems. It is not! In another post-Odyssey twist – and real Housewives of Aeaea situation – Circe and Penelope end up living together on Circe’s island, and Circe and Telemachus eventually marry. Write that sequel, Christopher Nolan! Tom Holland as nepo-baby Telemachus, who ends up marrying Circe. Universal Pictures via AP Calypso (Charlize Theron) A sea nymph and minor goddess and possibly the daughter of the Titan Atlas (the Titans ruled before they were overthrown by Zeus etc). She enchants Odysseus and keeps him as her (sex) slave for seven years on the island of Ogygia, while he cries on the beach and sleeps in a cave. Again, this is not in the movie! In the film, she eventually helps Odysseus on his way, but in Homer’s telling, Zeus and Hermes have a stern word before she lets him go. Polyphemus A giant man-eating cyclops who lives in a cave in Sicily tending to his sheep and making artisanal cheese (this is not in the original text). The son of the sea god Poseidon (who is the brother of Zeus and Hades, the god of the underworld), Polyphemus is blinded by Odysseus, who was trying to steal his sheep (again, Odysseus is the, ahem, hero in all of this). As revenge, Polyphemus prays to his father, who then curses Odysseus’ trip home. It works.



Related Article Podcasts The Odyssey has called it: Guilt is good The Laestrygonians More giants who also enjoy eating humans. They, apparently, came from one of Poseidon’s sons, making them the nephews of Polyphemus (kind of). They destroy 11 of 12 of Odysseus’ boats. Not happy. The Underworld and Tiresias On the advice of Circe, Odysseus and his men head to the Underworld, which is ruled by Hades, to honour the dead (including the Greek soldier Sinon, played by Eliot Page, a character Nolan borrowed from Virgil’s Aeneid) and seek guidance from the blind prophet Tiresias. In Greek mythology, he’s considered a bit of a gender bender, having also spent seven years as a woman before switching back. In the film, Tiresias is the one giving Odysseus good but dangerous advice about getting home, whereas in the original text, it’s Circe who points Odysseus correctly in the right direction. #justiceforcirce. Robert Pattinson as the ultimate jerk, Antinous, in The Odyssey. Universal Pictures via AP

World.title: Australia had a chance to do something big. Then came weak leadership and fatal errors
World.content:
Under the terms initially laid out by Prime Minister Anthony Albanese , states and territories were meant to agree to reforms by March, and legislate the changes no later than July 1. Both deadlines have come and gone, and a mooted September start date in NSW is looking unlikely.

Of Australia’s eight states and major territories, just two are proceeding with a post-Bondi buyback: NSW and the ACT.

Mikac had hoped to witness a similar national moment following December’s Bondi terror attack , in which 15 people were killed and many more physically and mentally scarred. But a potential repeat of Howard’s 1996 triumph has collapsed under the weight of shifting politics, absent leadership, and disagreement over who foots the bill.

Spurred on by the note, which is now held at the National Museum of Australia, Howard announced his legacy-defining national gun buyback scheme . Some 644,000 newly prohibited semi-automatic and pump-action firearms – one-third of all privately owned guns in Australia – were eventually handed over and destroyed.

“As the person who lost his wife and two beautiful daughters at Port Arthur, I am writing to you to give you the strength to ensure no person in Australia ever has to suffer such a loss,” he pleaded with the then-prime minister.

A little over a week after his wife Nanette and six-year-old daughters Alannah and Madeline were gunned down in Australia’s deadliest mass shooting , Walter Mikac sat down to write a letter to John Howard.

In the Jewish community, patience is wearing thin. Farmers and recreational shooters who will be caught up in the fallout are also in a state of limbo.

To make matters worse, the small number of jurisdictions that do want to take part in Albanese’s scheme still haven’t been able to finish the design of the scheme and strike a funding deal with Canberra.

Howard told this masthead this week: “Although the circumstances do vary, I am very disappointed that Anthony Albanese hasn’t got everybody on side.”

It took Howard just five months to announce, negotiate and begin his national gun buyback scheme following the Port Arthur massacre. By contrast, more than seven months have passed since the Bondi Beach antisemitic attack with no agreement.

Queensland is also out, as is South Australia. Tasmania won’t have a cap and Western Australia has just had 83,000 guns returned under a voluntary return program and feels no need to tie itself to Albanese’s proposal.

Victorian Premier Jacinta Allan rejected a key recommendation by her own independent expert, Ken Lay, to place a cap on how many guns a person can have, fearful of regional voters angrily handing back firearms at the same time as her beleaguered Labor government heads to the polls in November. Victoria Police also wanted a cap and was ignored.

The first was who would pay. Unlike Howard’s buyback, which was federally funded via a temporary increase to the Medicare levy from 1.5 to 1.7 per cent, Albanese’s model called for a 50:50 cost sharing with the states.

But there were three problems with the prime minister’s commitment that meant the idea was fatally flawed from the start.

Billed as “the largest since the Howard government in 1996”, Albanese said the buyback was critical and argued there were now 4 million firearms in Australia – more than at the time of the Port Arthur massacre.

The rot set in the day Albanese announced his plan for a national buyback nearly a week after father and son duo Naveed and Sajid Akram allegedly opened fire on Jewish families at Bondi Beach.

The failure to land a new national gun buyback scheme – one of the key policy responses to flow from the Bondi atrocity – offers an insight into the state of politics in 2026 and the profound power of self-interest.

Albanese eventually relented and agreed to a royal commission – but the father of gun reform speaking in such negative terms offered conservatives cover to shirk bipartisan support.

“I do not want this debate post this horrible event to be used, the focus on guns be used, as a pretext to avoid the broader debate about the spread of hatred of Jewish people and antisemitism,” Howard said in December.

Ironically, Howard – who supports the principle of a fresh buyback – damaged its chances of success in the days after Bondi. Savaging what he said was a failure of Albanese to combat antisemitism, Howard dubbed the prime minister’s proposed buyback a “ diversion ”.

Guns about to be destroyed as part of the 1996 buyback.

Albanese’s second failure was his initial refusal to announce other strong measures. His stubborn resistance to calling a royal commission into the deadly attack meant the measures outlined in his early response – however well-intentioned or needed – suffered by association.

Either way, an argument over costs gave leaders an easy way to sidestep the scheme. Northern Territory Chief Minister Lia Finocchiaro was the first leader to baulk at forking out. “We welcome the federal government to have a gun buyback scheme, but Territorians won’t be the ones footing the bill,” she said. “I’ve been very upfront and honest about that from day one.”

Would the deal have got up had Albanese stumped up 100 per cent of the funding? “I’m not so sure,” Australian Gun Safety Alliance convenor Stephen Bendle said this week. “What we’ve seen is that there has been political hesitation more than financial.”

Estimates based on current Victorian firearms ownership data have revealed that less than 20 per cent of the state’s firearms users would be impacted by the cap rejected by Allan.

Critics don’t buy it. The leader of the Victorian Greens, Ellen Sandell, said Allan’s refusal to support a cap was a “total capitulation to One Nation, the gun lobby, or probably both”.

Federal Labor MP Dan Repacholi, who represents the NSW seat of Hunter, supports a buyback scheme but has criticised the four-weapon cap for recreational shooters proposed by NSW Premier Chris Minns . Allan, the Victorian premier, holds the regional seat of Bendigo East but denies her political survival was a factor in not following the lead of her NSW Labor counterpart.

Costs are one factor. However, the rise of One Nation and its leader Pauline Hanson has seriously spooked state leaders and oppositions. One Nation, which is vehemently opposed to a buyback and has pledged to repeal it, poses a real threat in Labor and Coalition-held electorates with high rates of gun ownership.

But there is much blame to go around. The majority of states have refused to take part even though Virginia Bell explicitly recommended a national buyback in her interim report from the Royal Commission on Antisemitism and Social Cohesion.

The third setback was Albanese’s apparent unwillingness to use his prime ministerial authority to campaign for the changes. Whereas Howard travelled around the country making the case for a buyback, Albanese has been nowhere to be seen. He has spoken of the scheme publicly just a handful of times since February, according to an analysis of Hansard and his own transcripts.

Despite that proportionately small number, 287,000 firearms could have been disposed of had she agreed to the limit and participated in the national buyback.

“Any leader worth their weight would do what’s necessary to keep the community safe after such a horrific massacre as Bondi,” Sandell said in an interview this week. “People expect leaders to stand up and do what is right, even if that might be difficult and requires you to show some guts.

“And that’s why this is so disappointing with what Jacinta Allan has done here – she just does not have the guts to do what must be done.”

One senior Labor figure defended Albanese’s handling of the matter and said weak state leaders like Allan were really to blame for the scheme’s collapse. “They all need to explain why they are ignoring the recommendation of a royal commission that everyone was demanding,” the source, who declined to be named, said.

Prime Minister John Howard addresses a gun rally with a protective vest under his jacket. Andrew Meares

The department of Home Affairs, the domestic spy agency ASIO and the Australian Criminal Intelligence Commission have also endorsed a buyback, arguing it would help manage individuals with violent extremist ideologies, and frustrate serious and organised crime from obtaining lawful access.

Stolen or missing registered firearms account for nearly 10 per cent of illicit longarms and around 31 per cent of illicit handguns in Australia. Authorities estimate there are at least 250,000 illegal longarms and handguns in Australia, and potentially as many as 500,000.

Bendle also said limiting access would have other benefits, noting the “No.1 cause of firearm deaths is still by suicide”.

Shooting Industry Foundation of Australia chief executive officer James Walsh argued a cap in NSW and other states would not target the right gun owners. “These policies are not going to take a single firearm off a terrorist or a criminal – you’re just taking guns out of a safe,” he said.

“Taking those guns doesn’t increase public safety. Go out and go hard in south-western Sydney and take all the illegal pistols, illegal firearms, and the semi-automatic firearms that are being used. That will actually have tangible public-safety benefits.”

The argument that law-abiding owners saddle the biggest burden in any buyback was given short shrift by Howard in 1996. In his response to Mikac’s emotional letter of early 1996, the then-prime minister replied, saying: “I regret that many people who have never done anything wrong in their lives will be inconvenienced by the new laws, but this is ultimately a small price to pay for a community that feels, and is, more secure.”

Of course, Howard could rely on the crucial support of his deputy, Nationals leader Tim Fischer, who was instrumental in persuading rural Australia of the need for change.

Nationals leader Matt Canavan during a press conference criticising the buyback. Dominic Lorrimer

Walsh said claims his industry and its lobbying arm had too much influence over the failed buyback were wrong. He claimed his organisation had to do little if any campaigning before most states pledged to not take part, and said the Minns government had “refused to speak to us”.

“We have his backbenchers calling, going, ‘there’s nothing that we can do. We know it’s going to cost us our jobs. We know we’re going to lose votes over this, but it’s a captain’s call. He won’t change his mind’.”

An analysis commissioned by his association recently found the cost of buying back weapons in NSW would be about $415 million before other costs such as compensation and administration were added. The government has not publicly disputed the findings of that study.

The delay in securing an agreement between Macquarie Street and Canberra has caused legitimate angst among recreational shooters and primary producers in NSW, who still have no idea whether the government will pay market value for a firearm, rather than a lower set price.

Walsh was scathing of Albanese’s handling of the issue, and his absence from the debate over recent months. “The prime minister seems to say a lot and then change his mind, doesn’t he?

“He came out in an emotion-fuelled speech saying he was going to do this and going to do that. But he hadn’t come to the industry. He hadn’t gone to the states. He didn’t know how many firearms are out there.

“There were questions he should have asked before he came out with this.”

The Herald and The Age asked the prime minister a series of questions, including why he had not been more forceful in his public advocacy for the scheme and whether promising to fully fund the program might have delivered more participation by the states.

In a statement, he said: “We’re continuing to work on the buyback scheme. We’re confident it will lead to a significant reduction in the number of firearms in our community, and that’s a good thing.

“I want fewer guns on our streets.

“The states and territories will make their own decisions about how they choose to participate – but all governments have a responsibility to do all they can to keep Australians safe.”

Chris Minns, whose premiership was redefined by the horror of Bondi, remains 100 per cent behind the gun buyback and has been overheard telling colleagues he thinks it’s an issue worth losing an election over.

Laws that passed parliament in December restrict firearms licences to Australian citizens, reduce the standard term for firearm licences from five years to two years, cap the number of firearms an individual may possess at four, with a higher limit of 10 for primary producers, and restrict access to pump-action, button or lever-release, or straight-pull firearms – such as those used in the Bondi attack – to primary producers.

However, progress on making those laws reality has been painfully slow. Some of the yet-to-be-resolved issues include whether the state can afford to offer market value for guns, which will increase the cost of the scheme, how much should be paid for ammunition and other soon-to-be redundant firearm paraphernalia, potential compensation for gun clubs and stores, and what other exemptions may need to be written into the regulation. There is also a huge amount of work being done on the mechanics of how guns would be collected and destroyed, which NSW Police have had to play a central role in navigating.

NSW Premier Chris Minns and Police Minister Yasmin Catley. Sam Mooy

One senior member of the Minns government, who declined to be named due to cabinet confidentiality, said the work had been frustrating, “but I am sure there will be a deal and this will go ahead”.

Minns and Albanese have been under little political pressure to hurry up because oppositions state and federally do not see a political dividend in supporting the buyback.

NSW Opposition Leader Kellie Sloane told a NSW Farmers’ conference in Sydney this week that while the NSW Liberals supported Minns’ gun laws in December, they wanted changes.

Bondi is personal for Sloane – she was one of the first on the scene to render assistance to the dead and wounded – but like her Victorian counterparts she is being squeezed by One Nation ahead of the March election.

“There were two terrorists that caused that attack,” Sloane told the crowd. “It was not farmers. I know you feel like you’re being punished. I know that those 10-gun caps in your communities feel unworkable. So I want to say that we are working with the government, with stakeholders, to make amends.”

Privately, the state government is angry at other states for capitulating to the threat of a backlash and does not blame Albanese.

Minns told this masthead on Friday: “There is goodwill from both the NSW and federal governments on this, and we’ll get it done. We remain absolutely committed to the buyback scheme.”

Minns has previously argued NSW will end up with the “strongest gun laws in Australia”. That may be true, but it would be easy for someone to cross a border and more easily obtain weapons in states with a higher supply.

Perhaps aware of the potential for states to go their own ways, the royal commission’s interim report warned against patchy laws. “There is a public interest in national consistency in firearms regulation in Australia, where extensive and largely unmonitored state and territory borders make it possible for people and firearms to move between jurisdictions with relative ease,” the report noted.

Bendle from the Gun Safety Alliance agreed things had not landed where he had hoped. “There was some hope among public health experts that there might be some light come out of the shadow of a Bondi,” he said.

He said while some states won’t sign up to a full national gun buyback, many may still alter their gun laws, and that would be a good thing. “But it won’t be the same as 1996.”

World.title: How to (safely) access the cash locked up in your property
World.content:
MoneyPlanning & budgetingBudgeting Opinion How to (safely) access the cash locked up in your property Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor July 25, 2026 — 5:01am

July 25, 2026 — 5:01am Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

There are times in your life – and possibly through different stages of your life – when your money requirements are larger than your income. I don’t mean a straight imbalance between your salary and your expenses. I’m talking about big ticket things like the need to renovate, replace a car (without an expensive personal loan), maybe pay for kids’ education last minute. Or it’s a retirement funding shortfall that’s making life, well, miserable. The big potential disadvantage from any reverse mortgage is compounding interest rates could take a big bite from the estate when the borrower dies and the outstanding loan is repaid. Simon Letch Perhaps, increasingly commonly, you want to financially help adult children when they need it most. Thanks to the huge rise in property prices benefiting the older generation, the so-called living inheritance to get the next generation into housing is growing in popularity. No matter why, there are options at every age to get out the equity you might think is locked in your property.



Until your mid-50s Mortgage refinance: Often – and particularly after three rate rises this year – a mortgage refinance is about cutting your monthly repayments. But sometimes it is about getting a larger loan. And it’s even possible that, with the combination of both, you could extract equity without increasing your minimum repayment. This option is available earliest – just as soon as you have built enough equity to withdraw and maintain the maximum loan-to-value ratio. For asset rich but cash poor Aussies, at every age there are options. But it’s also an opportunity that evaporates as your retirement approaches, as lenders don’t love retired borrowers. So, if it’s something that features in your financial strategy, don’t leave it too late – keep a close eye on that retirement date.



And be aware, too, that if you extend your loan term, though it’s another way of keeping repayments low, you could end up paying way more interest overall. Editor's pick Opinion

Income tax The five tax return mistakes that could get you audited Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon Money contributor From your mid-50s Downsize: Don’t miss that the cheapest way of using your home for a cash injection is to sell it and buy something of a lesser value (bearing in mind that many people who trade a house for an apartment end up down-sizing but up-pricing). From age 55, the government has also increased the incentive by allowing you to deposit $300,000 of the proceeds into super, where they can grow with only 15 per cent tax on earnings (for balances under $3 million), becoming tax-free once you retire or turn 65.



The further beauty is that each person in a couple can do this. The only restriction is that you need to have owned the property for 10 years. But there are two ways to get out equity without selling, also usually from age 55... The reverse mortgage and home reversion scheme: A reverse mortgage is still a type of home loan but works the opposite way in that the debt ratchets up rather than whittles down. Available as a lump sum or income stream, you make no repayments. Instead, the ultimate debt is repaid by other funds if you choose, or from the sale of your house earlier or on your death (check that all options are available). The interest due will roll up until that time, and because you will pay interest on interest, can become large. Of course, the value of the property might also increase over that time. Most importantly, a no-negative-equity guarantee means the debt can never grow to more than the value of the property, and you can never be evicted for this reason (see if there are any other reasons though).



The home reversion scheme is an alternative with different advantages and disadvantages. Here, there is no interest payable, rather this is a shared ownership arrangement from the outset. Editor's pick Opinion

Ask an expert Should I sell my home to help my three children buy a house? Noel Whittaker Money columnist You sign over a portion of your home that is then recouped by the financial institution, again from your other funds if you choose or from your property’s sale before or on your death (check). It’s essential to get advice before making either a reverse mortgage or home reversion move. Some considerations are that with a home reversion scheme, you have an immediate liability … say, 40 per cent of your home is gone the day you settle. Of course, your – in this case – 60 per cent could still increase in value. You can delay this liability with the reverse mortgage approach – the debt only grows over time. The less time it has to grow, the better, and you might also have the option not to draw down on your funds until you need them.



The longer you wait before taking out either product, the more money you can extract. Finally, both moves can potentially deplete your kids’ inheritance – just so you know. And there may be less money left to fund aged care down the track. Speaking of, there is a cheaper option available later in life… From age 67 Home equity access scheme: At age 67, a government opportunity kicks in for people eligible for the age pension. The home equity access scheme via Services Australia is like a reverse mortgage in that you take out a loan against your equity that rolls up. However, the interest rate is far cheaper – it’s currently 3.95 per cent versus, say, 8 per cent for a commercial reverse mortgage. Being an official scheme, however, you can also get out far less and only as a small lump sum and then regular income. Your pension and loan payment can’t be more each fortnight than 1.5 times the full age pension.



Know, though, that for asset rich but cash poor Aussies, at every age there are options. Nicole Pedersen-McKinnon is author of How to Get Mortgage-Free Like Me, available at nicolessmartmoney.com. Follow her on Facebook, X and Instagram. Advice given in this article is general in nature and is not intended to influence readers’ decisions about investing or financial products. They should always seek their own professional advice that takes into account their own personal circumstances before making any financial decisions. World.title: Commonwealth Games: Erika Fairweather wins NZ's first medal of the 2026 Games, silver in the women's 400m freestyle
World.content:
New Zealand's medal campaign at the 2026 Commonwealth Games is underway after swimmers Erika Fairweather and Lewis Clareburt claimed the country's first podium finishes with a pair of silver medals on the opening night of finals in Glasgow.

Fairweather collected the first medal of the Glasgow Games for New Zealand with silver in the women's 400m freestyle, before Clareburt backed it up minutes later with a thrilling runner-up finish in a gripping final of the men's 200m individual medley.

Australia's Lani Pallister dominated the women's 400m freestyle, pulling away over the closing stages to win in 3m 59.56a. Fairweather finished second in 4m 2.65s, more than three seconds behind, having stayed in touch with the Australian through the opening 300m before fading over the final 100m.

"It was definitely to stay as close to her as possible," Fairweather said of her race plan.

"It wasn't my best performance today, but you can't be mad with the outcome that I got."

Fairweather appeared disappointed with her performance in her favoured event. Michael Steele/Getty Images

Despite appearing frustrated after the race, Fairweather said finally winning a Commonwealth Games medal after missing the podium in Birmingham four years ago was a special moment.

"I was gutted last time when I didn't get one, to know I'm going home with one in my suitcase now is super special."

New Zealand teammates Caitlin Deans and Eve Thomas also featured in the final, finishing sixth and eighth respectively.

Clareburt then produced one of the races of the night, storming home over the freestyle leg to claim silver behind Scotland's Duncan Scott in front of a vocal home crowd.

Scott successfully defended his Commonwealth title in a Games record time of 1m 56.38s, with Clareburt touching second after sitting third at the final turn before producing a blistering finish. England's Tom Dean claimed bronze in 1m 57.22a.

The silver was Clareburt's fifth Commonwealth Games medal, adding to the two gold medals and bronze he won in Birmingham in 2022, as well as bronze on the Gold Coast in 2018.

More importantly for the 26-year-old, the performance delivered a long-awaited personal milestone.

"The medal didn't mean as much to me as the time," Clareburt said.

"To be able to do a personal best on this stage is such a good feeling. I've been on the 1.57 mark for eight years, so to dip under that today and to get a silver on top is a cool feeling."

Clareburt finished second to local favourite Duncan Scott, and England's Tom Dean. Michael Steele/Getty Images

Clareburt admitted he had little idea where he was positioned over the closing stages of the race.

"To be honest I was breathing the wrong way and I couldn't see anyone. I knew that I was probably going to be close and I sort of had a glimpse and at some point I saw the TV, and all I could see was blue, which was what Duncan was wearing, so I knew he was ahead, but I had no idea where I was."

He also had no idea Fairweather had already opened New Zealand's medal tally.

World.title: 'Severe' magnitude 5.9 quake hits North Island
World.content:
A strong earthquake jolted the central North Island early on Saturday.

Geonet said the 'severe' magnitude 5.9 quake happened around five kilometres southwest of Taumarunui at 4.51am.

The earthquake was nine kilometres deep and the intensity was severe.

The quake was reportedly felt across much of the North Island, including Auckland, and as far as the top of the South.

By 6am, nearly 23,000 'felt reports' had been filed to Geonet.

At least seven aftershocks, ranging between magnitude 2.7 and 3.7, followed.

Fire and Emergency said far it had recieved only a sprinkler-related callout stemming from the big quake.

Minor slips reported

Manawatū-Whanganui Emergency Management Group urged motorists to take care while driving after minor slips were reported in the area.

"Emergency services and roading crews are assessing the situation, but a fuller view of any impacts is unlikely to be available until daylight," it said.

No injuries or other damage had been reported.

The Emergency Management Group expected aftershocks to continue throughout the morning.

"If people feel them, they should drop, cover, and hold. If you are in bed, the best thing to do is to stay there and cover your head and neck with a pillow."

'Strong and long' in the lower North Island

The earthquake felt like it would not end in Whanganui, according to a resident in the suburb of Springvale.

Cushela Robson described the tremor as a very strong, prolonged rolling motion.

"I thought, should I get out of bed? And if I did, could I stand? So I thought, no, probably, because I grew up in Wellington, I thought, no, I think it's probably better to stay in bed."

World.title: New US tariffs likely to face court challenges
World.content:
New Zealand's special agricultural trade envoy says new tariffs imposed by the United States could be challenged in the United States' courts.

The Trump administration has imposed a 12.5 percent tariff on most exports, replacing the current 10 percent one.

Former government minister Nathan Guy, also chair of the Meat Industry Association, said exporters across the board are bracing for more uncertainty.

"The Liberation Day tariffs last year, they were repealed through the Supreme Court. Refunds as a result have been flowing back to exporters, and these new tariffs could well be challenged through the courts over there as well."

Guy said the administration had decided to launch trade investigations ahead of the tariff announcements, which were considered due process, and could be harder to challenge.

US trade representative Jamieson Greer had claimed the new tariffs were designed to combat imports made with forced labour.Guy rejected this, saying a lot of information was provided through the Ministry of Trade and Foreign Affairs on the supply chains of all exporters.

He could "hand on heart" say there was no forced labour in supply chains here, but ultimately "our voices weren't heard".

Guy said he could not tell whether the administration would follow through on tariff threats, during his meetings in Washington.

"The summary that I took away, if anyone knows or can predict, has a crystal ball at the end of their bed or on their shelf in their office and knows what is going to happen next, then they're telling porkies. No one knows.

"We worry about this ... We thought something could be going to happen from this forced labour investigation. And obviously it has."

One positive was that the seed industry and animal feeds have had a tariff reduction which could equate to $100 million for those industries, he said.

In terms of the red meat industry, Guy said there was still strong demand for sheep meat in the United States.

"Certainly the value we get for the mid-loin cuts for the US is very significant. So any tariff just distorts trade, it impacts on consumer demand, it whacks them in the back-pocket so we say it's completely unnecessary and we're very disappointed."

The Dairy Association of New Zealand agreed.

Dairy Companies Association of New Zealand executive director Kimberly Crewther. Supplied / DCANZ

Executive director Kimberly Crewther said the new tariff disadvantaged New Zealand dairy exports, compared to competitors like the European Union and Australia.

Crewther said she was disappointed exemption requests from US customers of dairy protein ingredients were declined. The products are used in specialised nutrition and not produced in sufficient quantities in the US, she said.

World.title: The battle for Southland's hills: Trans-Tasman soldiers train for combat
World.content:
On the hills near the small Southland town of Waikaia, a battle is underway.

Trenches are set into the hilltop and soldiers have spent days climbing the grassy slope to prepare for the big offensive, often in the cold and mud.

Explosions and soldiers are not usually a common sight in the town of just over 100 residents, but Waikaia has been hosting Exercise Tauwharenīkau.

It is the largest Reserve Force-led warfighting exercise conducted in the South Island in decades, with close to 500 New Zealand Army and Australian Army Reserve personnel joining forces.

Legs burn as soldiers each haul at least 30 kilograms of kit up and down the surrounding hills, trying to scout for the enemy.

Close to 500 New Zealand Army and Australian Army Reserve personnel are joining forces for Exercise Tauwharenīkau. RNZ / Tess Brunton

That enemy has included Lance Corporal Stephen Potter, an Invercargill-based doctor and a medic in the Reserve Force.

For the last week, he has been disrupting, delaying and harassing the opposing side.

"We had a good fight in a quarry where we had actually fortified up with rocks and they had to come up quite difficult terrain and they actually came up with quite an intelligent way to come up one of our blindspots," he said.

"It's about trying to make it so it's realistic enemy. We were trying to counter that by putting patrols in to try and spot them so trying to adapt."

Exercise Tauwharenīkau is the largest Reserve Force-led warfighting exercise conducted in the South Island in decades. RNZ / Tess Brunton

They train regularly, but he said the terrain was rough.

"Certainly seeing a lot of people pretty tired with the hills. I think the North Islanders find it a wee bit cold, being a local I don't find it too bad," he said.

"But it has been pretty rough ... having to have the warm kit ready, making sure our Australian comrades are wrapped up well.

"I think Southland gives a really good training ground to actually build a good amount of resilience and I think that it's nice to be in my own backyard."

A trench near Waikaia. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Speaking the day before the battle, he was looking forward to seeing how the other force would try to claim the hills they were based on, which overlook Waikaia.

Opposition Force Commander Major Dion Becker said the hills were prime territory.

"It dominates the air in front of us. It's sighted to stop enemy forces coming up this valley so a lot of it is, as you can see, is laid out with interlocking arcs just to deny that bit of real estate," Becker said.

But their kit did not make it an easy climb.

"Some of our specialists units, they could be carrying up to 60 kilograms and this is a great environment to really build that resilience of carrying that weight over really undulating terrain, sorting out our lower limbs and things like that so that we can get to the high ground and fight when we're there," he said.

Opposition force commander Major Dion Becker said soldiers were carrying at least 30 kilograms of kit through the Southland hills. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Among the kit was an assault rifle that fired blanks - no live ammunition was used in the exercise

"We've also got attached lasers that connects to sensors that people wear so that we can, in real time [say], 'that was a close shot' or 'that was a good shot'," he said.

"They get feedback with a verbal tone and our umpires can then download a lot of that information and just see trends and do some analysis on that "

Soldiers would be positioned in trenches, including ones that were camouflaged under mounds of grass.

1 Field Squadron Captain Dean Burke said engineers would also be working in the final assault by helping the infantry to break in and removing the obstacles.

"Survivability is about hardening the defensive position as we've done here and so for the opposing forces, [they're] given a greater chance of survival in this structures [sic] that [we've] provided them," he said.

Captain Dean Burke said part of the challenge would be breaking through the defences of the opposing force. RNZ / Tess Brunton

Further south, at the Waimumu Forward Operating Base, Catering Sergeant Katie Emmett and eight others help to put out roughly 1000 meals a day.

There were two transportable kitchens decked out with ovens, kettles, grill plates and a deep fryer.

"It's really good to have in mind what they're going to be doing, and that's running as fast as they can, getting into position as fast as they can, medicating as fast as they can and communicating as fast as they can," she said.

"Ideally it's going to be hearty. It's going to make sure they have enough carbs."

Catering Sergeant Katie Emmett said nutrition was an important part of properly fueling soldiers. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The menu was varied.

"Spaghetti, baked beans in the morning. An egg option and they'll have a protein, whether it be bacon, sausages, and a specialty item, just create that morale.

"You've got your pancakes, maple syrup, squirt of cream, and hash browns."

Supply company IC Corporal Daniel Dunn said 100 people could use their diesel-fuelled showers over two hours.

Special transportable showers can be used by 100 people over two hours with spaces for people to put their dirty and clean clothes as well as their boots. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The cubicles were a bit cramped, but they put out 40 degree water, he said.

"Basically soldiers can come in, put all their uniform and stuff in here, pull the handle and then they've got water for a 20 second period and they can do that multiple times."

Back at the front-line, Reserve Force Executive Officer Lieutenant Colonel Darren Young said the Southland terrain was putting soldiers through their paces.

"The size and scale of the areas that we're training in is a really good opportunity," he said.

Reserve Force Executive Officer Lieutenant Colonel Darren Young said Southland terrain was putting soldiers through their paces. RNZ / Tess Brunton

The exercise was a great chance to build foundational skills, build their confidence and work as a team, he said.

Saturday's battle would put the skills they had honed to the test, he said.

"They've been practicing their assaulting skills, navigation, all the basic soldiering skills to get them to a point where they can work together as two companies, assaulting an objective which is where we are standing," he said.

World.title: Green Party determined to return to government benches, co-leader says
World.content:
Green Party co-leader Marama Davidson says the party is determined to return to the government benches, ahead of its annual general meeting.

Party members, delegates, MPs, and candidates have gathered in South Auckland to prepare for the campaign ahead.

Ahead of the AGM, Davidson told RNZ the Greens were committed to "getting rid of this government," and having a strong influence on the next one.

The party has already rolled out its tax policy, as well as its policies for water and energy.

Co-leader Chlöe Swarbrick is set to announce a further policy on Sunday afternoon, with the rest of her speech focusing on rallying the membership for the campaign ahead.

Davidson will deliver a speech focused on the party's values and release the party's election manifesto.

The manifesto, which is developed by the wider party membership, contains the party's broader priorities.

This year, Davidson said there had been a large uptick in volunteers, phone calls, and door knocks, compared to this stage of previous election years.

"There's energy there that I don't think even we were expecting, all due to the sort of vision and solutions that the Greens have been putting out."

Unlike New Zealand First, which opens up its remit sessions to the media, or ACT, which promotes its AGM as more of a public rally, the Green Party's meetings are more like a conclave.

The notoriously closed-door meetings have been full of drama in recent years, from the decision to vacate James Shaw's position as co-leader in 2022, to the agonising over Darleen Tana in 2024 that led to three Pasifika members leaving the party.

Compared to the Greens' tumultuous first year back in opposition, the party goes into the election more cohesive and relaxed.

Davidson said there had been aspects of the last few years that had been "traumatising," but the party was stronger for it.

"No doubt we have gone through a lot this term, and even into last term. We've come through more than a lot, actually. Let's be straight up. So to have come through that and know you can make it through to the light, the members are just really focused now on this election."

While constitutional matters and remits are left for the other years, the membership will still vote on the party's leadership.

Both co-leaders are set to be re-confirmed, but Davidson was not taking anything for granted.

"We have that yearly confirmation for a reason, because our members really do decide if we get the privilege of serving year after year. So I can't rule out anything, but we're hoping that we have good relationships across the party, and we will be campaigning hard to keep the roles that we're going after."

The party was on 10.3 percent in the latest RNZ-Reid Research poll, up 0.2 points from the previous poll, but still a slight dip on the 11.6 percent the Greens got at the 2023 election.

It would give the Greens 13 seats in the House, two down from its current total.

The party's final list, was published in April.

While current polling would see much of the current crop of MPs return, Scott Willis (15th) and Mike Davidson (20th) are in danger of losing their spots, and the highest-ranked new face is Tania Waikato, in 13th.

But Davidson was not deterred.

World.title: Commonwealth Games: Kiwi swimmers to contend for medals after qualifiers
World.content:
New Zealand swimmers have made a flying start in the pool at the Commonwealth Games in Glasgow, putting themselves in contention for medals on opening day.

Erika Fairweather posted the fastest time of the 400 metre freestyle heats, qualifying first in a time of 4 minutes 6.42 seconds, with team-mate Caitlin Deans qualifying third in the same race on Friday (NZT).

The Kiwi pair were separated by Australian Amelia Weber in second.

Fairweather would look to go one better at Glasgow after narrowly missing the podium in the 400 metre freestyle final at Birmingham.

Eve Thomas also placed third in her heat for the same event, behind Australian pair Lani Pallister and Jenna Forrester.

The trio of New Zealand women would face off in the 400 metre freestyle final due to happen about 6.05am Saturday morning (NZT).

Meanwhile, Lewis Clareburt, who clinched double gold and bronze at Birmingham in 2022, qualified second in the 200 metre individual medley, behind Englishman Thomas Dean.

Clareburt's qualifying time was 1.2 seconds shy of his bronze-medal performance at Birmingham.

The 27-year-old would vie for a fifth Commonwealth Games medal in the 200 metre medley final about 6.15am Saturday (NZT).

Hazel Ouwehand also booked a final berth finishing second in a tightly-contested 50 metre butterfly heat.

The 26-year-old's time of 26.4 seconds was 0.16 seconds behind Jessica Thompson, of South Africa.

Zoe Pedersen also finished second in her 50 metre butterfly heat, completing the swim in 26.6 seconds, 1.05 seconds behind Australian Alex Perkins.

World.title: Respected public servant Dame Helene Quilter dies
World.content:
Dame Helene Quilter, who was honoured for her work in the public service over 45 years, has died.

The Public Service Commissioner, Sir Brian Roche, said Dame Helene died overnight.

Dame Helene served as Secretary of Defence, Deputy Commissioner of the State Services Commission and, most recently, as Deputy Public Service Commissioner at the Public Service Commission Te Kawa Mataaho.

She retired as deputy Public Service commissioner in February 2023.

She was recognised as a Dame Companion of the New Zealand Order of Merit in 2023 for services to the public service and the arts.

Her citation noted her advocacy for diversity and inclusion in public sector appointments, her leadership in strengthening public service capability, and her commitment to serving New Zealand through some of its most important institutions.

Sir Brian said Dame Helene was one of New Zealand's most respected and influential public servants.

"Over a career spanning 45 years, she dedicated herself to strengthening the institutions that serve New Zealanders and to upholding the values of integrity, professionalism and public service," Sir Brian said.

He said she played a central role in the appointment and development of Public Service chief executives, championed greater diversity in leadership, supported the public service through the Covid-19 response, and brought extraordinary wisdom and judgement to some of the most important issues facing government.

"She combined intellectual rigour with humanity, integrity with courage, and a deep understanding of what it means to serve the public good," Sir Brian said.

"Throughout her career, she helped shape the modern public service and was a trusted adviser, mentor and leader to countless public servants. She believed strongly in developing people, building diverse leadership, and leaving our institutions stronger than she found them.

"Those who worked with Helene knew her as someone of immense capability, wisdom and generosity. She challenged us to be better, supported others to succeed, and never lost sight of the purpose of public service - improving the lives of New Zealanders."

World.title: Battle lines drawn over proposed LNG facility
World.content:
Proposed LNG import terminal unlikely to cause disruption Checkpoint Download MP3 3m

Port Taranaki has reassured nearby residents that initial assessments of a proposed LNG import terminal indicate it is unlikely "risk management zones" will impact on the community or popular recreational areas like Ngāmotu Beach and Breakwater Bay.

In a letter sent to hundreds of local properties, port chief executive Simon Craddock confirmed both shortlisted proposals involved a ship being moored alongside the Main Breakwater.

Opponents of the project argue Port Taranaki is the wrong place for a liquid natural gas (LNG) import facility.

Former oil and gas industry project manager Rob Green's home on Port View Crescent overlooks Port Taranaki.

"I can look straight down on the port, all the ships at anchor here, and I can see all the logs and so on. So, I'm looking straight down on the port at the Main Breakwater and all those berthing possibilities for ships," he said.

"It's very close, all the noises from the port operations I can hear. I'm looking straight at it."

Green was not convinced the port, about 1km from his apartment, was the right place for an LNG import facility.

"I keep hearing that safety is the top priority, but quite frankly I won't believe it until I can see the risk assessment analysis for myself.

"Here we are bulldozing on to a contract the government seems totally committed to regardless to the concerns of the neighbourhood."

Port Taranaki's letter and an article on the Ministry of Business Innovation and Employment's LNG webpage explain that the vessel to be moored at the Main Breakwater would store LNG and be capable of regasifying it and distributing it into existing transmission pipelines.

Other vessels from suppliers overseas would deliver LNG - which was frozen - to the moored vessel.

The Main Breakwater was about 200m away from popular recreational areas at Ngāmotu Beach, Breakwater Bay and the Lee Breakwater, where recreational fishers both surfcasted and launched boats.

Port Taranaki referred questions about the safety assessment to MBIE, which was managing the procurement process.

In a statement, MBIE said safety was the bottom-line and the plant would not get built if it could not meet safety standards.

"An initial safety evaluation has been undertaken as part of both of the providers' feasibility work, and detailed health and safety assessments will be carried out through the Safety Case process under the Health and Safety at Work Act 2015 once the preferred provider is contracted," it said in a statement.

"This includes a quantitative risk assessment which is location-specific and will cover the facility and all phases of its operation, as well as generating risk contour lines (or 'buffer zones') to keep the community safe."

MBIE said it was inappropriate to make the initial safety assessment public as it was commercially sensitive.

In statement, WorkSafe said it had no role in the choice of location, but it would work with the preferred provider on the more detailed Safety Case.

"Before the facility can be built and operated, the preferred provider must submit both a design notice and a Safety Case to WorkSafe.

WorkSafe would assess these to determine whether the facility could comply with major hazard facility requirements and that risks had been identified and appropriately managed.

"WorkSafe will either accept or decline the Safety Case. If it is declined, the facility will not go ahead."

The regulator said it didn't publish safety cases in full.

However, if the LNG project was designated a major hazard facility, prescribed information must be published on the WorkSafe website.

This would include an explanation of activities undertaken at the facility, hazard classifications of substances that could cause or contribute to a major incident, and the characteristics of those substances that made them dangerous.

General information about how the public would be warned in the event of a major incident would also be published, and information on how the public should act and what precautionary steps they should take if a major incident occurred.

Taranaki Energy Watch's Sarah Roberts RNZ / Robin Martin

Taranaki Energy Watch spokesperson Sarah Roberts said that would be a case of too little too late.

"What we're saying is this location is not the right place for an LNG import terminal. We know that there's a known potential worst case fatality distance to approximately 2km from these types of facilities. There are thousands of people and a number of schools in this area."

Roberts said right from the outset former Minister of Energy Simon Watts talked about working alongside the Port Kembla Energy Terminal in New South Wales.

"Over there, they have built a new terminal and they have the 2km separation distance between the terminal itself and the nearest residence."

Roberts worried people in the area surrounding Port Taranaki would be hurt if something went wrong.

"We feel like they're purposely avoiding the RMA and Fast Track legislation to get something through that should have been looked at primarily at the beginning. Looking at the location, seeing if there's any alternatives, and making it publicly available, making the safety assessments publicly available."

MBIE said the exact size and details of the safety buffer zones around the LNG import facility at Port Taranaki would be determined independently to the procurement process, once it had been completed.

"It is inappropriate to estimate the exact size of the buffer zones ahead of this detailed Safety Case process. Until the Safety Case is accepted, the import facility will not be built."

People walking along Ngāmotu Beach and at Breakwater Bay had mixed views on the LNG proposal.

Kevin said he accepted it was necessary: "I suppose we have to have the gas to run the country. There's no great place to put it. Everyone wants it somewhere else, but Taranaki has had all the gas and gas production over the years."

His mate, Denis, wasn't so keen: "I'm not really in favour of the whole thing. It's all imported fossil fuels and a bit close to a residential area."

Don had an alternative idea and reckoned the infrastructure was mostly already in place: "Pipe it in, which would eliminate any need for changes around the harbour area."

Robyn was willing to put her trust in the process: "They've got very stringent safety things, that's the big thing with oil and gas."

Grant worried about access to recreational areas: "Not very happy at all.

"There's a lot of people who use this area here. So, is there going to be an exclusion zone for people walking around here? And what about the cafes here, are they going to remove those?"

Graham said he could see both sides of the dilemma: "It's probably no more dangerous than anything else, but it is an unnecessary addition to danger, and the actual plant itself is unnecessary."

Bernard's home was within 2km of the proposed site: "I think it is a bit risky. It is a highly volatile thing and that. I would prefer them going back to Marsden Point and doing it there."

World.title: What it feels like to have your sport dumped from the Commonwealth Games
World.content:
As the Commonwealth Games kicked off on its first full day of competition, plenty more sat at at home, many wishing it could be them.

Organisers in 2026 ditched badminton, hockey, wrestling, road cycling, mountain biking, rhythmic gymnastics, rugby sevens, squash, table tennis, triathlon, beach volleyball, cricket and, the most storied of all, diving.

It has been held at every edition since the first Empire Games in 1930, until this year.

Of the 22 Commonwealth Games diving events, Anabelle Smith went to the past four, including Glasgow 2014.

Twelve years ago she won bronze in the women's synchronised 3m springboard with Maddison Keeney, but not in Glasgow like the rest of her team.

This dive for Smith (left) and Keeney was at Glasgow 2014 in name only. (Getty Images: Quinn Rooney)

The Scottish capital did not have a facility to allow for diving, so Smith, Keeney and Co were shipped to Edinburgh, the site of the 1970 and 1986 Games.

"[There was] obvious disappointment from the divers … but also an understanding," Smith told ABC Sport.

"It made sense they weren't just gonna ship the divers up to Edinburgh, disappointing but they'll power on and look ahead now."

The 33-year-old had not been planning to defend her 3m synchro gold medal from Birmingham 2022, but is instead attending her fifth Games as a spectator and part of the Australian team's connection and belonging squad.

How we got to Glasgow 2026 The bumpy road to Glasgow 2026 has produced a Commonwealth Games that will look a little different than the ones that came before.

She's joined by other athletes who have seen their sports axed, including beach volleyballer Chris McHugh and Melissa 'Milly' Tapper.

Her sport of table tennis was also axed after being included in six straight Games from 2002 to 2022.

Tapper, an Olympian and Paralympian, embodies the inclusive and integrated nature of the Games perhaps better than anyone.

She won team bronze at Glasgow 2014 and singles gold on home soil on the Gold Coast in 2018, and is still getting the chance to flash her skills in the team lounge at the decked-out Glasgow Argyle Hotel.

Loading Instagram content

"I've got a little bit of a call-up having the table tennis table in there," she said.

"We've had plenty of athletes and even some staff come through and challenge. Being around athletes everyone's competitive. It's a lot of fun.

"So even though table tennis isn't technically in the Games, it's still a part of the Games."

Table tennis was a "core sport" for the Commonwealth Games and falls into the category of many of the 2026 events, in that it could be held in existing halls.

Melissa Tapper has represented Australia at the Olympics, Paralympics and Commonwealth Games. (Getty Images: Matt Roberts)

Field hockey, however, requires a bit more space and bespoke facilities. Its history in the Commonwealth Games is not quite as long as diving's, but it had an elevated status as a "core sport".

In 2014, it was held at the Glasgow National Hockey Centre, which remains operational and is located along the River Clyde, within the 13-kilometre corridor of the pared-back 2026 Games.

When cuts were being made for 2026, the International Hockey Federation (FIH) and Commonwealth member nations lobbied for the sport's inclusion, but they missed out as organisers opted largely for indoor sports with athletics the only outdoor event.

Glasgow 2026 events 3x3 basketball/wheelchair basketball

Artistic gymnastics

Athletics

Bowls

Boxing

Judo

Netball

Para powerlifting and weightlifting

Swimming

Track cycling

The Kookaburras have won all seven men's gold medals since 1998, while the Hockeyroos have also never missed the podium, boasting four gold, two silver and a bronze.

Kookaburras captain Eddie Ockenden carried the flag in the Birmingham 2022 opening ceremony, as evidence of the sport's standing in Australia's Commonwealth Games movement, so Hockey Australia was "naturally disappointed" to miss out in 2026.

"Our national teams only play a finite number of international tournaments, making every opportunity to compete in one incredibly valuable," high performance director Bernard Savage said.

"The Commonwealth Games have always been one of those opportunities that our teams have genuinely looked forward to. Beyond the competition itself, the Commonwealth Games provide a unique multi-sport environment that our athletes look forward to and aspire to be a part of.

"The broader interest in the Games has provided an opportunity for our athletes and teams to inspire the next generation of hockey players across Australia and the Commonwealth.

"While this has been disappointing news, our focus remains firmly on our preparation for the 2026 FIH Hockey World Cup."

The World Cup will be played in Belgium and The Netherlands from August 15-30, shortly after the end of the Glasgow Games.

World.title: Cats down Dees, Dockers flex muscle against Eagles in derby
World.content:
Jye Amiss has kicked five goals and Murphy Reid produced a third-quarter clinic as Fremantle continued their western derby dominance with a 70-point win over West Coast at Perth Stadium.

The Dockers led by just eight points at half-time of Friday night's match before kicking 11 goals to one in the second half to race out easy 16.16 (112) to 6.6 (42) winners.

(Getty Images)

Amiss took seven marks inside 50m on the way to 5.1, while last year's Rising Star winner Murphy Reid (26 disposals, one goal) snared the Glendinning-Allan medal as best afield after turning the contest on its head with a mesmerising nine-possession third quarter.

Matthew Johnson (29 disposals, six clearances) and Caleb Serong (26 disposals, seven clearances) also had big games in front of 56,616 fans — a record home crowd for a Fremantle regular-season game.

There was late concern for West Coast mid-season recruit Oliver Francou when his right knee was gashed open after sliding over the studs of Andrew Brayshaw during a tackle.

Eagles players immediately signalled to the bench for help as Francou lay on his back and lifted his leg high in the air to stop blood from gushing out.

Star West Coast midfielder Harley Reid battled hard on the way to 30 disposals, 12 clearances, while Tim Kelly (31 disposals, 603m gained) and defender Marcus Herbert (36 disposals) were prominent.

The Dockers have now won five derbies on the trot — and 10 of the past 11 — to close to within three in the overall head-to-head ledger (33-30).

The result means Fremantle (17-2) will finish the round at least three wins clear on top of the table with just four rounds remaining, putting them in an excellent position to snare just their second minor premiership.
