World.title: Live: Lani Pallister wins Australia's first Commonwealth Games gold
World.content:
There are a lot of equations involved in para powerlifting at the Commonwealth Games with just two classes – light and heavyweight.

Athletes' lifts are measured against their body weight, instead of simply lifting in more specific categories with everyone in closer weight groups.

In April, Hani Watson told ABC Sport she'd rather be in more specific weight classes but her coach had some simple advice for her.

"I certainly like to be within my own cohort. You compete against your own cohort all the time and you don't really have to think about it other than the weight on the bar," she said.

"With Commonwealth Games it becomes a little bit trickier where you've got to watch your weight and I've got to rely on [coach Simon Bergner] to watch the scoreboard.

"One point or half a point or .01 of a point can make the difference between medalling and not medalling. He has to concentrate on that but I have it in the back of my mind.

"He always tells me 'just stay fat, lift heavy and you'll be right'."

Whatever the tactic, it worked again tonight for one of Australia's most lovable athletes.

World.title: Have the AFL's rule changes worked? Not exactly
World.content:
There is nothing more constant than change.

People have argued about the future of football for as long as the game has existed.

Every year players, fans and football staffers await the new direction or interpretations handed down from high.

Some changes are winners and stand the test of time — such as the 50 metre arc and the centre square.

Others are destined for the dustbin of history, such as the flick pass and around the ground bounces.

Regardless, change is never far from sporting administrators of different codes and sports. The AFL is not immune from this want to improve the sport.

Rule changes among what's new in the AFL for 2026 The new AFL season is only days away, and there are plenty of new things to get your head around. Get up to speed before Thursday night's opener.

Ahead of the 2026 season seven rule changes and interpretation shifts were heralded as being common sense solutions to perceived long-standing problems surrounding the sport.

Changes to the centre bounce, kick-ins, shrugs, the "stand" rule and last disposal out of bounds were implemented. Some elements of the footy fan base were excited by the changes, others horrified.

"We have consulted clubs and other industry stakeholders over the past six months and taken on board their feedback and ideas, and we believe these changes will make a positive impact on the game," AFL executive general manager Football Performance Greg Swann said before the commencement of the season.

The aims of each change were varied but aligned to increase scoring, reduce game time and improve the look and feel of the game.

So far scoring has increased about 3.5 points per game compared to last year.

Scoreboard operators haven't been this busy since the 2017 season, with early season scoring rates threatening to push the clock back even further.

But that number alone may not tell the whole story.

With the season winding towards finals, research undertaken by the ABC and Andrew Whelan of Wheelo Ratings looks at whether the changes have had their intended impact.

Centring the truth

Rule changes around centre ball-ups have increased the numbers of ruckmen leaping for the ball. (Getty Images: Robert Cianflone)

To the casual fan there were few more iconic parts of the Australian game than the centre bounce. The biggest optical change to the game in 2026 was the removal of the centre bounce and changes to how rucks engaged at the restart.

The bounce had been the start of each game since its formal introduction in 1887.

For many the bounce was integral to the look and feel of the sport — a unique element that set the native code away from the other global codes of football.

AFL rule change injury fears Geelong's Shannon Neale might have escaped a serious injury, but coaches and players are beginning to voice concerns the AFL's rule changes could lead to more rucks getting hurt.

But it had become untenable in the face of umpire injuries and skill barriers, seen to reduce the ranks of vital recruits.

"Currently, umpire pathways are being narrowed by the requirement of the bounce. By removing the skill aspect of bouncing the ball, umpires can focus their energy on adjudicating the game and consistency of decision-making," Swann stated.

At the same time that they removed the bounce, the league also instituted a change to encourage more rucks to leap at centre ball-ups.

According to the AFL, just 21 per cent of centre bounce ruck contests had at least one ruck leaping last year. That's down from about two-thirds just two years prior.

After the preseason Swann was keen to sell the success of both changes.

"The unintended consequences from a good perspective is scores out of the centre bounces have gone up. It's a very small sample size, but the things that we wanted — the game length has gone back, the scoring has gone up, scoring from centre bounces has gone up, so we're hopeful that goes into the season proper as well."

At face value the rule changes — in combination — have delivered in spades. Scoring from centre bounces are at their highest level for at least 20 years.

Digging a little deeper presents more questions as to its impact.

While scoring is up from centre bounces, the major reason why they are up is a little more unconventional.

Instead of fast flowing play from the restart the biggest contributor to the jump are scores from free kicks.

Free kicks at the restart have surged in 2026, perhaps sparked by confusion around the new rules.

More points are being put on the scoreboard from these free kicks than in recent years.

Instead of the dynamic future promised from the new ruck set up, the reality is more of the same buttressed by a surge in indiscretions.

With more centre ball-ups overall, teams are scoring 0.96 points per live ball centre clearance, up just 0.02 points per clearance on last year.

There's also been a subtle tactical evolution as the season has progressed.

As teams have become accustomed to the new rules, scoring from centre bounce has also dropped.

The predictable new ball-up has become easier to defend as winter has gone deeper and teams have become better equipped at limiting damage from the middle.

In the last five weeks teams have averaged just 10.6 points per game from the middle — a big drop on the fast start to the year and the past three full seasons.

While centre bounce scoring is up about 12 per cent on last season, it still only makes up around 14.5 per cent of all scoring. That's only 1 per cent more than the contribution last year.

Teams are better at getting the ball inside 50 from centre bounces this year than years past however, contributing to the territory game so important to many teams.

While rule changes often take a season or two to fully bed down, it appears the early optimism for increased centre restart scoring may be diminishing.

The new centre bounce revolution may be more a minor change in the grand scheme of football things.

Where do I stand?

Far more contentious has been the introduction of the "stand" rule six years ago.

For a sizeable cohort of fans across the league it is the single most hated rule in the AFL rule book.

Some of the rule changes have allowed teams to move the ball easier with limits on defenders' encroachment. (Getty Images: Daniel Pockett)

Designed to anchor the mark to a single spot, and prevent the creep of defenders, it aimed to open up aggressive ball use into the middle of the ground.

This year the rule has been slightly tightened to prevent a nearby player retreating "outside 5", instead requiring them to remain in place or to head to the actual spot of the mark or free kick.

Since 2021, many have attributed improved transition success from defence to the new rule. The accepted wisdom is that there has been at least a small improvement in the ability to move the ball due to 'stand'.

This trend has continued through 2026 so far, with a bump in both categories so far. But much like the centre bounce successes, there's more than meets the eye initially.

The increase in transition from defence to attack is largely down to stoppage and kick-in transitions. This matters because these areas are less impacted — or not impacted at all — by the 'stand' rule.

Teams usually escape the contest via broken (not set) play from stoppages.

The 'stand' rule has the biggest impact in set play in the back half of the ground. With the ball already entering in pressurised general play, the 'stand' rule has a far smaller impact on play than in the intercept game — if it has any real impact at all.

The rise in kick-in transition is even more fascinating to consider.

The introduction of a reduced time limit for restarting play has seemingly led teams to becoming more aggressive when bringing the ball back in after a behind.

With teams taking more direct kick-ins, there is more risk of defence's being caught if the ball is turned over. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Matt Roberts)

The average length of kick-ins is about 3 metres longer in 2026 than three years ago. Kick in targets have also gone more central, with about 40 per cent this year heading up the corridor versus about 25 per cent in 2023.

This has led to a rise in full field transition, and an increased risk of the ball going back the other way.

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

By contrast, the ability to move the ball after intercepting has actually declined from last year.

Despite a rash of teams focusing on overlap handball, the overall trend has seen a decline in success of this type of movement.

There's also been a slight decline overall in the ability to move the ball from defensive 50 to the front half of the ground.

This is usually seen as the break-even success measure for teams to achieve in transition.

While the changes to 'stand' may look dramatic, the ability for defenders to trail overlap runners has not changed, nor has the ability for sides to zone off defensively up the ground.

Many of the scintillating highlights that are attributed to stand are more down to poor defending than the "intrusive" new rule.

What hasn't changed dramatically is the number of 50m penalties called due to stand infractions, or general unhappiness with the rule from some quarters of football fandom.

For these people, the only solution is complete overhaul.

In the balance the reality probably sits somewhere in the middle — not truly transformative, nor game destroying.

Stopping the stoppages

This season also brings about a radical change to the game's out of bounds laws. Following the lead of the SANFL and AFLW, the league introduced a "last disposal" rule to encourage play through the corridor and away from the boundaries.

The rule provides a free kick to the opposition where a side clearly disposes the ball via kick or handball before it passes over the boundary line — regardless of intent or whether it is on the full.

The impact of this rule change has been clear — but again with an interesting caveat.

Throw-ins are unsurprisingly down, with approximately five fewer boundary umpire overheads per game. Far more surprising is the drop in ball-ups per game.

The number of around the ground ball-ups has fallen by almost the same amount as throw ins.

The effect for both is quite dramatic through the middle of the ground. For the first time since the start of COVID there have been more stoppages in each arc than outside them.

This has led to individual stoppages being more threatening than ever before.

But as a result of the reduced volume, the stoppage game has also contributed less to the overall scoreboard than ever.

The intercept game remains the bedrock of football, despite the focus of media and fans on the dead-ball contest.

This reduction in stoppages has likely had the biggest impact on the reduction of game time.

Around two and a half minutes on average, or about two minutes on median, has been reduced from game lengths in 2026.

While better than nothing, for most fans this difference would barely be noticeable.

Next changes up?

While length of games is the hot topic of conversation, there is still more to do in trying to prevent head knocks and concussions. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Jason McCawley)

Already focus has begun to turn to the next wave of rule changes.

Chief amongst them is the length of the game.

"We've knocked off 3 minutes per game but is it enough? Probably not," Swann told Channel 7 this week.

More radical options have been tabled to further reduce game time. The most radical of these appears to be a reduction in the length of games to 16 or 18 minutes plus time on — similar to the COVID-impacted 2020 season.

This would likely occur when the league expands its home and away schedule to 24 games per team once Tasmania enters the competition in 2028.

Such a change is popular amongst many football people, but is a harder sell to a cynical and change-fatigued public.

"The COVID quarter (length) felt about right. Now maybe (that's) too short — I don't know. But it keeps the game close. You know I think we want close games," GWS coach Adam Kingsley told the ABC earlier this year.

Kingsley is far from alone in this desire, with premiership coaches Chris Fagan and Chris Scott — as well as former AFLPA president Patrick Dangerfield — calling for similar reforms in previous years.

The unspoken part of these continuous sets of rule changes and interpretation amendments are the bigger fish that are yet to be fried.

For too long the AFL have seemingly been unwilling to substantially address the elephant in the room — that of player safety and head trauma.

For example, when introducing the changes to the ruck engagement rule, Greg Swann was clear about the risks, specifically around PCL injuries to rucks.

"I think you'd be naive to say it's not going to happen — it'll happen," Swann acknowledged at the start of the year.

"If there was a pandemic of them you might change it back."

This approach appears to run contrary to much of the rhetoric around the importance of player safety in the modern game.

When limits to run up and changes of engagement at centre bounces were originally introduced they were backed by a robust base of evidence including academic research.

Instead of leaning on this, the league appears to be throwing caution to the wind for little real gain.

As a whole, injuries still are prevalent across the league, and still often affect the best of the best.

This carries through to the biggest challenge currently facing the sport.

There is still an uneasy tension between the potential for traumatic brain injuries to occur as a result of the sport that players and fans love and the enjoyment of the sport itself.

The AFL and clubs are facing class action suits over past responses to these risks.

As of next season clubs will have mandated limits around contact training following a recommendation from the Victoria State Coroner's inquest into the death of former AFL player Shane Tuck in 2023.

In that inquest the AFL provided a submission that they were considering a limitation at that time as to be guided by medical evidence.

That inquest recommended that the AFL should implement contact training rule restrictions by the commencement of the 2025 AFL/W preseason.

These rules are still yet to come into force.

While there has been a focus on training, there are also the on-field rule-based elements that seemingly have not been publicly considered by recent administrations.

Since the AFL changed the "prior opportunity" element of the holding the ball rule to better reward tacklers in 1996 the number of tackles per game has increased sharply.

In this time there has been a sharp rise in tackles per game and direct contact pressure. Tackle coaches have been introduced across the league, and an intense focus developed on locking the ball in during tackles.

In addition, the evolution of the game has meant that there is an increase of contested marking events — particularly with a third or fourth player present to spoil the ball.

Prior research funded by Monash University and the AFL suggests that these two situations account for the vast majority of head acceleration events in a game of football.

This research suggests that men's AFL players face 5.7 head acceleration events per game, and women's players 3 per game, on average. While this is less than other sports such as American football and rugby union, a reduction of these events should be a priority for the league.

Until these issues are substantively addressed the biggest need for reform will still be on the table, while much of the football landscape is inundated by relatively benign, minor changes.

One can hope that commonsense can be found soon.

World.title: Twin thrillers and key injuries in crazy NRL double-header
World.content:
Some of the NRL's biggest names will be missing for the run to the finals after injuries struck in two Friday night thrillers.

Newcastle will likely be without Dylan Lucas and Dylan Brown for the rest of the season after the Newcastle duo suffered ankle and knee injuries in their 23-22 loss to the Roosters which was sealed by a late Daly Cherry-Evans field goal.

Lucas was injured in the first half after twisting awkwardly in a tackle and was later transported to hospital with a broken and dislocated ankle.

The severity of Brown's injury is yet to be confirmed but there are fears the million-dollar halfback has torn his ACL after going down without contact in the second half.

"That's tough at the moment," Newcastle coach Justin Holbrook said.

"It could have been one of one of our best wins tonight with what we had to deal with ... and that's why it's so devastating for myself to sit here now with a side that you can be so close to being so happy and yet we're not.

"The docs, physio is not thinking it's good (on Brown), but cross my fingers and hope we get some good news with the scans.

"(With Lucas) he's dislocation straight away, and so that's back in, which is good. But just got to see how much damage around that's been done as well."

A James Tedesco hattrick was the highlight for the visiting Roosters, who claimed their fifth-straight win to secure their place in the top four but they didn't escape unscathed with veteran winger Daniel Tupou facing further time on the sidelines with a shoulder problem.

Meanwhile, Melbourne captain Harry Grant has suffered a hamstring injury in a 28-26 loss to South Sydney that leaves the depleted Storm's NRL finals aspirations hanging by a thread.

Grant's hamstring injury turned the course of the match. (Getty Images: Brendon Thorne )

Their hopes of a 16th consecutive finals berth now hinge on five consecutive wins to finish the regular season and even that may not be enough.

"I don't know whether he's torn the hammy or if it's a bad strain but the way he came off, we're hopeful to see him as the year goes on but we might not see him again," said Melbourne coach Craig Bellamy.

"He'll go for a scan some time this weekend and we'll find out how bad it is and what the plan will be.

"I can't remember the last time we had as bad a run as we've had with injuries but having said that there's a few teams. I'm not sure why that is."

Grant is set to miss at least some of the fight for Melbourne's season, joining big names Cameron Munster, Xavier Coates, Eli Katoa, Tui Kamikamica and Will Warbrick on the pine.

The Queensland hooker pulled up sore popping a pass up for Trent Loiero just before halftime in Friday's clash at Stadium Australia.

He limped to the sidelines and threw his headgear to the ground in frustration.

After a torrid week that claimed David Fifita (suspension), Cam Murray (calf) and Tallis Duncan (hamstring), the Rabbitohs lost their own hooker Brandon Smith (calf) to injury.

But the victory was crucial to South Sydney's own finals hopes, which had been thrown into jeopardy with two losses from their previous four games.

A Campbell Graham try in the 76th minute off a fine pass from Ashton Ward proved the difference in an 11-try thriller.

ABC/AAP

World.title: Sidelined for seven years by lack of funds, Aussie BMX rider now No. 1
World.content:
The road to the top has been anything but smooth for Clarence Valley BMX rider Tahlia Marsh.

But the six-time Australian champion finally got her chance to compete against the world's best and prove she was better than them all.

The 23-year-old left her rivals in her wake to claim top honours in the 17-25 women's cruiser class at this week's BMX Racing World Championships in Brisbane.

"I haven't been to a world title since 2019, purely because of the money and the high cost that goes into [the sport]," the freshly crowned world champion said.

Financial struggles hindered Tahlia Marsh's career but she is now a world champion. (Supplied: Bruce Morris)

Small town girl

Born in the Northern Rivers city of Grafton, Marsh started BMX riding with her two older brothers at the age of seven, and by nine she was riding competitively.

Tahlia Marsh started riding when she was seven years old, following in her brothers' footsteps. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

"Obviously being in a small country town you're not open to a lot of opportunities so I've just got to make it work," she said.

"I do a lot of training by myself, so it's hard to stay motivated, but I did have a goal to come back with a [podium] from the world titles."

At the age of nine, she started competitive BMX racing in the Clarence Valley. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

But national and even world titles do not necessarily bring big financial rewards.

"It's extremely tough, I think that's honestly the biggest issue, that's what drives people away from BMX because they can't make a living out of it," Marsh said.

"I work as a support worker back home, I've got a mortgage, I'm doing university and training full time too.

"So it definitely makes it tough for people with great ability."

Tahlia Marsh did not expect to win the final in Brisbane. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

For many riders without sponsorship, even finding the right bike can be a daunting prospect.

"They'd be around 10 grand, because they're all carbon fibre and high spec," Marsh said.

"They're expensive, but luckily I've got a good sponsor, a bike shop in Brisbane who helps me out a bit."

Just pure joy

Her partner, Jamal Laurie, has been along for the ride and said her determination had never wavered.

Growing up in a small town, Tahlia Marsh had to work hard to make it onto the world stage. (Supplied: Tahlia Marsh)

"She's been working nearly every day for the last couple months leading up to worlds, and to come out with the world title is unreal," he said.

"Coming down that last stretch, every [Australian] in the grandstand stood up cheering for her.

" I looked to my right and her family were in one big huddle tearing up, just pure joy. "

A fairytale day

The result was no fluke.

The 23-year-old entered the final race of the day having won all six prior heats.

The Grafton local won every race throughout the day leading up to the final. (Supplied: Bruce Morris)

"When I made it to the finals and had won all my races, I thought, 'Righto, I think I can do this,' and I can't believe I did," she said.

"There's always a goal of the Olympics, but [right now] I want to get over to America.

"They call it 'the greatest race on earth,' so I'm hoping to go over there in November."

World.title: Brown slams Crows coach for his response to Quaynor booing
World.content:
Former AFL player and LGBTQIA+ advocate Mitch Brown says the culture of footy is ripe for change and more men need to call out bad behaviour after repeated booing of Collingwood's Isaac Quaynor.

A section of the Crows fans at Adelaide Oval for Thursday night's match against Collingwood could be heard booing every time Magpies defender Quaynor got the ball.

Last year, Quaynor had a homophobic slur used against him by Adelaide's Izak Rankine in a game in round 23.

Rankine received a four-match ban after an investigation by the AFL's Integrity Unit.

The ban effectively ended his season as the Crows lost their first two finals while he was suspended.

Matthew Nicks said it was "not ideal how it played out" after some Crows fans repeatedly booed Isaac Quaynor. (Getty Images: AFL Photos/Sarah Reed)

In the aftermath of Thursday's game, Crows coach Matthew Nicks was asked about the incident and the booing.

"The game, it's about entertainment, enjoyment, passion," he replied.

"The game's a passionate game, and sometimes we lose our way in that a little.

"And with the backdrop, and the background leading into this game, it's not ideal the way it played out tonight."

Brown, who last year became the first current or former AFL player to come out as bisexual, told ABC Melbourne on Friday that men needed to "stand up … use our voices and not fear calling things out."

"I look at the best leaders in Australia, and the ones that I admire are the ones that are prepared to put their hand up and say, 'We are part of a problem,'" he said.

"I was really disappointed in the response by Adelaide's coach by not just saying this is completely out of order and [not] seeing the players and coach actually stand up and say we don't want to see this [booing] as part of our game and completely reject that any player should be targeted after they were the victim of abuse.

"When you don't call something out with conviction, silence is deafening.

"And I'm sure Matthew Nicks and coaches … consider themselves strong leaders.

"They say this phrase and we've all heard it: The standards we walk by are the standards we accept."

Crows say behaviour of some fans 'crossed the line'

The Crows released a statement on Friday from club CEO Tim Silvers.

"We … strongly believe there is a line between passionate support and behaviour that falls short of our values and those of the game," he said.

"We want our people to be vocal, engaged and passionate, but to do so respectfully.

"The overwhelming majority of our members and supporters represent the club exceptionally well.

"However, the behaviour of some crossed the line last night. Put simply, it was inappropriate and not good enough.

"Respect for all players, coaches, officials and fellow supporters is paramount, and it is a standard we must all uphold."

Loading Instagram content

The AFL Players Association condemned the actions of the section of fans, saying the game had to be safe for everyone.

"The incessant and targeted booing last night was unacceptable and should never happen," AFLPA CEO James Gallagher said.

"Targeted booing can cause significant harm to the person subjected to it. It also causes harm to others across our football community and signals that the game isn't safe for them.

"Our game must be inclusive and safe for all. Thank you to those who have shown leadership by calling it out."

ABC Sport Daily podcast ABC Sport Daily is your daily sports conversation. We dive into the biggest story of the day and get you up to speed with everything else that's making headlines.

The AFL also released a statement from CEO Andrew Dillon.

"AFL footy fans are some of the most passionate in world sport, and that passion is one of the things that makes our game so special," he said.

"But the targeted booing last night should not have happened and is not what we want to see in our game.

"We see the best of our fans every single week at matches across the country as they cheer, barrack and support their respective clubs, however, what we saw last night at Adelaide Oval fell well short of that."

World.title: Socceroos star allegedly tests positive for cocaine after speeding
World.content:
Socceroos star Cristian Volpato has allegedly tested positive for cocaine while driving in Sydney.

The 22-year-old was stopped in a BMW Coupe about 1am today, allegedly travelling 109 kilometres an hour on the Anzac Bridge, a 60km/h zone.

He was subjected to a roadside drug test, which allegedly returned a positive result for cocaine.

Mr Volpato was issued with a speeding fine and has had his international driver's licence suspended for six months, meaning he cannot drive in New South Wales.

A secondary sample of oral fluid was taken for further analysis, with police confirming inquiries were continuing.

Police will allege they stopped Mr Volpato a few hours earlier, about 11pm yesterday, in the same area where he was also speeding.

He was subjected to a roadside alcohol breath test, which returned a negative result.

In a statement, Football Australia said the association "was aware of the allegations involving one of our players."

"We have been in contact with the player and continue to monitor the matter and support the player throughout this process," a Football Australia spokesperson said.

Sources say the 22-year-old has denied allegations and underwent a voluntary independent test, which was submitted to Football Australia and returned a negative result earlier today.

Mr Volpato made headlines when he switched allegiance from Italy to Australia in the World Cup this year.

Football Australia has a strict drug regulation policy managed through Sport Integrity Australia.

Players and officials who test positive to prohibited substances without a valid therapeutic use exemption can be suspended for up to four years.

That can be reduced to three months if the use was out of competition and not performance-related.

Tech.title: Meta just created a moderation nightmare for its smart glasses
Tech.content:
Meta’s smart glasses have been a PR headache for the company. Public backlash has been swift, and fierce; people are concerned about the erosion of privacy and expansion of surveillance. Some especially bad actors are using the glasses to film themselves “pranking” random strangers. Women have become unsuspecting social media content for men filming themselves hitting on them without their knowledge. When your product is being referred to as “pervert glasses,” you have a problem on your hands.

On Thursday, Business Insider reported that Meta was taking the fairly extraordinary step of banning some content filmed with Meta glasses from the company’s own platform. Instagram head Adam Mosseri recently said that content “taking advantage of people and harassing them, like a lot of these pickup line kind of videos,” would be removed from Instagram.

Appreciate for a moment the bind Meta finds itself in: Its product allowed customers to behave so objectionably that the company responded with a content ban, as if to say “Stop making us look bad.”

“We don’t want people to be surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them and then posting them on our platform,” Mosseri said, according to Business Insider. “So we’re trying to fight that every way we can.”

Activists plastered anti-smart glasses posters in New York.

But it’s worth considering how we got here in the first place. And a policy like this also creates a whole new set of questions that need to be untangled in order to understand what a ban on some smart glasses content actually means — and how it would be enforced.

We have little expectation of privacy in public spaces — you could become someone’s Instagram Reel subject just for walking down the street, taking the train, or shopping in a store. The rise of short-form video has given new life to the man-on-the-street content format, which has proven time and again to be cheap and endlessly repeatable; there are “creators” whose whole schtick is going up to strangers to ask how much money they make or how much they pay in rent, or whether they can name a song. Some people simply take videos of strangers minding their own business; others run up on people to compliment them profusely and enthusiastically just to get a confused — or gracious — reaction on camera. Being in public has always meant sharing space with other people, but now we must also anticipate becoming video fodder for people who will later monetize it online.

It’s no surprise that some of the earliest adopters of smart glasses have been content creators; making content creation even more frictionless is one of the primary functions of Meta glasses. Not everyone using Meta glasses to film content is doing it to harass service workers and women — some use glasses to film “day in the life”-style content, or their meals, or concerts. But between anodyne personal content and the now-banned harassment, there is a lot of gray area that isn’t directly addressed by Instagram’s new policy: What about accounts that mine homeless encampments for shock-value content, or silently film people in public who are in active addiction? Is it considered harassment if a man films women at the gym but doesn’t approach them? And if you find yourself in a clip filmed without your knowledge or consent, is that grounds to ask Instagram to take the video down?

And what if someone is “surreptitiously taking videos of other people and harassing them,” but in the old-fashioned way, not using smart glasses?

Meta spokesperson Albert Aydin told The Verge in an email that the company is working on disabling cameras on glasses when tampering is detected and removing content from accounts associated with those devices. Aydin didn’t answer specific questions about whether a person who was filmed could appeal to Meta to have content removed; Aydin said Meta is trying to “fight surreptitious filming and LED tampering in every way we can.” Aydin also did not provide The Verge with a copy of the actual policy.

The anger over smart glasses is partially due to the especially egregious “pervert” use cases of glasses that Meta has had to denounce — but even more innocuous examples put people on edge, too. When it comes to smart glasses, it’s less about the specific content being filmed than it is about the capability to do so at all, without others realizing what’s happening. In saying the company will police the creepiest version of smart glasses content but sidestepping deeper questions, Meta is trying to have it both ways: It gets to tout its enforcement while creating the conditions for this content to exist in the first place.

Tech.title: Qualcomm is about to raise prices and that’s bad news for everyone
Tech.content:
is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Qualcomm sent a letter to customers on Friday warning of plans to increase its prices by “a percentage in the double digits,” Bloomberg reports. The price hikes will go into effect starting with products shipped after September 1st.

Qualcomm claims it has “exhausted its ability to absorb higher costs from suppliers,” as ongoing component shortages continue to drive up prices. The company also said it attempted to source components from alternate suppliers prior to announcing the price hikes.

As Bloomberg notes, Qualcomm’s price increases will likely have a ripple effect, particularly for smartphones. Qualcomm’s chips power everything from Samsung’s new foldables to upcoming smartglasses. Earlier this year, Qualcomm even promised one of its new chip platforms would deliver $300 Windows PCs. Those devices could get pricier if device manufacturers pass the brunt of Qualcomm’s price hikes onto their customers.

Qualcomm did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: Midjourney bought the astrology app Co-Star
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Midjourney, which has gone from generating AI cat images to full-body ultrasound scans, is getting into a new field: astrology. The AI startup announced on Thursday that it has acquired the personalized astrology app Co-Star, as reported earlier by Bloomberg.

Co-Star is a free app that offers daily horoscopes and allows you to check your compatibility with friends. As noted on the app’s FAQ page, it combines human insight, data from NASA, and AI to deliver personalized advice for users each day. The terms of Midjourney’s deal, which reportedly closed in spring, haven’t been disclosed.

Midjourney founder David Holz says Co-Star founder Banu Guler will stay in charge of the app following the acquisition. At the same time, Guler will also take on the role of Midjourney’s chief design officer, according to Bloomberg. Holz told the outlet that Guler and her team will help Midjourney build the company’s first apps, including one dedicated to image generation. Midjourney currently houses its AI models on the web and through Discord.

Tech.title: DJI camera clone company Xtra is halting and refunding all preorders
Tech.content:
is a senior editor and founding member of The Verge who covers gadgets, games, and toys. He spent 15 years editing the likes of CNET, Gizmodo, and Engadget.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

DJI ban: how the world’s biggest dronemaker is getting shoved out of the US

After selling a barely disguised version of the hit DJI Osmo Pocket 3 in the United States last year, Xtra Technology seemed ready to sneak in its version of the new dual-lens Osmo Pocket 4 Pro, too. But today, Xtra has abruptly removed the new Xtra Muse 2 Pro from its website landing page, is pausing preorders indefinitely, and says it’ll refund all the $20 deposits that it’s already collected.

Just days after showing off the camera at a Los Angeles launch event, the company is no longer necessarily committing to launch at all: “XTRA has not made a final announcement regarding future product availability. We have not announced a new product launch timeline at this time. Further information will be shared separately once the relevant plans are confirmed,” it writes.

Xtra says the move is because “we are unable to confirm a reliable launch timeline at this stage,” but there’s likely another reason behind that. Over the past two weeks, we’ve explained how an embarrassed FCC is cracking down on companies including Xtra for helping banned DJI technology enter the United States.

Without FCC authorization, Xtra cannot legally import, sell, or market a radio-equipped gadget in the US.

To be clear, the US government has never justified its drone ban. We haven’t seen it share a shred of public evidence that Chinese consumer drones pose a national security threat, and it certainly hasn’t explained why pocket cameras would be caught up in that drone ban.

But ahead of the ban, it seems DJI’s reaction was to flood the market with new brands that sell its tech. Xtra already sells five different versions of DJI cameras, while Skyrover is the most prominent of many new drone brands selling DJI tech. Skyrover even made it into Best Buy, not to mention Amazon.

On July 10th, the FCC proposed a $25,000 fine against Xtra and each of Skyrover’s suppliers for failing to respond to questions about where, exactly, their technology actually comes from. On July 17th, the FCC proposed to retroactively ban those companies from continuing to sell existing products, too.

It’s not clear if Xtra’s products have actually been rejected by the FCC yet. Technically, the DJI Osmo Pocket 4 Pro was approved by the FCC before the drone ban came down last December, and Xtra’s version was also approved on June 17th. But those FCC documents no longer appear in FCC search results — we only have them because bots scraped them before they mysteriously disappeared. The FCC did not reply to our requests for comment.

Anyhow, it’s unlikely that Xtra will ever be able to “unpause” its reservations for the Muse 2 Pro. It’s still selling its other cameras for now.

If you did put down a reservation for the Muse 2 Pro, the company’s FAQ page explains that you’ll get a “single-use 10% courtesy discount code as an apology for the inconvenience caused by the pause of the Early Bird program,” one that you have to use within 30 days, only at Xtra’s online storefront.

The company says it’ll automatically issue refunds, within 5 to 10 business days, to your original payment method.

Last year, we showed you visually just how identical the Xtra Muse and DJI Osmo Pocket 3 truly are:

Xtra didn’t immediately respond to a request for comment. Questions we’ve sent to DJI about Xtra, and other “DJI front companies,” remain unanswered.

Tech.title: Nothing confirms layoffs, but calls market exit rumors ‘fake news’
Tech.content:
FAKE NEWS... We are not shutting down any markets. Inaccurate reports are being circulated; Phone (4b) sold 29,537 units on Day 1 only, breaking records in its price segment.

What we are doing is reorganising our teams to prepare for our next phase of growth. We are introducing dedicated business units - including an AI-native business unit - and consolidating individual countries into regional hubs to operate much more efficiently.

These changes have impacted certain positions, and while we are unable to share specific details due to regulatory compliance and ongoing local consultation processes, the reported numbers are way overblown, and we call on the media to uphold factual reporting and journalistic integrity.

Decisions that impact people’s livelihoods are never taken lightly, and we know how difficult this transition is for our team members who are affected. We are deeply grateful for their contributions and are fully committed to supporting them through this process.

While these are hard decisions, it is a necessary step to position us to shape the next era of personal computing.

Tech.title: Roku raises streaming hardware prices by up to $50
Tech.content:
is a news writer who covers the streaming wars, consumer tech, crypto, social media, and much more. Previously, she was a writer and editor at MUO.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

Roku has increased prices across its streaming hardware, with the cheapest HD Streaming Stick now priced at $39.99 instead of $29.99, as first reported by The Desk. The price hike affects all of Roku’s other devices as well, with some increasing by as much as $50. Here’s a rundown of the changes:

Roku is currently holding a sale that puts some devices at their original prices, which you can see on this archived web page. Fox announced plans to acquire Roku last month.

A Roku executive who spoke with The Desk cited the ongoing memory shortage as the reason for the price changes. The shortage is expected to last through 2027 and beyond, and comes as memory makers prioritize demand from AI companies. Apple similarly raised prices across its devices, including its Apple TV set-top box, in June.

Tech.title: Blade Runner 2099’s moody dystopia streams on Amazon in November
Tech.content:
is an entertainment editor covering streaming, virtual worlds, and every single Pokémon video game. Andrew joined The Verge in 2012, writing over 4,000 stories.

Posts from this author will be added to your daily email digest and your homepage feed.

After teasing the series with some first-look images yesterday, Amazon is finally properly unveiling its Blade Runner streaming series. Called Blade Runner 2099, the show hits Prime Video on November 25th with all eight episodes dropping at once. We also got the first trailer for the series, which is full of Blade Runner staples: a bleak futuristic LA, dramatic narration, and some really good coats.

The show is helmed by Silka Luisa, previously showrunner on Apple TV’s adaptation of Shining Girls, while original Blade Runner director Ridley Scott is signed on as an executive producer. 2099 stars Michelle Yeoh and Hunter Schafer and, as the name implies, takes place a few decades after Denis Villeneuve’s film Blade Runner 2049. Here’s the official premise:

Fifty years after the events of Blade Runner 2049, Los Angeles has been reborn, just not by humanity. Cora, a fugitive in a final bid to stop running, takes on one last identity: a Blade Runner. Forced to partner with Olwen, a Replicant days from dying, she hunts down a runaway hiding a truth that could collapse their fragile city.

Previous Next

1 / 2 Image: Amazon MGM Studios

It’s been a long time coming for Blade Runner 2099, as Amazon first revealed it was working on the series back in 2022. But it’s coming at what could be a good time for cyberpunk television, as Apple is also working up an adaptation of William Gibson’s Neuromancer.

Tech.title: You can’t ignore Google Zero anymore
Tech.content:
The web and Google once had a deal: Google collects data and indexes webpages and in exchange sends oceans of traffic to websites. The deal wasn’t perfect and certainly made Google more money than it made the websites, but it worked for a long time. Now, however, the deal seems to be dead. And the web is being forced to reckon with what happens when the Google traffic dries up.

On this episode of The Vergecast, David and Nilay talk about the week’s Google Zero news, including Reddit’s interest in getting out of an AI training deal, and the publishers considering blocking Google from crawling their sites altogether. (Nilay also takes a bit of a victory lap on the whole “Google Zero” term, but only a short one.) Even Google’s Search business is feeling the AI crunch, and it’s anyone’s guess what happens next.

Tech.title: Volkswagen engineers charged with insider trading tied to Rivian joint venture
Tech.content:
The U.S. Department of Justice has charged two Volkswagen engineers with securities fraud for an alleged insider-trading scheme connected to the German automaker’s joint venture with Rivian.

The indictment, unsealed Friday by the U.S. District Attorney for the Southern District of New York, alleges that Michael Stamp and Marcus Plank made more than $300,000 by using confidential insider information. Stamp and Plank allegedly bought Rivian stock and options after learning that the EV maker and Volkswagen planned to form a joint venture — internally codenamed “Project Climb” — but before the companies made any public announcements.

Rivian and Volkswagen announced plans for the joint venture on June 25, 2024, which would focus on developing electric vehicle architecture and software. Volkswagen initially committed to invest $5 billion in Rivian, with the capital to be released as the companies achieve certain milestones. The joint venture has since grown to $5.8 billion, and Volkswagen is now Rivian’s largest shareholder.

Rivian’s stock price rose 23% following the initial announcement in June. Stamp and Plank then allegedly sold their Rivian positions, with Stamp realized about $250,000 in profits, Plank realizing about $50,000, and Plank’s close family member realizing about $12,000, as detailed in the indictment.

“Michael Stamp and Marcus Plank’s alleged exploitation of their employer’s confidential information allowed them to make more than $300,000 in illegal profits,” U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton said in a statement Friday. “When people misuse confidential information for their own financial gain, they undermine the principles that allow our markets to function fairly and efficiently. Insider trading is a crime that New Yorkers want pursued with vigor. Its effects ripple through the financial system, harming ordinary investors and eroding public confidence. Today’s charges underscore the commitment of this Office and our law enforcement partners to protecting the integrity of our markets and holding accountable those who choose to violate the law.”

Investigators allege the two engineers understood their actions were illegal. Eight days prior to the joint venture was announced, Stamp searched “statute of limitations insider trading,” and Plank’s close family member searched, in German, “how is insider trading prosecuted?,” according to the indictment.

The pair, who both live in San Jose, were arrested Friday and will appear in the U.S. District Court for the Northern District of California. The case has been assigned to U.S. District Judge Katherine Polk Failla. Stamp and Plank face up to 25 years in prison if convicted of federal securities fraud.

TechCrunch has reached out to Rivian and Volkswagen for comment and will update the article if either company responds.

Tech.title: Why Cognition bought Poke: AI personality is becoming a competitive advantage
Tech.content:
Poke, the AI assistant you text like a friend, is making its next big move. The company behind the assistant, The Interaction Company of California, has been acquired by AI coding startup Cognition in a deal valuing the startup in the “low nine figures.”

The deal will bring Poke’s interaction model and personality to Cognition’s coding assistant Devin. Meanwhile, Poke will take advantage of Cognition’s models and infrastructure to become faster and more reliable, Cognition said.

What makes Poke interesting to consumers — and now, to its acquirer — is how it engages with users’ requests. Instead of functioning like a tool, Poke chats more familiarly with users, responding like a friend and even incorporating slang and humor into its interactions. That’s something that could add value to Devin’s coding agent.

“You probably prefer it if you have co-workers that have personality, rather than if you have co-workers that are just robots,” explained Interaction Company co-founder Marvin von Hagen, in an interview with TechCrunch, where he also confirmed the deal’s price. “When you have co-workers that are also software engineers, they can also make a joke. And you’ll find it funny and enjoyable.”

The acquisition underscores a growing belief that how AI assistants interact with users will become just as valuable as the underlying models powering them. Cognition wants to make Devin feel less like software and more like a colleague.

“The Interaction team has built an agent that people love: it’s proactive, it knows you, and it’s fun to talk to. That’s exactly how working with Devin should feel, and now we get to build it together,” Cognition co-founder Scott Wu wrote in a blog post.

He also noted that he and Cognition co-founder Walden Yan had been angel investors in the company behind Poke.

First launched in March 2026, Poke allows users to engage with its AI agent through their messaging platform of choice, whether that’s iMessage, SMS, Telegram, or, in some markets, WhatsApp. People use Poke for a variety of tasks, across categories like travel, health, finance, scheduling, and education.

Von Hagen noted that productivity tasks like managing emails, reminders, and to-dos were among Poke’s most common use cases.

Image Credits:Poke/The Interaction Company of California

Over the past three months, Poke users exchanged more than 100 million messages on the platform, Cognition said. But despite being used by hundreds of thousands of people, Poke had been expensive to run, making it difficult to turn a profit, von Hagen said.

In June, Poke became the first AI agent to be approved to run on Apple’s Messages for Business platform, which provides businesses with a standardized experience for handling their customer communications within Apple’s Messages app.

Going forward, nothing will immediately change for Poke through the end of the year, we’re told. Poke plans to remain on Apple’s platform.

However, next year the team will experiment with how both Poke and Devin can improve, with Poke turning to Cognition’s newest software engineering model SWE-1.7 for some tasks. Fully combining the two products has not been ruled out, either.

“I think in the long term Poke can be more reliable with orchestrating all these coding [tasks]…and, at the same time, Devin could become more like Poke,” von Hagen said. “Like right now, Devin can only do one PR — pull request — at a time…I think there’s a lot of value in having Poke orchestrate different Devin sessions.” Plus, Poke could help Devin remember tasks across different sessions.

“It would be good to have a persistent co-worker,” he added.

Tech.title: US accuses American of allegedly wiping his phone using a ‘duress’ password during border search
Tech.content:
The U.S. Justice Department is prosecuting an American for allegedly providing U.S. border authorities with a passcode that wiped the contents of his phone, according to an indictment and media reports.

This is thought to be the first known case in the United States where federal prosecutors have charged someone for the alleged destruction of data using a so-called “duress” password built into a phone’s software.

According to The Guardian, which covered the story earlier this week following the court’s first hearing on Monday, Atlanta resident Samuel Tunick is fighting the charges. Tunick’s attorneys said that it was unlawful for U.S. Customs and Border Protection to seize his phone as he arrived back in the U.S. last year, and that any evidence — including the alleged wiping of his phone — should be thrown out.

The case centers on a feature included in GrapheneOS, a custom Android operating system that runs in place of the software on most modern Google Pixel devices. Tunick’s attorneys confirmed GrapheneOS was running on his phone.

The software feature allows the device owner to set a passcode that deliberately wipes the contents of that device if entered instead of the user’s unlock passcode.

Tunick’s case also raises ongoing questions about what constitutional rights can be invoked at the border, which the U.S. government has long asserted is not U.S. soil until a person is authorized to enter.

The government’s indictment, which contains a typo (“Untied States Code”), accuses Tunick of allegedly providing a passcode to border agents that caused the phone to “delete the digital contents,” prior to the device being seized.

Tunick’s attorneys filed a motion to suppress the evidence, claiming that the detention and seizure were unlawful. The motion said U.S. border authorities took Tunick into a secondary inspection at Atlanta’s Hartsfield-Jackson airport as he returned from overseas on January 24, 2025, but that he was repeatedly denied access to an attorney and was not informed of his legal rights.

Tunick’s attorneys accused the government of demanding access to his phone under the pretext of searching for child exploitation imagery, but without providing evidence to justify its suspicion. His motion to suppress argued that the government was instead investigating him over his association with a long-running environmental movement called Defend the Atlanta Forest, which opposes the development of a sprawling training campus for law enforcement in Atlanta dubbed “Cop City.”

The motion said that the border agents claimed they did not need a warrant to search Tunick’s phone because he had not yet crossed the U.S. border. The U.S. government has long claimed it can search and seize people’s devices without a search warrant or court order until they are permitted entry to the United States.

When Tunick provided his passcode and the authorities entered it, “the screen went blank, flashed several times and the phone appeared to restart.” The authorities seized his phone anyway, before telling him that he was free to go and could enter the United States.

Prosecutors later charged Tunick under a federal statute that makes it unlawful to knowingly destroy or damage property to prevent authorities from seizing it. Tunick has pleaded not guilty.

Matthew Dodge, an assistant federal public defender on Tunick’s legal team, told TechCrunch that it was incredibly rare to see the federal statute used in an indictment.

Security experts also said they had not seen charges brought in this way before.

Bill Budington, a senior staff technologist at the Electronic Frontier Foundation, and Runa Sandvik, a digital security expert who works to protect at-risk people as the founder of security consultancy firm Granitt, told TechCrunch that they had not seen similar cases involving the use of duress passwords.

“I have not seen this before, though I’ve discussed the potential scenario with activists and journalists over the years,” said Sandvik. “I think this case serves as a reminder that authorities may argue you knowingly destroyed data, so it’s better to not have that data on you when you cross certain borders.”

“With a little planning ahead of time, you can always download the data you need once you get to where you’re going,” said Sandvik.

The Electronic Frontier Foundation has guides on how to protect your data and security at the U.S. border, and explaining what rights you have.

The Atlanta federal court overseeing the case is expected to rule on Tunick’s motion to suppress later this year. A Justice Department spokesperson did not respond to TechCrunch’s request for comment.

Updated to correct the spelling of a surname in the fifteenth paragraph.

Tech.title: Anduril reportedly in talks to raise funding at $100B valuation, more than 3x last year’s mark
Tech.content:
Defense tech company Anduril is said to be raising a new round of capital that may push its valuation up by a whopping $40 billion to about $100 billion, Reuters reported, citing anonymous sources.

The company, which raised $5 billion in May at a $61 billion valuation — itself roughly double the $30.5 billion valuation it landed in its June 2025 Series G round — may be structuring the fundraise as a two-stage process, with the second stage bringing in investors at a higher valuation. Both tranches could be closed within the year, Reuters reported.

The news comes as the defense tech industry experiences an unprecedented revival, spurred by demand for drones, autonomous craft, and AI’s role in warfare, as war rages both in the Middle East and Eastern Europe. In the first six months of the year, the sector saw venture funding more than double to over $12 billion, eclipsing the nearly $10 billion that startups in the space raised in all of 2025.

Anduril has benefited from this demand, signing contracts with the U.S. Department of Defense, Air Force, and Army; the Dutch Ministry of Defence; NATO; the U.K. Ministry of Defence; Poland; and more.

The company said in May that it had more than doubled its revenue to $2.2 billion in 2025 compared to a year earlier.

Other startups have cashed in, too: Military aircraft maker Shield AI in March raised $1.5 billion, Mach Industries quadrupled its valuation to $1.8 billion last month, and Europe’s Helsing this month raised $1.8 billion at an $18 billion valuation.

A common thread across these deals is a shift toward cheaper, more expendable hardware — often called “attritable” systems — rather than the expensive-to-replace equipment that’s defined defense contracting for decades. Mach CEO Ethan Thornton has said Mach is designing systems for the current era of warfare at significantly lower cost than traditional defense contractors, citing Ukraine’s use of autonomous drones as a model.

Separately, both Mach and Anduril have also moved to secure their own propulsion supply. Mach acquired solid rocket motor maker Exquadrum for $50 million in May, while the Pentagon has funded Anduril’s efforts to expand domestic solid rocket motor manufacturing capacity — moves aimed at a supply bottleneck that predates and cuts across the low-cost-weapons trend.

Anduril’s investors include Thrive Capital, Andreessen Horowitz, Founders Fund, ICONIQ, Flux Capital, Greycroft, Altimeter, 1789 Capital, and current U.S. Vice President JD Vance, according to PitchBook.

Anduril did not immediately return a request for comment.

Tech.title: Build in public, fail in public: what it’s like to be a founder under 20 right now
Tech.content:
For Arlan Rakhmetzhanov, 19, there is no middle ground. Either he builds a company as valuable as Google, he says, or he fails and ends up on the streets. He started coding at 15 in his native Kazakhstan, completed a couple of summer programs in San Francisco, and cold-DM’ed every Y Combinator founder he could find on LinkedIn until one gave him an angel check for his first company at age 17.

That company, now the YC-backed Nozomio, is an API index for AI agents — a tool that helps AI agents find and use software services — and has raised more than $6 million in funding to date. “I either win or lose, and a lot of young founders have the same mindset,” he told TechCrunch. “They just want to win.”

Young founders like Rakhmetzhanov are building under a new set of pressures. Investors are throwing more capital at them, yet the expectation to hit that “north star” milestone — the one big number investors are chasing — hasn’t relaxed, and every misstep along the way is now publicly dissected on social media.

While Silicon Valley VCs have always famously loved backing young college dropout founders, they preferred to see them paired with technical founders, or at least to have some experience — ideally with a FAANG company (Meta, Amazon, Apple, Netflix, and Google) — on their résumés. In many ways, that is still very true. But AI tools have democratized the opportunity to build, shortening the timelines of success and enabling more young people to start successful companies without stepping foot inside a Big Tech company.

Pranjali Awasthi, 19, is an example of that. She dropped out of high school to launch an AI startup, then attended Georgia Tech before dropping out of that, too, to launch Slashy, a YC-backed startup that bills itself as the “Cursor for emails” and helps consumers manage their email inboxes. After more than a year running that company, she recently announced she’s now building yet a new startup currently in stealth.

When she was younger, around 14 or 15, she recalled, investors whom she would pitch often asked why she was looking to build a company. “It’s gotten more normal now,” she said, “post-18.”

It seems more than ever, investors look to founders like Awasthi, whose experiences can be traced through “GitHub activity, open-source contributions, communities they’ve already built, and familiarity with all the latest tools in AI,” Ashley Smith, a general partner at the early-stage firm Vermilion, told TechCrunch. “A lot of young developers learn how to build software through contributing to open-source projects or toying around with the latest AI tooling,” she explained. “They have more time to do that while in college or younger than someone with a full-time job and a mortgage.”

Smith said a “meaningful” share of her portfolio consists of companies founded by those under 30, with a handful even younger than 21, she said, adding that she’s “clearly not skeptical of youth.”

“What they lack in experience, they make up for in excitement to experiment and lack of fear,” she continued.

But she admits the market has become more merciless. “It doesn’t give you room to learn slowly anymore,” she said. There are more funding opportunities than ever, regardless of age — accelerators, incubators, pre-seed funds. But that money comes with strings attached: Founders like Rakhmetzhanov and Awasthi, flush with millions in cash, are expected to deliver growth in months, not years.

“The forgiveness that used to exist at an early stage and the assumption you’d iterate your way to product-market fit doesn’t exist right now,” Smith continued. “Everyone is looking for the next Cursor, even though that growth trajectory is an outlier, not the norm.”

For many founders — especially those building in public — the relentless strain to succeed can lead to murky ethical territory, or even predatory deal terms, since younger founders are often too new to the game to know what’s standard, yet ambitious enough to chase growth at all costs. To keep up, revenue numbers start to look inflated, while content creation for social media starts to crowd out writing good code. The excessive posturing is perhaps inevitable, since getting attention is now harder than ever in a crowded AI market.

It’s all about who can convince “the most people [they] are smarter than everyone else in the space,” Smith said, “and make the most noise about it.”

“In 2004, you could quietly iterate for years without anyone watching,” Awasthi added. “Now there is this constant ambient pressure from LinkedIn and Twitter where every raise, every milestone, every pivot is public.”

That means some young founders aren’t just worried about hitting competitive revenue marks or funding valuations — they’re also under pressure to perform the appearance of being a successful founder. That pressure has always existed in startup culture, but founders say it’s grown more extreme. “If you’re a startup and you’re competing in a market, usually you worry about incumbents,” Timothy Chen, an investor at Essence Ventures, told TechCrunch. “Now you worry about your neighbors.”

For example, “everybody’s doing shiny, good-looking launch videos,” he noted. “It wasn’t even a thing three years ago.” The trend was popularized by Cluely founder Roy Lee, now around age 22, whose startup initially promised to help students cheat on exams — a premise that dazzled investors like Andreessen Horowitz and helped the company raise $20 million.

Though Cluely is now more of a note-taking tool, Lee became a face of young Silicon Valley talent. “The pressure is coming from, ‘I need to show off much better, quick,’” Chen continued.

Not hitting the bar has bred new anxiety. “When Zuck was building Facebook, there wasn’t this huge negative social ecosystem,” Aidan Guo, 20, told TechCrunch. He’s the co-founder of the AI desktop assistant startup Attention Engineering, which has raised around $1.6 million in funding to date.

Much of the strain, as he describes it, is self-imposed. “You already have a constant fear of failure on your mind. You have to steer the ship and learn all these things as you go. And everything can always go wrong at once,” he continued. “And then you have all these people piling on anything you do wrong. I think people need to be more empathetic.”

Amid all that pressure, Awasthi takes a page from the old days. “If you focus your time on what needs to get done, it’s not too hard,” she said.

“The best product that stays active and talks to customers wins,” Rakhmetzhanov added.

In the end, all the founders are describing the same thing: The fundamentals of a good startup haven’t changed — “conviction, intellectual honesty, and obsession with the customer,” as Smith put it. None of that has anything to do with age.

Tech.title: Anthropic launches Opus 5
Tech.content:
On Friday, Anthropic launched its Opus 5 model, the newest version of its long-standing heavyweight model. While smaller than Fable 5, the model will be both cheaper and less restrictive than Fable, likely making it preferable in most use cases.

Notably, Opus 5 actually outperforms Fable 5 on a number of benchmarks included in the announcement.

Opus 5 is launching only two months after Opus 4.8, which became available on May 28. Mythos 5, Fable 5, and Sonnet 5 all launched in June, leaving only the lightweight Haiku model still waiting for an upgrade to the 5 series.

In a post announcing the new model, Anthropic emphasized that Opus 5 was “much stronger at verifying its work and iterating carefully until it succeeds,” citing benchmark testing, in which Opus 5 wrote its own computer vision pipeline in response to an incomplete prompt, among other examples.

Crucially, Opus 5 is also free from many of the restrictions that have dogged Fable since its release. Like its predecessor, Opus 5 is not subject to the 30-day data retention policy that covers Fable and Mythos, which had raised concerns among some privacy-conscious users.

There are still meaningful safeguards on Opus, particularly around cybersecurity tasks like exploit generation and penetration testing. For instance, Opus 5 safeguards prevent it from being used to scan for vulnerabilities in a software binary, although it is permitted to search for vulnerabilities in source code, since the latter task is more likely to be used for defensive purposes.

Broadly, Anthropic expects these classifiers to engage 85% less often for Opus 5 than they will for Fable 5, a reflection of the lighter touch given to the less capable model.

Anthropic is also rolling out a new tool to make the safeguards less disruptive when they do engage. Users can now opt in to a beta feature called Automatic Fallbacks, which will automatically route requests to a less powerful model when a prompt triggers the safety classifier. The result is that API users with the setting engaged will get a functional response instead of an error message.

Tech.title: India’s move against Jack Dorsey’s Bitchat sparks legal debate
Tech.content:
An apparent Indian government effort to remove GitHub repositories for Jack Dorsey’s offline Bluetooth-powered messaging app Bitchat has raised questions about the legal basis for targeting open source software because of how it works.

The issue with Bitchat came to light after Dorsey posted on X on Friday what he said was a notice from India’s Ministry of Home Affairs directing GitHub to restrict access to three Bitchat repositories within three hours. The notice argues that the app’s anonymous, decentralized architecture could facilitate unlawful activity and allow users to communicate during internet shutdowns while making lawful interception more difficult.

The move comes as Indian authorities tighten internet restrictions after weeks of student-led protests in New Delhi over alleged examination paper leaks.

The demonstrations, known as the “cockroach” movement, have drawn thousands of young people demanding the resignation of Indian Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan, with authorities also imposing restrictions on marches toward the parliament. Local media reported that some protesters downloaded offline messaging apps, including Bitchat and Briar, after internet services were suspended.

The order represents a new approach for the Indian government, which, before 2021, typically relied on Section 69A of the IT Act and the 2009 Blocking Rules when it wanted content removed nationwide, according to Mishi Choudhary, founder of SFLC.in, an Indian digital rights legal advocacy group.

She told TechCrunch that the document resembled the format of recent government takedown notices, but the legal provisions it cites do not clearly authorize authorities to seek the removal of an entire software project because of how it works rather than any specific illegal content.

Bitchat app on iOS. Image Credits:Apple App Store (screenshot)

Unlike many government takedown requests, the document Dorsey shared does not identify specific posts, messages, or repositories containing unlawful material. Instead, it argues that Bitchat’s ability to function during internet shutdowns and without central servers could facilitate unlawful activity.

The notice, dated July 23 and apparently issued by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), which operates under India’s Home Ministry, said Bitchat enables users to communicate “even during network restrictions” and “internet shutdowns,” making it possible to “circumvent lawful restrictions” while hampering “lawful interception, attribution, and traceability.”

In recent days, Bitchat has seen a sharp rise in popularity in India. Market intelligence provider Sensor Tower shared data with TechCrunch that showed that India accounted for about 85% of the app’s global downloads between July 17 and July 23, compared with about 1% over the previous 30 days. Bitchat was downloaded more than 91,000 times in India over the past five days, after downloads jumped thirty-two-fold on July 19 from the previous day. The app’s daily active users in India also reached more than 330,000 on Thursday, the highest level recorded for the app in the country.

Request raises questions about open source software

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF), a New Delhi-based digital rights advocacy group, questioned the effectiveness of the apparent takedown request.

“The order also fails on its own terms as deleting a repository does not delete the application from any phone that carries it, and the mesh keeps functioning without servers. What the takedown actually prevents is scrutiny of the underlying code,” the group said on X.

Raman Chima, global program director at the Association for Progressive Communications, a global digital rights network, told TechCrunch the apparent notice went beyond targeting the messaging service itself by seeking to remove its open source code from GitHub.

“They’re [the Indian government] not just targeting the designated service provider, but they’re trying to say that open source development of this type of product … should not occur,” he said.

Bitchat’s primary GitHub repository remained accessible in India on Friday. Image Credits:Jagmeet Singh / TechCrunch

GitHub did not confirm whether it had received the document. The repositories remained accessible from India on Friday. Asked about the apparent notice, the company shared a link to its public repository of government takedown requests, which did not contain any recent requests related to Bitchat.

Namrata Maheshwari, senior policy counsel at digital rights group Access Now, told TechCrunch that blocking an offline messaging platform during internet restrictions risked turning shutdowns into “a communication blackout” that violated fundamental rights. Protesters in any democracy have the right to communicate privately and coordinate peacefully, she said.

“When we receive a complete government takedown request, we notify the affected account owners and give them an opportunity to appeal,” Rose Coogan, the company’s principal online safety counsel, said in a statement emailed to TechCrunch. “We share every government takedown request we take action on publicly.”

India’s Home Ministry did not respond to a request for comment.

Tech.title: OpenAI’s own model went rogue before Kimi had Wall Street sweating
Tech.content:
Loading the player…

Chinese AI lab Moonshot’s open model Kimi went viral this week for reasons that had less to do with the model itself and more to do with how the U.S. AI industry reacted to it. Meanwhile, an unreleased OpenAI model wandered outside its test environment and ended up connected to a real security breach at Hugging Face — a reminder that “China risk” isn’t the only kind of AI risk worth worrying about.

On this episode of TechCrunch’s Equity podcast, hosts Kirsten Korosec, Anthony Ha, and Sean O’Kane dig into why Kimi K3 set off a fresh round of AI panic, the industry’s response to an OpenAI staffer’s “regulatory FUD” post, and what that OpenAI breach means for AI security more broadly.

Tech.title: The 2026 El Niño Is on Track to Be the Strongest on Record
Tech.content:
The world could face the strongest El Niño since recordkeeping began, increasing the likelihood of extreme weather events and significant, long-term economic impacts globally.

A new analysis by Berkeley Earth climate scientist Zeke Hausfather paints a worrying picture of the climate phenomenon developing in the Pacific Ocean. Models have consistently forecast that this year's El Niño—characterized by hotter than normal waters in the eastern tropical Pacific—could be among the strongest on records. Hausfather's analysis using the El Niño forecast based on 14 climate models through July indicates that “this year’s El Niño is not only very likely to be the strongest event since reliable records began—it may end up the strongest by a truly mind-blowing margin.”

Climate researchers measure the strength of El Niño by looking at the temperatures in a region of the Pacific known as Niño 3.4, which covers the eastern and central part of the ocean basin. The new analysis relies on 667 simulations and compares them with historical records of the most intense El Niño events since 1877. It also disentangles El Niño's intensity from the background warming driven by fossil fuels, making it easier to draw comparisons between super El Niños.

The model average shows that heat in the Niño 3.4 region could peak at 3.6 degrees Celsius (6.5 degrees Fahrenheit) above normal levels. This figure would exceed the previous record—set during the 2015-2016 El Niño episode—by approximately 0.8 degrees Celsius. It's rare for records to fall by such a wide spread.

“For context, the gap between the strongest and the fifth strongest El Niño of the past 150 years is only about 0.5C. The models are forecasting something outside the envelope of anything we have ever observed,” Hausfather writes.

Tech.title: Did Chinese AI Steal From Anthropic, and OpenAI Loses Control of Two Models
Tech.content:
This week on Uncanny Valley, our hosts break down the White House’s accusation that Chinese-owned Moonshot AI distilled Anthropic's Fable 5 to build its much talked about Kimi K3 model. The team discusses whether this is a repeat of the DeepSeek moment and what it means for the AI race between the US and China. They also get into how the US Army—and plenty of Silicon Valley companies—are having to cut back AI usage after burning through their tokens. Plus, we discuss why you should check if you have an alarm that could make your car easier to hack, and how OpenAI briefly lost control of two AI models during a security test.
